full_judgment:
Mr. Sharif Uddin Chaklader, J: This rule for condonation of delay of 191 days in tendering the Appeal from Original Decree against judgment and decree dated 29.10.2007, passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 212 of 2006 rejecting the plaint under Order VII Rule II of the Code of Civil Procedure, after framing issue as per provision of the Order XIV Rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

2. The facts disclosed, briefly are that, plaintiff-appellant filed the aforesaid suit for a declaration of title against the defendants that the land measuring 1.54 acres with ponds, homestead, viii, road and passage, described in schedule Ka, belongs to the plaintiff, with further declaration for delivering possession after removing the structure from there.

3. Defendants appeared in the suit and filed two application one, under Order VII Rule II of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of the plaint as it is barred by law and another, under Order XIV Rule 2 of the Code for framing issued to that effect. The learned Judge framed issue as to the maintainability of the suit and after hearing both the sides rejected the plaint on the ground of maintainability. In passing the order, learned Judge found that against the application filed under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, plaintiff did not file any written objection as plaintiff submits as “বাদী/প্রতিপক্ষ আপত্তি দাখিল করেন নাই এবং মৌখিকভাবে জানান যে, তাহাদের আপত্তি দাখিলের আবশ্যকতা নাই।”

4. Learned Judge after hearing both the parties, was of the opinion that, by Dhaka gazette notification dated 29.02.1956 and also in 1965, at serial No. 31, rent receiving interest of Surujbala Bibi and others have been taken over by the Government and also the learned Judge on consideration of C.S. and R.S. Khatian, finally came to the decision that, plaintiff has no title in instituting the suit.

5. Against this judgment and decree, plaintiff filed this appeal before this Court out of time of by 191 days and filed an application for condonation of delay of the aforesaid days. This Court issued rule upon the defendant-respondents to show cause as to why the delay in filing the appeal should not be condoned.

6. Mr. Md. Abdul Haque learned Advocate, appearing for the plaintiff-appellant, submits that, the delay has been explained in the supplementary-affidavit, as such, this Court should condone the delay. Learned Advocate frankly submits that, originally, in the application for condonation of delay, delay of 191 days was not been properly explained. Learned Advocate further submits that, since the plaintiff filed advolerum Court fee of Taka more than forty thousands, the delay should he condoned.

7. Mr. Md. Khalilur Rahman, learned Advocate, appearing for the defendant-opposite parties, submits that, usually he did not raise objection for condonation of delay of 191 days in preferring the appeal but he submits that, no effective result will be available to the plaintiff, save and except dragging this matter for unlimited period and thereby hanging the defendants as plaintiff failed to prove title for instituting the suit and did not file any written objection against the averments made in the application for rejection of the plaint, in Court below, as such the delay should not be condoned. Learned Advocate taken us to the annexures with the counter affidavit filed against the application for condonation of delay, particularly annexure-1, and submits that by gazelle notification published on Monday, March 24, 1952, in exercise of the power conferred by sub-section (I) of section 3 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (East Bengal Act No. XXVIII of 1951), Government notified for the information of all concerned that the Governor is pleased to acquire, with effect from the 14th April 1952, all interests of the rent-receivers named in column I of the schedule, in the estates and taluks and tenures, the particulars whereof are given in column 2 of the schedule, against their names, including all their interests in all sub-soil and rights to mineral in such estates and taluks and tenures and in column, the name of the plaintiff appeared and also in column 2(a), particularly, Mirash Raja Rajendra Narayan Roy, under Sukimi Taluq Krishna Prosad Khojanehi, Mohal No.49 has been acquired by Government with all rent receiving interest from March 24, 1952. Learned Advocate in support of his submission, relied on the decisions, of People's Republic of Bangladesh, represented by the Dy. Commissioner, Sylhet and others vs. Sri Sri Madan Gopal Jew Bigraha, 33 DLR (AD) 13, 53, the case of Anwara Begum Chowdhury vs. Nur Jahan Begum and others, 27 DLR (AD) 109, the case of Samatannessa Bewa vs. Haibatulla Sacker, 41 DLR (AD) 105, the case of Gopal Das Soni and another vs. Government of Bangladesh and ors, 13 BLC (AD) 69, the case of Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, Ministry of Works and other vs. Mr. Alauddin 21 BLD (AD) 35, the case of Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and others vs. Md. Jahangir Ali and others 21 BLD 215, the case of Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and others vs. Md. Jahangir Ali and another 53 DLR (AD) 365.

8. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates of both sides. From the judgment itself it appears that the plaintiff did not file or raised any objection to the application filed by the defendant-respondent-opposite party for rejection of the plaint, on the ground that it is barred by law. Before this Court, from the original application for condonation of delay the plaintiff explained the delay of 191 days in paragraphs 5 and 6, that is:-

"5. That the law officer after receiving the certified copies produced the concerned file to the Manager of the Court of Wards Bhawal Raj Estate who produced proceed the file to the Chairman of the Land Reform Board, Ministry of Land, Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh through the Member, Land Reform Board. The Chairman, Land Reform Board passed his orders to produce the matter before a Committee formed with some learned panel Lawyers headed by member Land management to examine and give opinion regarding filing of the appeal before the Hon'ble High Court Division.

6. That the committee meeting held on 20.02.2008 and the matter was discussed in the meeting and it was decided that the Senior Law Advisor (a retired District Judge) of the Court of Wards Bhawal Raj Estate will peruse the case record, impugned judgment and decree, necessary documents and will to through the related laws and will give his opinion in respect of the Case. Accordingly the file was given to the Senior Law Advisor on 13.04.2008 and the Senior Law Advisor perused the record, impugned judgment and decree and other necessary documents and opined on 23.04.2008 to prefer the appeal before the Hon'ble High Court Division."

9. Having been in difficulty, plaintiff filed supplementary-affidavit where the plaintiff explained the delay as, after the judgment, file was produced by the Manager, Court of Wards Bhawal Raj Estate to the Member; Land Reform Board, Ministry of Land on 22.11.2007. The Member, Land Reform Board after perusing the file, asked the Manager, Court of Wards to take opinion from the Senior Law Advisor (in respect of filing of the appeal) by his order dated 26.11.2007; thereafter, the file was again sent to the Chairman, Land Reform Board, Ministry of Land. The Chairman approved the proposal by his order dated 26.11.2007 and the file was sent to the law Officer on 27.11.2007 and the law officer produced the file to the Senior legal advisor on 27.11.2007 and the Senior legal advisor proposed to submits the matter before the Board Meeting (authority) for decision; the Senior legal advisor sent the file to the law officer on 10.12.2007. The law officer consulted about the matter with the authority and produced the file on 26.12.2007 to the Manager who produced the file on the same day to the Member, Land Reform Board, Ministry of Land, who passed his order dated 27.12.2007 to take step. Thereafter, it was proposed to produce the matter before the Land Reform Board and the proposal was approved by the Chairman, Land Reform Board, on 02.01.2008, on 07.01.2008. the law officer produced the file to the Manager, Bhawal Raj Estate, for fixing a date of holding meeting and the date was fixed on 15.01 .2008. But, unfortunately, the manager had to take leave from Office for his personal difficulties and the concern lawyer of the Bhawal Raj Estate could not appear in the meeting. On 21.01.2008, the file was produced by the law officer for fixing a date of meeting and the Chairman, Land Reform Board fixed the date of holding the meeting on 29.01.2008. Thereafter, the Member, Land Reform Board, decided to hold meeting with the learned Advocate of the Land Reform Board for taking a decision in respect of dismissal of the Title Suit No.2(2 of 2006 and thereby, the day was fixed on 20.02.2008. Then it has been written that the authority with a view to file appeal, referred the matter to Mr. Md. Faijul Kabir, learned Advocate, who opined on 06.03.2008 that appeal cannot be file against the order of rejection of the plaint of the Title Suit No.212 of 2006, on 29.10.2007. But as per decision of the authority dated 20.02.2008, appellant took step for filing appeal and accordingly, Law Officer proposed on 12.03.2008 to appoint Ms. Ferdous Akhter Wahida, learned Advocate for filing the appeal. The authority approved the proposal on 23.03.2008. Then the learned Advocate, Ms. Ferdous Akhter Wahida, orally refused to receive the brief, as such, the file was produced before the Manager, Court of Wards, on 01.04.2008 for appointing a new Advocate. Manager consulted with the Member and Chairman, Land Reform Board and they referred the matter to the Senior Legal Advisor on 02.04.2008. The Senior Legal Advisor opined on 03.04.2008 to file the appeal and to take opinion from the newly appointed senior legal advisor and the law officer proposed on 06.04.2008 to appoint Mr. Md. Abdul Haque, Advocate for filing the appeal and proposal was made to the authority to sent the file to the senior legal advisor for opinion. The proposal was approved on 10.04.2008 and the file was sent to the senior legal advisor on 13.04.2008. Senior legal advisor after perusing the record, impugned judgment and decree and other necessary documents, opined on 23.04.2008 to prefer the appeal before the Hon' ble High Court Division.

<u>10. The facts disclosed in the supplementary affidavit are the inherited bureaucratic methodology smeared with note-making, file pushing and passing of the back ethoes, delay on part of the appellant is less difficult to understand but more difficult to approve. The entire statements of the application for condonation of delay with supplementary affidavit reflect the appellant callousness, negligence, slothful manner and indolent attitude.</u>

<u>11. It appears that appeal was tendered before this Court on 27.08.2008 without Second judge's copy, which was filed on 27.08.2008. From the aforesaid narration of fact for explaining the delay in supplementary-affidavit, we do not find that, even if we consider the entire explanation given in the supplementary-affidavit as true and genuine, then also we do not find any explanation for the period from 23.04.2008 up to 27.08.2008, that is, about 4 months. This delay of 4 months has neither been sought for not explained. It appears from the aforesaid facts that condonation of delay has been sought for in piecemeal basis. Application was filed on 27.08.2008 and supplementary affidavit was filed on 01.12.2008 which shows how much negligent and careless the petitioner was in the matter of prosecuting the appeal. In the case of Bangladesh vs. Abdul Wahab and others reported in 45 DLR 30 where it has been held that "petitioner having knowledge of limitation and without sufficient cause slept over the matter and allowed the period of limitation to run out and as such the delay cannot be condoned."</u>

12. In the Case of Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh vs. Mr. Alauddin, 21 BLD (AD) 35, it is observed. "It is really surprising to know that more than one year and nine months was consumed to start a part file and to file the leave petition. This is gross negligence of the part of the Solicitor wing which should not be condoned."

13. In the Case of Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and others vs. Md. Jahangir Ali and others, 21 DLR 315, it is held that negligence of an agent or servant of the Government is not sufficient cause to condone the delay.

14. In the Case of People's Republic of Bangladesh vs. Sri Sri Madan Gopal Jew Bigraha, 53 DLR (AD) 13, it has been held, while seeking condonation the Government officials concerned are to explain the delay for each day. In the application the condonation, a general explanation has been given without proper explanation for delay of each day.

15. In the Case of Province of East Pakistan vs. Abdul Hamid Dargee, 21 DLR 824, Bangladesh vs. Suppliers and Building Corporation, 1991 BLD 194, Subash Chandra Chowdhury and another vs. Govt. of Bangladesh, 46 DLR 663 and many other decisions of this sub-continent it has been held that as litigant, the Government stands on the same footing with ordinary litigants. As such delay of each day when not satisfactory explained no one could get any premium whether he is a private individual, corporate body or government.

16. A question may arise that delay being of 191 days appellant paid court fee of more than Tk. 40,000/- and appeal is a matter of right, why the delay should not be condoned? Mr. Khalilur Rahman raises the question that after whole sale acquisition of rent receiving interest of the Zamindars by the Government, appellant lost his locus stands to initiate any case.

17. In the Case of Gopal Das Soni and another vs. Government of Bangladesh, 13 BLC (AD) 69, it has been held, it is seen from the judgment of the High Court Division that the land in suit being the land within periphery of Khulna Hat and Bazar, compensation roll has been prepared and finally published in the gazette and that being the undisputed fact relief sought in the it suit was not available to the plaintiffs so long compensation roll is not revised and the land is being shown as retainable class of land. It is also seen froth the judgment of the High Court Division that compensation roll in respect of the land in suit was prepared as back as in 1962 upon assessing considerable amount of money and thereupon compensation roll has been published in the gazette. It is further seen from the judgment of the High Court Division that a sketch map has been prepared some time in 1975 by the Government in respect of the land in suit and the same has been shown within the periphery of the Khulna Hat and Bazar. The High Court Division, on consideration of the materials on record, particularly the fact of preparation of compensation assessment roll and publication thereof in the gazette as well as the sketch map prepared in 1975 showing the land in suit within the periphery of Khulna Hat and Bazar set aside the judgment and decree of the courts below. The learned Counsel has submitted that compensation assessment roll in respect of the land of the plaintiffs and publication thereof was illegal and that publication of the said illegal assessment roll can no way take away the title of the plaintiffs in the land which is of retainable class of land and that also not within the periphery of Khulna Hat and Bazar. He has also submitted that the sketch map said to have been prepared in 1975 showing land within periphery of Khulna Hat and Bazar is an unauthorized and illegal act of the respondents and, on the basis thereof plaintiffs cannot be deprived of their tenanted land which they are legally entitled to retain. The submission of the learned Counsel as of no merit since preparation of the compensation assessment roll and the publication thereof has the legal presumption that the land claimed by the plaintiffs is of non-retainable class of land and that as on the publication of the compensation assessment roll in the gazette, the land has vested in the Government the plaintiffs are not entitled to raise any claim in the land and as such, relief sought in the suit was not available to them. Moreover as back as in 1975 the Government prepared the sketch map showing the land in suit within the periphery of Khulna Hat and Bazar and that as it appears the said sketch map has been prepared in the background of the publication of the compensation assessment roll in the gazette the same carries legal weight in arriving at the decision as to the class of land in suit. As in the background of the materials on record the High Court Division has arrived at the finding the Courts below were in error in decreeing the suit, in our view, the finding so arrived at by the High Court Division is in accordance with law and suffers from no infirmity and illegality.

18. In the Promod Ranjan Shaha vs. Govt. of Bangladesh, 33 DLR 53, it has been held; there are can be no denying the fact that the plaintiffs sought to challenge the acquisition of their hat and Bazars made under the general notification dated 02.04.56 issued under section 3(1) of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, and so it is directly hit by Presidents Order No.90 of 1972, which gives a clear mandate of law that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, on the commencement of the Order, all suits, appeals, applications and of the legal proceedings pending or continuing or deemed to be pending or continuing in any court against the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh in which the legality of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (E. B. Act No. XXVIII of 1951), or of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance 1956 (E. B. Ordinance No. III of 1956) or of any other law making any amendment in the said Act or of the acquisition of any property made under any provision thereof is challenged or called in question shall abate, and all orders, including orders of injunction and other interlocutory orders passed in suits, appeals, applications and other legal proceeding shall cease to have any effect: and no Courts shall entertain and no person shall bring any fresh suit, appeal, application or other legal proceedings in which the legality or validity of any such law or requisition is challenged or called in question.

19. In the Case Anwara Begum Chowdhury vs. Nur Jahan Begum, 27 DLR (AD) 109, it has been held; it appears that mention of the different classes of tenants or occupants has been made in the above quoted provisions of law. It was argued that sub-section 1 of section 24 of the Act clearly indicates that no under-raiyati holding would remain in existence at the time of the preparation of the record-of-rights which would be subsequent to the Notification under section 3 of the Act. Rule 18 provides for the preparation or revision of the record-of-rights on the basis of which the compensation Assessment-roll would be prepared and published and rule 61 says that the different classes of tenancies would cease to exist with publication of the Notification under section 3 of the Act and that entire chain of interests of rent-receivers would be eliminated only after the publication of the Compensation Assessment-roll. Thereafter a Notification would be published under sub-section (2) of section 43 declaring that the compensation assessment-roll in respect of that area had been finally published and after this publication of Notification, the whole of Part V of the Act would come into operation. The sum and substance of the contention of the learned Counsel is that raiyati interest did not cease to exist and that under raiyat was not upgraded before Part V came into operation. With a view to strengthen his argument the learned Counsel relied on a decision in Afran Ali Sheikh's case reported in 14 D.L.R. (Dacca) 791. It is a Single Bench decision by Idris, J. of the Dacca High Court. The said case was under section 26F of the B.T. Act. In that case the question arose as to whether there was an automatic elevation of under-raiyats to the status with effect from 14.04.56 when all rent-receiving interests vested in the Government. The learned Judge held that publication of Notification under section 3 of the Act did not eliminate the different classes of tenancies till publication of the compensation assessment-roll, i.e., till Part V of the Act came into operation. In coming to that decision Idris, J. it appears, relied on an unreported decision by Asir, J., in Civil Revision Nos.1129 and 1130 of 1960 of the Dacca High Court. On the authority of the decision of Idris, J. and the provision of law referred to above, the learned Counsel submitted that pre-emption was not available in the present case to an under-raiyati even if he had occupancy right.

<u>20. From the aforesaid discussion it appears that plaintiff has no subsisting interest in instituting the suit. The impugned Gazette notification was published under Section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act with reference to particular estates, taluks, tenures, holding and tenancies and in respect of all rent receivers whose properties were under the management of court of wards Act, 1878. Sub-Section (2a) was enacted and introduced Section 3 of the Act by Ordinance No. 111 of 1956. It is after this amendment general notification dated 2nd April, 1956 was issued district wise in regard to all rent receiving interest which thereafter vested in the government with effect from 14.04.56 in terms of those notifications. As such, after 14.04.56 the plaintiff has no right take interest or possession in itself, whatever it has under the Government, not of it in any individual from to initiate any proceeding. A title less person has no legal character to initiate any proceeding as such no effective result would be available to the appellant in appeal be admitted on condonation of delay.</u>

21. In the decision of Santannessa vs. Hapitullah Sarker, 41 DLR (AD) 105 it has been held that when no useful purpose will be served in allowing the restoration of appeal and the plaintiff will be driven to fruitless litigation instead of being benefited in any manner if restoration is allowed impugned order does not call for any interference. We have already seen that plaint was rejected, as per provision of Order VII rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, as it is barred by law and by framing of issue as per Order XIV rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Plaintiff as it appears from all the documents produced before as and produced before trial court, that he has no title it's title has been eaten up by the Government as per gazette notification of Monday, 24th March, 1952 published under provision of section 3(1) of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (East Bengal Act No. XXVIII of 1951), as such if the appeal be registered on condonation of delay, the plaintiff instead of being benefited in any manner will be driven to a fruitless litigation as it appears that the defendants after getting the land from the land owners and also from Government, is possessing the same for 50 years.

22. We find no reason to condone the delay.

23. In the result, the rule is discharged without any orders as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Mr. Goutam Kumar Roy, D.A.G. with Mr. Arobinda Kumar Roy, A.A.G ------ For the petitioner.
Mr. Md. Mahbub Ali, Advocate ------ For the opposite party Nos. 1-5.
parties:
Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Sylhet ------ Defendant No.1-appellant-petitioner.
Versus
Syed Rashid Ahmed Ehsan @ Syed Abdur Rashid and others ------ Plaintiff-respondent-opposite parties.
full_judgment:
Mr. Sheikh Abdul Awal, J.:- This Rule-was-issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1-5 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree of affirmance dated 3.02.2003 passed by the teamed Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Sylhet in Title Appeal No.332 of 2001 should not be set-aside. 

2. Material facts of the case as necessary for disposal of the Rule are that the opposite —1 party Nos.1-5 as plaintiffs filed a suit being Title Suit No.136 of 1998 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Sylhet for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession and also for declaration that the judgment and decree dated 15.6.1998 passed in Title Suit No.7 of 1995 by the same Court was collusive and not binding upon the plaintiffs on the averments that the suit land along with other lands were originally belonged to Sudhir Chandra Dutta and Subid Chandra Dutta, the Proforma-defendant Nos. 4-5 who while possessing in equal share comprising 0.3603 acre out of .7206 acres of land in plot No.5137 transferred their share to Most. Jahurunnessa Khanam (proforma defendant No.3) by registered kabala No.15310 dated 15.11.1989 corresponding to 1st Agrahayan, 1396 B.S. at a consideration of Tk. 85.000/00, subsequently who in necessity of money transferred the said land in favotir of the plaintiffs through his 'attorney, Ishtiaque Khaled by a registered deed dated 5.10.97 and defendant No.2, Monjur Ahmed transferred his share to plaintiff No.5, Md. Abdul Wadud by executing a registered-deed dated 7.9.98 and accordingly, the plaintiff Nos. 1-5 became exclusive owner of the suit land; that entire land of the suit plot including the structure thereon was requisitioned by the then Government on 26.9.47 from the ,defendant Nos. 4-7, the original owner of the land including the suit land for the purpose of residence and office of the Government officials and employees; that out of .7206 acre of suit plot, the then Zaminder Khan Bahadur Dewan Eklimur Raja of Sylhet town purchased .1801 acre of suit plot and one Muzibur Rahman purchased .1801 acre of suit plot; that the defendant Nos. 4-5 while possessing .3606 acre out of which in southern portion .1650 acre was acquired by the defendant No.1, Deputy Conimissioner, Sylhet in L.A. Case No.14/69-70 for Agricultural Development Bank and rest .1927' acres remained under possession of the plaintiffs by purchase; that the suit land situated within the Zindabazar Commercial Area of Sylhet town and the structure, houses standing thereon were old of 50/60 years approximately; that the building was not useable as dwelling house and for construction of multistoried commercial building and market the plaintiffs purchased the land; that the plaintiffs by purchase acquired title over total 0.1927 acre; that the plaintiffs applied for de-requisition of their purchased land and to pay all arrear of rent enclosing all the relevant documents relating. to their ownership of the suit land but after long lapse of time the land acquisition officer in the middle part of May, 1998 all on a sudden disclosed that the plaintiffs have no right ownership in the suit land and as such question of de-requisition does not arise at all which cast a cloud over the title of the plaintiffs; that the defendant 'No.9, Md. Nazrul Islam has no right, title and possession over the suit land, who beyond the knowledge of the plaintiffs filed Title Suit No.7 of 1995 and on 22.6.98 obtained a collusive decree by practicing fraud upon the Court which is not binding upon the plaintiffs, hence the suit. 
3. The defendant No.1 contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material allegations of the plaint contending, inter-alia, that the entire area of suit plot comprising 0.7206 acre of land originally belonged to defendant Nos. 4-7; that the said land was requisitioned by the then Government vide R.S. Case. No. 1 B/47-48 and allotted as residence of the then District Controller of Civil Supply, Sylhet and subsequently, allotted to different Government officials; that on 7.5.48 Khan Bahadur Dewan Eklimur Raja purchased 1/4th  share of Subinoy Dutta and received the rent of requisitioned house from 8.5.48; that on 27.6.61 one Mujibur Rahman claimed '/4th share of Snail Dutta and the Government defendant on examining his document paid rent to him for his 1/4th share; that said Mujibur Rahman transferred his share on 21.02.63 in favour of Bedora Begum alias Afsara Begum and others, who accepted the rent since 21.02.63 in respect of 0.1801 acre; that said Khan Bahadur Eklimur Raja 'applied for release of his property and the then Government of East Pakistan allowed his prayer and released 0.1801 acre of land; that 0.3352 acre of land was acquired for Agricultural Development Bank vide L.A. Case No.14/69-70 and as such the suit land remained as1 requisitioned land wherein the Government officials have been living ; that the plaintiffs claimed their title over the suit land on the basis of collusive deeds and as such the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

3A. At the trial the plaintiffs examined in all 5 (five) witnesses namely, PW-1, PW-2, PW-3, PW-4 and PW-5 and exhibited a series of document in support of their right, title in the suit land while the only contesting defendant No.1 examined one witness namely DW-1. 

4. The trial Court after closing of the evidence and hearing argument of the parties by his judgment and decree dated 8.11.2001 decreed the suit holding that the plaintiffs have been succeeded to prove their right and title in the suit land on the basis of their registered kabala deed. 

5. Against the said judgment and decree dated 8.11.2001 defendant No.1 as appellant preferred Title Appeal No.332 of 2001 in the Court of District Judge, Sylhet. The said appeal was subsequently transmitted to the Court of Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Sylhet for disposal. During the pendency of the appeal the defendant-appellant submitted additional written statement and adduced 1 witness namely DW-2 and also exhibited documents namely, Ext. "Ka- and "Kha" to fortify his case. The learned Additional District Judge, Sylhet upon hearing of the appeal and on considering the materials on record by the impugned judgment and decree dated 3.02.2003 dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial Court with a direction to deliver possession of the suit land to the plaintiff-respondents within 120 days from date. 

6. Being aggrieved and dissatisfied with the aforesaid judgment and decree of two Courts  below the present defendant-appellant-petitioner has come before this Court and obtained the present Rule.  

7. Mr. Goutam Kumar Roy, the learned Deputy Attorney General appearing for the petitioner submits that the Court of appeal below acted illegally in dismissing the suit and affirming the judgment of the trial Court below without considering the additional evidence as adduced before it. He next A relying on the decisions reported in 6 BLD (AD) 342 and 24 BLD(AD) 56 submits that admittedly the property in question was requisitioned by the then Pakistan Government and the plaintiff after failing to get back the suit property by way of de-requisition filed the instant suit for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession and in view of the bar imposed by the provisions of section 14A of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 the suit was not maintainable. 

8. On the other hand, Mr. Md. Mahbub Ali, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-opposite party Nos. 1-5 upon referring the prayer portion of the plaint submits that the argument of the teamed Deputy Attorney General in the facts and circumstances of the case with regard to maintainability of the suit is plainly misconceived inasmuch as in this case the plaintiffs having not challenged the so-called requisition order of the then Pakistan Government. He adds that in the cited decisions namely the decisions reported in 6 BLD(AD) 342 and 24 BLD(AD) 56 the order of requisition of the suit property under section 3 of the (Emergency) Requisition Property Act, 1948 was challenged but in the present case it is apparent from the prayer portion of the plaint that the suit was filed for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession and as such the principles laid down in those cited cases are not applicable in the present case. 
9. To appreciate the submissions of Mr. Goutam Kumar Roy, the learned Deputy Attorney General and Mr. Md. Mahbub Ali, the learned Advocate for the opposite party Nos. 1-5, we have studied those decisions along with the contents of the plaint to the best of our ability. It appears that plaintiffs in their plaint did not challenge the order of claimed by the plaintiffs that there is a requisition. 

10. In the case of Nur Mohammed & others Vs. Moulvi Mainuddin Ahmed and others reported in 6 BLD(AD) 342, it has been observed as follows: 

"Appellants who are plaintiffs filed O.S. No.19 of 1977 in the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong misleading respondent No.1 as defendant No.1 along with other defendants for a decree for establishment of title and confirmation possession with a prayer for permanent injunction and alternately  for khas possession on setting-aside an  order of requisition of the suit property  under section 3 of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948. Plaintiffs also filed an application under Order 39 Rules 1 and 2 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for temporary injunction restraining defendants from dispossessing them till the disposal of the suit." 
(the under linings are mine) 

11. In the case of Director of Housing and Settlement, Segunbagicha, Ramna, Dhaka 
Vs. Abdul Majid Howlader and others reported in 24 BLD(AD) 56, it has been observed as follows: 

"The suit was filed alleging, inter-alia, that the property in suit was acquired in L.A. Case No.159/61-62 and the acquisition was finally notified in the gazette on October 22, 1970. It was contended by the plaintiffs that although Government acquired the land but possession thereof was not taken over by the Government and the plaintiffs are in possession of the land. It was also claimed by the plaintiffs that there is a Mosque and a Madrassa in the land in suit. It is the contention of the plaintiffs that they are in enjoyment of the property in suit and they prayed for release of the property but their prayer was rejected and thereunder the Government threatened to dispossess them and as such they are constrained to file the suit. " (the under linings are mine) 
From the above, it appears that in those cases the plaintiffs challenged the order of acquisition and requisition and we have already indicated that in the present case the plaintiffs having not challenged the order of requisition. 

12. In the case of Alizan Vs. Bangladesh reported in 37 DLR(AD) 161, it has been held that the requisition must be for the public purpose. But in this case that is lacking inasmuch as on assessment of the evidence on record, we find nothing on record to show that the property in question was requisitioned by the then East Pakistan Government for public purpose. Moreover, the question of maintainability of the suit as per provisions of section 14A of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 was not raised by the contesting defendant -petitioner before the Courts below at any point of time. 

13. In view of the above, as to the first submission of the teamed Deputy Attorney General on the, point of maintainability of the suit appears to be without any substance. 

14. Mr. Goutam Kumar Roy, the learned Deputy Attorney General next submits that the very nature of transfer of the suit property to the plaintiffs by way of a registered deed is not free from doubt inasmuch as it is apparent from the record that the whereabouts of the original owners of the suit property namely Sudhir Chandra and Subir Chandra was totally unknown to the defendant-petitioner since 1947 to till date but both the Courts below without considering this vital aspect of the case mechanically decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiffs. 

15. On the other hand, Mr. Md. Mahbub Ali, the learned Advocate relying on the decision reported in 32 DLR 252 submits that the proposition of law is well settled that a registered kabala is an evidence of title which will prevail over other records of rights as such until and unless such kabala is cancelled on specific allegation of fraud by any civil Court in an appropriate civil suit and in this case the original owners of the suit land transferred the land to Most. Jahurunnesa Khanam, who subsequently transferred the same to the plaintiffs by registered deed dated 5.10,97 (Ext.I-Ka) and there is nothing on record to show that during pendency of the suit before the Courts below the defendant No. 1, Deputy Commissioner, Sylhet at any point of time took step to detect the whereabouts of the original owner of suit land that is Sudhir Chandra and Subir Chandra who were impleaded as defendant Nos.4 and 5 in the suit by the plaintiffs and therefore, the contentions as raised by the learned Deputy Attorney General that the Courts below having failed to consider about the nature of transfer, of the suit is without any legal basis whatsoever. 

16. In the case of Sultanuddin Chowdhmy Vs. Government of the People’s Republic of Bangladesh and others reported in 32 DLR 252, it has been held as follows: 

"In the foregoing facts and circumstances of the case the petitioner's valid purchase of the property from the said Sushil Kumar Gangali remains undisputed until now. This is quite evident from the order passed on 15.3.77 by Mr. M. A. Samad, Joint Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms of the Government of Bangladesh, wherein it was held that the petitioner's property was never listed as a vested property nor was it made khas property of the Government. In such circumstances it was further ordered that it was not necessary to treat the property in question to be under any unauthorized possession of the petitioner and on that account the petitioner's eviction was avoided. It is surprising to note that only after four months on 22.7.77 another order was passed by Mr. S. Hossain. Khan, Joint Secretary in the Ministry of Land Administration and Reforms of the Government of Bangladesh wherein it was held that the property in question appeared to have been held as vested property and on 15.3.77 was reviewed and revised. In passing the subsequent order of 22.7.77 it was observed that the petitioner's title in the property in question was doubtful. Apart from the act that the petitioners title is based upon valid purchase of the property by a duly registered deed. The authority in the Government could not question and annul the validity of such title by an executive order. If the Government wanted to claim in such Property if could only do so by way of an appropriate suit for declaration of title and cancellation of the petitioner's registered kabala as such. Be that as it may it is surprising to note that a Joint Secretary in the Ministry of Land Reforms could revise an order passed only four months before by his predecessor, another Joint Secretary in the said Ministry of land Administration and Land Reforms. The subsequent order passed by joint Secretary Mr. S. Hossain Khan on 22.7.77 is obviously based on Illegal assumption of fact and as such suffers from clear illegality." 
17. As we have already noticed that both the Courts below after discussions of the entire materials on record arrived at a common finding that the plaintiff’s title is based upon valid purchase of the property by a duly registered deed. The authority in the Government did not or could not raise any question in any civil Court for cancellation of the plaintiffs registered deed. The learned Deputy Attorney General could not show from the record that the concurrent findings of the Courts below on the point plaintiff’s title based on misreading of the evidence on record or misinterpretation of any material document. Therefore, in the facts and circumstance of the case and in view of the submission of Mr. Md. Mahbub Ali, vis-a-vis the above quoted decision reported in 32 DLR 252 we are unable to accept this branch of argument of Mr. Goutam Kumar Roy, the learned Deputy Attorney General. 

18. The learned Deputy Attorney General further submits that the proposition of law is by now well settled that in a suit for recovery of possession the question of dispossession is required to be proved by adducing sufficient convincing evidence but in this case there is nothing on record to show that at any point of time the present plaintiff-opposite parties had possessed the suit land or there is nothing on record to show that on a specific or particular date the plaintiff-opposite parties were dispossessed from the suit land although both the Courts below without applying its judicial mind to this vital aspect of the case mechanically decreed the suit with a direction to hand over the possession within 120 days. 

19. To this, Mr, Mahbub An, relying on the decision reported in 44 DLR(AD) 100 submits that in such a case the plaintiffs can get recovery of possession only if the title is not lost by adverse possession and in this case both the Courts below found the title of the plaintiffs to the suit land and there is nothing on record to show that at any point of time the title of the plaintiffs was lost.

20. In the case of Abdus Sattar Vs. Abdul Rahman @ Abdur Rahman and others reported in 44 DLR(AD) 100, it has been held as follows: 

"The first ground urged by Mr. Khondker as to the application of Article 144 of the Limitation Act instead of Article 142 as applied by the learned Judge of the High Court Division appears to be of little practical consequence inasmuch as it has been found that the defendants had acquired title by adverse possession. If this finding remains then the suit will be indisputably barred also under Article 144. Therefore, the main question for consideration is whether the finding as to adverse possession was correct and this brings us to the second ground on which the appeal was mainly pressed. Even so, it may be observed that the question of limitation falls to be decided initially on the plaintiffs own case as set out in the plaint. In the present case the plaintiff asserted that he was in possession of the suit land upon taking settlement in 1357 BS but was dispossessed by the defendants in 1368 BS and as such Article 142 applies in terms. The courts below, however, disbelieved the plaintiffs case of alleged possession and dispossession but at the same time found his title to the suit land. In such a case, time plaintiff can get recovery of possession only if the title was not lost by adverse possession of the defendants for over twelve years. As the defendants have specifically pleaded adverse possession, the suit will have to be decided on the basis as to when the possession of the defendants became adverse to the plaintiff. In this way, Article 144 gets attracted subsequently although the initial onus was upon the plaintiff to prove his possession within twelve years before the institution of the suit." 

From a reading of the above quoted decision together with the facts and circumstances of the case, we find there is a good deal of substance in the contention raised by Mr. Mahbub Ali, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff opposite parties that the Courts below in the facts and circumstances of the case committed no illegality in decreeing the suit as prayed for inasmuch as in this case both the Courts below found the title of the plaintiffs to the suit land on the basis of registered Kabala and there is nothing on record to show that at any point of time the title of the plaintiffs was lost. 

21. Mr. Goutam Kumar Roy, the learned Deputy Attorney General further relying on the decision reported in 4 BLD(AD)199 submits that the power of attorney dated 3.8.89 (Ext.4) was not proved as per the provision of section 67 of the Evidence Act and as such subsequent transfer on the basis of power of attorney including the registered deeds are illegal and not acted upon as well. 

22. On the contrary, Mr. Mahbub Ali, the learned Advocate submits that all the registered deeds including the power of attorney were properly proved and exhibited. He also adds that a registered kabala is an evidence of title which will prevail over other records of rights as such until and unless such kabala is cancelled on specific allegation of fraud by any civil Court in an appropriate civil suit and in this case the Government did not file any suit for declaration of title and cancellation of registered kabala or power of attorney dated 3.8.89 (Ext.4). 

23. To appreciate this branch of argument of the learned Deputy Attorney General and the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite parties from a correct angle, we have carefully examined the evidence of PWs. and DWs. together with the documentary evidence on record. It appears that PW-1 (plaintiff No.2) in his deposition stated that the defendant Nos.4 - 5 that is full brother Sudhir Chandra Duna and Subir Chandra Duna executed a power of attorney in favour of Mrinal Kanti, who subsequently transferred the suit land to Jahurunnesa Khanam on 15.11.89 by executing a registered deed dated 22.11.89. This witness also proved the said power of attorney as Ext.4 and it also appears that Ext. No.4 and other documents including the kabala of the plaintiffs all are registered documents no one filed as yet any suit for cancellation of those registered documents. 

24. In the case of Sultanuddin Chowdhury Vs. Government of the People’s Republic of Bangladesh and others reported in 32 DLR 252, it has been held as follows: 

"This is a well-established principle of law. A registered kabala is an evidence of title which will prevail over the other records of rights as such until and unless such kabala is cancelled on a specific allegation of fraud by any civil Court in an appropriate civil suit." 

In this case it is also found that all registered documents including power of attorney (Ext.-4) and registered deed of kabala dated 5.10.1997 and power of attorney dated 5.10.89 ( Ext.-1 & Ext. ka) which were produced from the custody of the plaintiffs and those documents are more than 10 years old documents. At the trial no dispute was raised in the trial Court as to its registration. Therefore, sitting under revisional jurisdiction, we are unable to accept the contention of Mr. Goutam Kumar Roy, the learned Deputy Attorney General that the power of attorney was not properly proved rather, we find considerable merit in the submission of Mr. Mahbub Ali. 

25. By now we have covered the points raised by the learned Deputy Attorney General. Now let as advert to some of the submission made by Mr. Mahbub Ali. One of the main contention raised by him relying on the decision reported in 17 BLD(AD) 199 is that a finding of fact whether concurrent or not arrived at by the lower appellate Court is binding upon the High Court Division in Revision except in certain well-defined circumstances such as non-consideration and misreading of the material evidence affecting the merit of the case and in the present case the judgments of 2 Courts below are well based on correct evaluation of the facts and materials of the case and as such question of interference does not arise at all. 

26. Mr. Goutam Kumar Roy, the learned Deputy Attorney General while elaborating his submission this Court asked him to address on the point that whether the judgments of two Courts below are based on misreading and non-consideration of the evidence on record. Mr. Roy could not satisfy as upon referring evidence from the record that the judgments of two Courts below are based on misreading or non-consideration of the evidence on record. The trial Court and the lower appellate Court are the final Court of facts. The suit having been concluded on concurrent findings of fact, it is very difficult to interfere with such findings sitting under the revisional jurisdiction, unless it is found that the concurrent findings of fact are perverse being contrary to law or evidence and materials on record. 

27. Another contention raised by Mr. Mahbub Ali, relying on the decisions reported in 55DLR (AD) 132 and I7BLD (AD) 77 is that in this case the petitioners were most illegally discriminated all along by the Government machinery inasmuch as it is evident from the record that a portion of the suit plot has been de-requisitioned while the prayer of the plaintiff-petitioners was not considered in accordance with law. It is found that all other property similar to the suit property has been de-requisitioned on the basis of the prayer of the owners of the land while the prayer of the plaintiff-petitioners for derequisition was not considered. So, the grievance of Mr. Mahbub Ali, the learned Advocate does not appear to be without substance. 
28. Furthermore, in this connection we want to quote hem few lines in the case of Abdur Rauf Vs Govt. of East Pakistan reported in 22 DLR(1970) 193, which reads as follows: 

"It must be remembered that no citizen can be asked to part with his property even  temporarily unless it is necessary for public purpose. Every citizen has a fundamental right to enjoy his property subject to the exercise of the State power of Eminent Domain only when it is necessary for a public purpose. Retention of property under requisition when there is no subsisting public purpose is indeed illegal and when the Government, by exercise of the power vested on it by the drastic provisions of section 3 of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, requisitions any property, it should act with promptitude in de-requisitioning the property as soon as it is found that it is no longer necessary to retain its possession." 

In this case we have already noticed that there is nothing on record to show that the property in question was requisitioned by the then East Pakistan Government for public purpose. 

29. Mr. Goutam Kumar Roy, the learned Deputy Attorney General at the end of the day having himself realized the weakness of the case by filing an application under Order XLI, rule 23 of the Code of Civil Procedure he has submitted that the plaintiffs are totally failed to prove the existence of defendant Nos.4-5 in Bangladesh and they even did not submit any voter list to prove that the defendant Nos.4-5 were in Bangladesh at the relevant time of alleged execution of power of attorney, the execution of the same clearly creates doubt or in other words the same was executed by false personation in order to grab the suit land taking the advantage of their absence in Bangladesh, both the Courts below committed an error of law in failing to consider the same and the same has resulted in error in the impugned decision occasioning failure of justice and thus, on such ground the suit may be sent back on remand to the trial Court for deciding it on all points after holding the trial afresh. 

30. On the other hand, Mr. Mahbub, the learned Advocate relying on the decisions reported in 54 DLR(AD) 73, 55 DLR(AD) 20 and 41 DLR(AD) 124 submits that the defendant-appellant got ample opportunity to adduce evidence before both the Courts below and since the deeds of the plaintiffs were proved' in accordance with law and both the Courts below after detail discussions of the entire evidence on record decreed the suit and when evidence on all material, points are there on record, it would not be justified sitting under reivisional jurisdiction to send the suit back on remand to have the, genuineness of the said deeds proved in accordance with law . 

In the case of Hosne Ara Begum and others Vs Montaj Ali and others reported in 55 DLR(AD) 20, it has been held as follows: 

"Though the learned Judge of the High Court 'Division quoted the relevant portion of the deposition of DW-1 as noticed by us, but he failed to consider the same properly resulting in error in his finding. Further, the legal position is that where evidence has been duly placed before the trial Court and it has decided the suit on merit the revisional Court has no power to' remand by shirking its duty, particularly solely for the purpose of writing the judgment afresh. This appeal, therefore, must succeed." 

In the case of Additional Deputy Commissioner, Revenue and Asstt. Custodian Vested Property, Chandpur Vs Tafumessa, wife of Ali Ahmed Mia and others reported in 41 DLR(AD) 124, it has been held as follows: 

"But a remand order is not to be granted as a matter of routine. Section 29 All 184 P.C. and 17 All 112 P.C. Mr. Moksudur Rahman found it difficult to pinpoint the area of investigation which could be done on remand. The crucial question is as to the physical presence of the vendor. It is presumed under section 60 that the registration was done in accordance with law and the requirement of the law was fulfilled. It is a rebuttable presumption, no doubt, but Mr. Moksudur Rahman could not argue, how the evidence as it is, has rebutted the presumption. The defendants got ample opportunity at the trial stage and no such rebuttal evidence was adduced. Hence the prayer for remand does not merit consideration. Since the point has been settled already on which the leave was granted, Mr. Ahmed is correct in saying the appeal has become of mere academic interest." 

In the case of Akitullah and others Vs Zafala Begum and others reported in 54 DLR(AD) 74, it has been held that remand as contemplated under Order 41 rule 23 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not of matter of course or to fill in the lacuna in any party's pleading. 

In the case of Golam Rahamn Vs Hazera Khatoon, reported in 1, MLR (AD) 211, it has been held that remand of a suit for fresh trial to provide opportunity for introducing a new case of adverse possession is not sustainable. 

In view of the long line of judicial decision is to the effect that the remand order should be avoided as far as possible, we are unable to accept the submission of the learned Deputy Attorney General that to send back the case on remand to the trial Court below for fresh trial since both oral and documentary evidence having been available on record to decide the case on merit. 

31. In view of our discussions made in the foregoing paragraphs it is by now clear that the instant Rule must fail. 

32. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The judgment and decree of affirmance dated 3.02.2003 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Sylhet in Title Appeal No.332 of 2001 is hereby maintained. 

33. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court stands vacated. Let a copy of the judgment along with lower Courts record be sent down at once.

End.

Mr. Md. Fazlul Karim with, Mr. Kazi Anowar Hosain ---For the petitioner (Pre-emptee).  
Mr. Shahidul Islam ---For the Opposite Party No. 1 (Pre-emptor)
parties:
Mosammat Saleha Bibi ------Petitioner.

full_judgment:
Mr. Md. Mozammel Haque, J: This Rule was issued directing the opposite parties to show cause as to why the judgment and order dated 11.12.73 passed in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 23 of 1973 by the Additional District Judge, Bogra, reversing the judgment and order dated 15.2.73 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 40 of 1970 by the learned Munsif, 1st Court, Bogra, should not be set aside. 

2. The present petitioner Mst. Saleha Bibi was the pre-emptee and opposite party No. 1 Tayeb Ali Molla as pre-emptor filed an application under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The pre-emptor instituted the aforesaid miscellaneous case for pre-emption on the ground that the deed in question is an out and out sale deed and he being a co-sharer by inheritance was entitled to pre-empt the case land. This pre-emption application was opposed by the present petitioner Mst. Saleha Bibi being pre-emptee. It is her case that though it is a sale deed, in fact it is a deed of gift and by mistake the scribe had written it as a deed of sale instead of deed of gift. The pre-emptee examined five witnesses. The opposite party No. 1 pre-emptee examined six witnesses in this case. After considering the evidence on record the learned Munsif by his judgment dated 15.7.73 dismissed the application for pre-emption holding that it is a deed of gift. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and order of the pre-emptor preferred an appeal which was registered as Miscellaneous Appeal No. 23 of 1973. This Appeal was disposed of by the learned Additional District Judge, Bogra who after considering the materials on record and hearing the parties set aside the judgment and order of the learned Munsif and sent the case back on remand for reconsideration after adding a person as party in the case. Being aggrieved by the judgment and order dated 11.12.73 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Bogra in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 23 of 1973 the pre-emptee preferred this revisional application and obtained the present Rule. 

3. Mr. Fazlul Karim, the learned Advocate appearing for the pre-emptee petitioner. submits that the remand order is good in view of the fact that the son of Kapashi ought to have been made a party in this case and since the son of Kapashi was not made a party the case was sent back for disposal after impleading the son of Kapashi as party. He further submits that since the evidence on record were not properly considered by the learned Lower Appellate Court this case ought to have re-heard by the learned Lower Appellate Court on the basis of the material evidence already on record. 

4. Mr. Shahidul Islam. the learned Advocate appearing for the pre-emptor opposite party No. 1, submits that on the basis of the materials on record the Lower Appellate Court utterly failed to consider the material evidence on record and the remanded the case only on some objection which was raised at the Appellate stage and not in the initial stage. In the case of Additional Deputy Commissioner, Revenue, Chandpur Vs. Safurnessa, 41 DLR (AD) 124, their Lordships totally discouraged the order of remand and held that it on the basis of the material evidence on record, the appeal could be disposed of by the Lower Appellate. Court. It should be disposed of in accordance with law on the basis of the material evidence on record without any order of remand. From the materials on record I find that the Lower Appellate Court could have finally disposed of this matter instead of sending this back on remand. It was also held by the High Court Division in another case of Zehad Ali Vs. Kharshed Ahmed, 41 DLR, 336. Mr. Shahidul Islam the learned Advocate submits that in this case the main question for determination is the interpretation of the documentary evidence namely the deed Ext, A.I.E. whether it is actually a deed of sale or a deed of gift. He submits that this Ext. A is a registered deed of out and out sale. On examination of the entire contents of this deed it cannot be construed as a deed of gift in any manner whatsoever. He submits that Sections 91 and 92 of the Evidence Act are very clear on this point. The pre-emptor opposite party No. 1 examined as many as six witnesses and by their oral evidence the pre-emptor has been able to make out a case that it is deed of sale. It cannot be said that by mistake it was written as a deed of sale by the scribe of the deed. 

5. Mr. Shahidul Islam submits that had it been so then the pre-emptee could have filed a suit under section 31 of the Specific Relief Act for correction of the deed, but it was not done. When this application under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was filed for pre-emption at that time this new case was made by the pre-emptee-petitioner. If I read the evidence of P.Ws and O.P.Ws and Ext. A in juxtaposition with the provisions of Sections 91 and 92 of the Evidence Act. It clearly appears to me that this Ext. A is an out and out sale deed and by no manner of interpretation it can be treated as a deed of gift. The oral evidence as given by the O.P.Ws cannot alter or change the contents of the sale deed. Ex. 4. I have gone through the evidence of PWs and OPWs in this case. It appears to me that if I read the deed of sale along with the evidence of PWs 1 and 2, it will be clear that it is a deed of sale out and out. The D.Ws wanted to prove by saying that due to love and affection this property was given to the plaintiff by way of gift and not by way of sale. This oral evidence is contrary to the deed. Ext. A. which cannot be accepted in view of the provisions of Sections 91 and 92 of the Evidence Act. So, on the materials on record. It hold that this Ext. A is a deed of sale out and out and it cannot be treated as a deed of gift in any manner whatsoever. 

6. As regards impleading of son of Kapashi, Mr. Shahidul Islam, submits that this objection ought to have been taken at the earliest stage, but it was not done. He submits that the objection which was taken by the pre-emptee at the initial stage were met by filing an application for amendment and addition of party by the pre-emptor. But this pre-emptee did not know the name of the son of Kapashi and this was for the first time mentioned at the appellate stage. Since the objection was not raised at the earliest stage, this cannot be accepted at appellate stage. Such an
objection will only linger the proceeding. In support of his contention Mr. Shahidul Islam has referred to the case of Akhtarunnessa Vs. Habibullah 31. DLR (AD) 88. Since the objection has not been raised earlier, it cannot be raised at an appellate stage. In support of his contention as regards oral evidence and the registered document as contemplated under sections 91 and 92 of the Evidence Act. Mr. Shahidul Islam has referred to the case of Joynal Abedin Vs. Aliar Rahman, 1983 BLD (AD) 105 and Nasir Ahmed Vs. Ismat Jahan 21 DLR (SC) 145. The decisions cited above have got relevancy in the facts and circumstances of the present case. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case and materials on record, I am of the view that the Lower Appellate Court committed an error of law in its decision occasioning failure of justice and as such the order of remand cannot be sustained. 

7. Second submission of Mr. Md. Fazlul Karim is that the case should be remanded back to the Lower Appellate Court for rehearing of the appeal on the basis of the Materials already on record. I am unable this contention of Mr. Karim in view of the fact that this pre-emption case was instituted in 1970 and now it is 1993. Long period of 22 years already passed and if I send it back on remand it will take more time. Further, it will also increase the sufferings of the parties manifold. Considering the above, for ends of justice I decided to dispose it of finally in this court on the basis of the materials on record and for that reason. I have discussed above the evidence of the parties both oral and documentary. Moreover, in this case the only vital point requires decision as to whether the deed in question is a deed of sale or a deed of gift. I have already found that in the eye of law the deed is actually a deed of sale and not a deed of gift. So in the facts and circumstances of the case and in view of the material evidence on record. I am of the view that this court can also pass an appropriate order in its Revisional Jurisdiction in deciding this case finally and conclusively without remanding it to the Lower Appellate Court. On this point this case finds support from the case of Sk. Abdul Latif Vs. Abdul Malek, 1984 BLD (AD) 15 (Para-81). 

8. In the result, this Rule is made absolute and the order of remand of the Lower Appellate Court is set aside and the order of the learned Munsif is also set aside and the application on the pre-emptor opposite party No. 1 under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act for pre-emption is hereby allowed. No cost. 

Send down the L.C. records immediately. 

End.
