full_judgment:
Mr. Shah Abu Nayeem Mominur Rahman, J: This rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause why the judgment and decree dated 21.7.94 passed in title appeal No. 298/89 by the learned Additional District Judge, Naogaon, allowing the appeal after setting aside the judgment and decree dated 28.10.89 passed in O.C. suit No. 53/87 by the learned Assistant Judge, Manda Upazilla, Naogaon, dismissing the suit, should not be set aside.

2. The Opposite Party as plaintiffs filed the suit for setting aside the judgment and decree passed in partition suit No. 47/84 by the learned Assistant Judge, Manda Upazila , Naogaon, allowing the partition contending that the plaintiff was made defendant No. 25 in the aforesaid partition suit and that the defendant was not served with the summons of the partition suit and that he was also not aware or had any knowledge about the partition suit and that the partition suit was decreed experte and that the plaintiffs came to know about the partition suit when the defendants came to take possession of the lands in execution of the decree and that thereafter on procuring certified copy of the judgment and decree passed in the partition suit, the plaintiffs came to know about the partition suit definitely and his land being affected by the experte decree he is compelled to file this instant suit. The defendant No. 3 is contesting the suit by filing written statement contending inter alia that the plaintiffs had no title and possession in the suit jote and that the plaintiffs name having been wrongly recorded in the records of right he was made a party in the aforesaid partition suit and that the plaintiff as defendant No. 25 appeared in the partition suit and filed written statement jointly with defendant Nos. 1 to 3, 7 to 9 and 24 of the said partition suit. But subsequently this plaintiff did not contest the said partition suit which was ultimately decreed experte on. 16.1.86 in preliminary form and the final decree was passed on. 29.11.86 and that the instant suit has been filed malafide to cause loss and injury to and to harras the defendant. The learned Assistant Judge on consideration of the materials on record and the writ-ten statement filed in the partition suit, which contains the thumb impressions of the plaintiff, being defendant No. 25 in the partition suit, held that the plaintiff had knowledge about the partition suit but allowed the said partition suit to be decreed experte and therefore dismissed the suit by his judgment and decree dated. 28.10.89. Being aggrieved the plaintiff preferred title appeal No. 298/89, which on transfer was heard and disposed of by the learned additional District Judge by the impugned judgment and decree. The appellate court allowed the appeal and thereby decreed the suit and set aside the judgment and decree passed in the partition suit. The appellate court although arrived at its finding as to the non service of the summons upon the plain-tiff appellant but did not advert to the finding 'of the learned Assistant Judge on the issue of knowledge about the suit. 

3. Mr. S. N. Goswami, learned Advocate, appearing of the petitioner submitted that the impugned judgment and decree is not a proper judgment of reversal and that the appellate court erred in law in not adverting to the findings of the trial court to the effect that the plaintiffs had knowledge about the partition suit and therefore, the finding of the learned Assistant Judge as to knowledge stands and if that finding of the learned Assistant Judge stands then the appeal cannot be allowed in as much as the suit is liable to be dismissed on the ground of earlier knowledge about the partition suit. The learned Advocate in support of his contention referred to the decision in the case of Ranjit Sarker Vs. Sree Sukendra Nath Biswas reported in 1997 BLT (AD) 15. 

4. Mr. Bhabesh Chandra Sarker, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party submits that there is no illegality in the impugned judgment and decree and since the appellate court has found that the summons of the partition suit was not property served the plaintiff had no knowledge about the suit as well as the decree passed in the partition suit and therefore, the said partition suit has been rightly restored to its original file and number. The learned Advocate further submitted that the appellate court allowed the appeal but did not discuss on the findings of the court below on the point of knowledge of the plaintiffs and hence it is a fit case for remand for a proper decision by the appellate court below. The learned Advocate submits that the partition suit has been disposed of experte, where in, in the schedule, his landed property measuring about 91 decimals of land are involved and if the experte stands then he will be highly prejudiced and shall suffer irreparable loss. The learned Advocate taking me through the judgment of the trial court submits that there is no evidence on record to show that the court has compared the alleged thumb impression of the plaintiff appearing in the written statements filed in the partition suit with the thumb impression of the plaintiff appearing in the deposition sheet dated. 2.5.88 of the trial court. Normally when the genuineness of the thumb impression is in question the court sends the same for opinion from hand writing expert provided an application is made. The learned Advocate submits that for ends of justice it is necessary that the thumb impressions as appearing in the written statement in the partition suit should be examined and compared with those of the plaintiffs appearing in the deposition sheet of this case of with the thumb impression to be taken in open court for arriving at an conclusive finding. 

5. I have perused the application and the materials on record and considered the sub-missions of the learned Advocates of the respective parties. The plaintiff has taken the plea that he was not served with the summons of the partition suit which was decreed experte and that he came to know about the partition suit when the execution case stated and that after procuring the certified copy of the judgment he came to a know about the case definitely. D.Ws. 2, 3 and 4 have proved that the plaintiff had knowledge about the partition suit, in which the plaintiff as defendant No. 25 filed a joint written statement. The D.W. 2 categorically stated that the plaintiff was also served with the summons of the partition suit in his presence and he is a witness to the said summons. The D.W.4 in his deposition stated that his wife being defendant No. 9 and the plaintiff being defendant No. 25 in the partition suit put their respective signatures on the written statement along with other contesting defendants in the partition suit. The appellate court though discussed on the issue of service of summons of the partition suit upon the plaintiff but did not consider the aspect of knowledge of the plaintiff about the partition suit as found by the trial court. Having regard to the decision in the case of Ranjit Sarkar Vs. Sukendra Nath Roy reported in 1997 ELT (AD) 15, wherein it has been observed that no relief to he granted without adverting the findings of the trial court and that in the instant case the appellate court did not advert the reasoning’s of the trial court and also did not discuss the material evidences which were considered by the trial court, and these hit the root of the merit of the cases and it also appears that the appellate court also did not comply with the requirements of Order 41 Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure in delivering the impugned judgment. In the circumstances I find that the impugned judgment and decree passed by the learned appellate court is not a proper judgment of reversal and has occasioned failure of justice. 

6. In the result the rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and decree dated 21.7.94 passed in title appeal No. 298/89 by the learned Additional District Judge, Naogaon is set aside and the judgment and decree dated. 28.10.89 passed in O.C. Suit No. 33/87 by the learned Assistant Judge, Upazila Manda, Naogaon, dismissing the suit is affirmed. Stay granted by this court stands vacated. 

7. Let the record of the courts below be sent down.

	End.

lawyer:
Mr. M Khaled Ahmed, Advocate--for the petitioners. 
Mr. AKM Enayet Hossain, Advocate -- for opposite party No. 1.
parties:
Sonali Bank, Head Office and others ----- Petitioners
Versus 
Md. Jalaluddin and another ----- Opposite parties
full_judgment:
Mr. Md. Abdur Rashid, J:This Rule was obtained by the defendants upon an application under Section-115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, in brief the Code, against judgment and order dated 28.08.95 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Kishoreganj in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 58 of 1992 affirming those dated 22.08.92 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, at Sadar, Kishoreganj in Review Case No. 20 of 1990. 

2. Facts are not disputed. On 22.01.77 opposite party-plaintiff joined the defendant Bank as typist in Kishoreganj Branch. On 09.05.81 the plaintiff was put under suspension pending decision of a police case lodged against him by the said Branch of the Bank. On 18.11.82 the plaintiff was dismissed from service under the service rules of the Bank. 

3. On 17.11.85 the plaintiff instituted Other Class Suit. No. 265 of 1985 in the Court of Senior Munsif at Kishoreganj for a decree for declaration that his dismissal from service was illegal, void and not binding upon him and that he continued in service of the Bank. But upon hearing the matter on the issue of maintainability at the instance of the defendants, the learned Munsif held that in view of the Administrative Tribunal Act (Act VII of 1981) 1981, shortly the AT Act, the civil court had no jurisdiction to try the suit and directed to return the plaint to the filing Advocate for presentation before the proper court by his order dated 05.07.86. 

4. Thereafter, on or about 09.04.90 the plaintiff made an application under Order-47 Rule- I read with Section-151 of the Code being Review Case No. 20 of 1990 before the Upazila Senior Munsif for review of the said order for return of the plaint. On hearing both the sides, the learned Munsif by his order dated 22.08.92 found the order for return of the plaint based on total misconception of law regarding the right of the plaintiff to sue in a civil court and accordingly, allowed the application for review and vacated the order for return of the plaint dated 05.07.85 and directed the suit to proceed with. 

5. On appeal there from at the instance of the defendants, the Subordinate Judge rejected the appeal and confirmed the decision of the Senior Assistant Judge by his order dated 28.08.95. 

6. Against this appellate order allowing the review, the defendants obtained the above Rule as stated earlier. 

7. In support of the Rule, Mr. M Khaled Ahmed appearing for the defendant  Bank, submits that the plaintiff is a worker within the definition Section-2(28) of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, 1965, shortly, the SO Act and as such, his remedy lies before the Labour Court and not before a civil court under Section-9 of the Code as the jurisdiction of Civil -Court stands impliedly ousted by the SO Act. Secondly, the defendant Bank having been brought within the ambit of the AT Act by an amendment dated 25.09.84, the plaintiff could have gone to an Administrative Tribunal under Section-4 of the AT Act if he claimed to be not a worker and the jurisdiction of a civil court is also impliedly ousted by this Act. According to him, after the dismissal of the statutory appeal on 25.09.84. only forum was open to him was that of the Administrative Tribunal. He then, submits, the review petition was hopelessly barred by limitation being cut of time by more than 4 years. Both the courts below erred in law in condoning such an inordinate delay in the absence of an application under Section-5 of the Limitation Act. He finally submits that both the courts below committed serious error of law in their decisions occasioning failure of justice in allowing the review. In support of his submissions, he also cited the decisions reported in 40 DLR (AD) 45, 43 DLR 395, 44 DLR (AD) 260 and 48 DLR 330. 

8. Mr. AKM Enayet Hossain appearing for the plaintiff cited the decisions of 29 DLR (SC) 39 and 29 DLR (SC) 41. He also filed a photo copy of an unreported decision dated 08.01.97 of the Appellate Division in the case of GM, Sonali Bank v Abul Khair being Civil Appeal No. 86 of 1994. He submits that as the plaintiff was removed from service on 18.11.82 when there was no scope for him to seek any remedy in the Administrative Tribunal under Section-4 of the AT Act as the defendant Bank was not yet included within the schedule of the Act. He also submits that the plaintiff did not qualify under Section-25 of the So Act to make 
any grievance before a labour court. Only doors according to him were open to him were those of a civil court. He therefore submits on the authorities that the concurrent order allowing review does not call for interference by this Division under Section-115 of the Code. 

9. In reply, Mr. Khaled Ahmed submits that the principle enunciated by the Appellate Division in the unreported case cited by Mr. Enayet has no manner of application to the facts of the instant case. 

10. After patiently hearing the learned Advocates, going through the entire record, perusing the revision application and the impugned orders, and reading number of decisions of this Division as well as of the Appellate Division as cited at the Bar, it appears to me that the question as to the right of a petty employee of statutory corporations to sue in a civil court 
against his removal from service facing the courts has not yet been finally settled even after so many authoritative decisions of the Appellate Division. 


11. The Supreme Court of Pakistan in Malik and Haq v Muhammad Shamsul Islam, PLD 1961 SC 531 held: 

"... in the absence of any statutory provision protecting the servant it is not possible in law to grant to him a decree against an unwilling master that he is still his servant. A servant 
cannot be forced upon his master." Following the decision, the Supreme Court in Eastern Mercantile Bank v M Shamsuddin, 21 DLR (SC) 365 set aside the decree obtained by an employee of a private Bank against his termination from service and dismissed the suit being of the view, 
"The declaration that the order terminating the respondent's service was null and void, etc. could not be covered by the provisions of Section-42 of the Specific Relief Act, ... the terms 
and conditions of the respondent's (plaintiff) service were not regulated by any legal instrument, it could not be said that the declaration asked for by him was in relation to any legal character," 

12. Whether the rule of master and servant is equally applicable in the cases of employees of statutory corporations and whether, in the absence of service rules, a suit of such employees is maintainable under Section-42 of the Specific Relief Act were seriously mooted before the Appellate Division in MD, Janata Bank v Hafizuddin Ahmed and others, 29 DLR (SC) 39 and 
BSIC v Mahbub Hossain, 29 DLR (SC) 41. 13. In the earlier case, Hafizuddin, a Grade-II Officer sued for a declaration against his dismissal from service. In the appeal of the bank preferred from the concurrent order rejecting an application of the bank u/o 7R. 11 of the Code, the then Supreme Court of Bangladesh held for the first time that an employee of a statutory 
corporation does not come within the master and servant rule as his service has a public character. So, he is entitled to a legal character and can maintain a suit for declaration u/s 42 of the Specific Relief Act.

14. The questions were thoroughly investigated in BSIC v Mahbub Hossain. Mahbub, an officer of the Corporation was on 31.05.73 dismissed under the service rules pursuant to a decision of the Board of Directors and in consideration of first Screening Board appointed by the Government. He successfully challenged his dismissal in an application under article-102(2) of the Constitution before this Division. On an appeal there from, the Appellate Division on review of various decisions, formulated the principles as to the law relating to the employees of statutory corporations or bodies. 
a. If an employee is dismissed or his service is terminated in contravention of a mandatory statutory provision, the employee has a right of action either in the ,Supreme Court in its writ jurisdiction or in a Civil Court, 
b. If the service of its employee is terminated in violation of the principle of natural justice, the employee has a similar right of action as in (a), 
c. If the office is a statutory one, the holder of the office has similar right of action as in (a), in case of termination of the said office not in accordance with the law under which the said office has been held, 
d. In spite of the office being a statutory one or of public character, terms and conditions of the office may be regulated by contract, and termination of service in contravention of such contract, but otherwise than in the manner mentioned in (a) and (b) is not actionable for the purpose of reinstatement in the office, and 
e. Terms and conditions of service pre-scribed by the rules, regulations or any other form of delegated legislation made by a body under statutory powers are not contractual, but have statutory force and the dismissal or termination of service in substantial disregard of them will entitle the employee to a right of action as in (a). 

15. An employee of a statutory corporation answering the description of a worker as defined in the SO Act May be removed from service either under such Act or under the service rules of such corporations. The cases against removal started coming before the courts with the moot issue, whether the suit of such an employee of a statutory corporation is still maintainable. In Dosta Textile Mills v Sudangshu Bikash Nath. 40 DLR (AD) 45, Sudangshu, Store-in-Charge on being discharged from a criminal charge on final report was proceeded under Section-18 of the SO Act and finally dismissed from ser-vice. He sued the Mills in civil court and got a decree against the dismissal from the appellate court and affirmed by this Division in revision. In further appeal to the Appellate Division, it was held that Sudangshu was a worker and that he was not an employee of the Corporation in which the Mill vested and the Service Rules of the corporation were not applicable to him. The Appellate Division also observed, 
"... the very moment it is found that the plaintiff is a worker, he is non-suited, because his suit filed under the Civil Procedure Code is not maintain-able, specific remedy of his grievance lies in a separate forum, the Labour Court, established under the Industrial Relations Ordinance. 1969, as amended up to date." The principle followed, 
"Where a right is created by a statute which also prescribes the manner in which that right may be enforced, the party complaining of any infringement of such right can only seek such remedy as is provided by that statute." The decision of this Division in Jogesh Chandra Datta v Bangladesh, 30 DLR 219 was approved. 

16. In Mujibur Rahman v Bangladesh, 44 DLR (AD) 111, the Appellate Division held that in view of clause 5 of Article 102 of the Constitution, a writ petition is not maintainable against judgment and order of the Administrative Tribunal established under Section-5 of the AT Act. It further held, inter alia, 
"A person in the service of the Republic who intends to invoke the fundamental rights in challenging the Ares of a law will seek his remedy under Article 102 (1) of the Constitution." 

17. After coming into force of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1981 (AT Act) bringing all classes of employees of statutory corporations, bodies or authorities within its sweep, the confusion around the questions appears to have heightened. In MD, Rupali Bank v Tafazal Hossain and others, 44 DLR (AD) 260. Tafazal, and Assistant Cashier of the bank got a decree against his termination from service and the decree was confirmed in appeal as well as in revision by this Division. He was terminated on 15.09.81. The statutory public authorities, including Rupali Bank was on 25.09.84 brought into the ambit of Section-4 of the Act by Administrative Tribunal (Amendment) Ordinance, (Ordinance No. LX of 1984) 1984. In 1987, he instituted the suit after spending six years seeking remedies before persons and authorities not contemplated in Section-4(2) of the AT Act. The Appellate Division held that his case goes out. of the ambit of the AT Act. For his case would be governed by the law which was applicable to him and was in force at the time of his termination in 1981. But Tafazal was found to be a worker and accordingly it was ruled that his remedy would lie before the Labour Court u/s 25(1) of the EL(SO) Act, 1965. The Appellate Division approved the view of a single bench decision in Md. Shahabuddin v Janata Bank, 41 DLR 94. But it could not be ascertained, whether the termination of was under the SO Act, 1965 or the Bank Service Rules. 

18, In GM, Sonali Bank v Abul Khayer & others, CA 86 of 1994, Abul Khayer a driver in the Bank instituted OC Suit 289 of 1986 for declarations that his termination from service dated 24.09.81 under the Sonali Bank Service Rules was void, illegal, inoperative etc and further that his service as driver was continuing with its salaries and facilities. Leave was granted against the order of the HCD affirming the order of the trial court rejecting an application of the Bank u/o 7 r. 11 of the Code for rejection of the plaint made on the grounds, 
a. the suit was barred by reason of the AT Act, 1980 which got exclusive jurisdiction to try such matter, 
b. the suit was barred u/s 42 of the SR Act, 
c. the matter was triable by the Labour Court, and 
d. the suit was barred under the Limitation Act. 

Relying the decision in Rupali Bank v Nazrul Islam, 39 DLR 167, the trial court held that the plaintiff was not a worker and hence his case was not triable by the Labour Court. Relying on the decision in 44 DLR (AD) 260, only point argued before the Appellate Division that since the plain-tiff was a worker his remedy would lie before the Labour Court and the jurisdiction of the Civil Court was impliedly barred. It was pointed out by this Division that the termination of the plaintiffs service was not done under the SO Act but under rule-17(ii) of the Bank's (Staff) Service Rules which is permitted u/s 3 of the SO Act. This Division also noticed that in 44 DLR (AD) 260 the termination was issued in 1981 and the Rupali Bank was brought into the ambit of AT Act in 1984. 
The Appellate Division confirmed the decision of this Division in holding that in view of the proviso to S 25 of the SO Act and the facts of the case, this Division correctly took the view that the door of the Labour Court was closed to the plaintiff and as such, the decision in 44 DLR (AD) 260 would not be a binding precedent in the instant case. The Appellate Division also noticed that the proviso to Section-25 of the SO Act was not brought to its notice. If the proviso was considered as above in 44 DLR (AD) 260 it would be difficult to resist the view taken by this Division. 
The plaintiff having been found to have no other forum either under the SO Act or Industrial Relations Ordinance. 1969 (Ordinance XXIII of 1969) to challenge the order of termination from service was found to be entitled to go to the Civil Court. The Appellate Division also held that if there is termination of a worker u/s 19 of the SO Act, there is no doubt that he has to follow the grievance procedure u/s 25 of SO Act. Then, the Appellate Division observed, 
"The terms of Section-19 of the (SO) Act providing termination of a 'worker' and those of rule 17(ii) of the Bank's Service Rules are found to different and therefore, it is difficult to say that a termination under the service rules of the Bank is covered under the SO Act. In such view of the matter also the plaintiff cannot be said to have a remedy under the (SO) Act." 19. Besides the above cases, I have also studied other cases on the issues. The principles enunciated so far may be summarized as follows: 
a. The standing of employees of a private company or authority remains the same to be covered by the law of master and servant and the rule of hire and fire in case of removal from service with the only exception that if such employee is a worker he may go to the labour court with his grievance. But he is not entitled to sue in a civil court under Section-42 of the Specific Relief Act, 
b. If an employee of a statutory corporation answering to the description of a worker as defined in the Employment of Labour (Standing Order) Act, 1965, shortly the SO Act, is removed from service either by termination or dismissal under the provisions of the Act, he must seek his remedy before the Labour Court established by the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969, 
c. If such employee is terminated under the provisions of the Act but he does not qualify to make his grievance under Section 25 of the Act, he may seek his remedy in a civil court, 
d. When such employee is removed from service either by termination or dismissal not under the provisions of the SO Act but under the service rules of such corporation, and before the coming into force of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1981 or before his corporation brought within the ambit of the Administrative Tribunal Act by subsequent amendment, he is entitled to seek his remedy either in a civil court or before this Division under Article-102 of the Constitution in writ jurisdiction, and 
e. After the coming into force of the Administrative Tribunal Act or bringing into the ambit of such Act by subsequent amendment, all 'employees of a statutory corpora-tion, bodies or authorities not covered by clauses (d) must seek his remedy against removal from ser-vice under the service rules of the corporation or otherwise, before an Administrative Tribunal under the provisions of the Administrative Tribunal Act. 

20. Now, in the 'case before us, I find from the record that after the plaintiff was put under suspension';' 'proceeded with under the Bank's Old Service Rules and finally dismissed from service on 18.11.82 under the Bank's Old Service Rule No. 39. His departmental appeal was also dismissed under Rule No. 43 on 25.09.84. All through he was proceeded with under the Service Rules of the Bank. This is permit-ted under Section-3 of the SO Act. On 18.11.82 when he was dismissed from service, the defendant Bank was not brought within the ambit of the AT Act. So, the plaintiff had no scope to seek remedy under the AT Act, 1981. Equally, as the plaintiff was not dismissed under any pro-vision of the SO Act, 1965 he had also no right to go to the Labour Court established under the Industrial Relations Ordinance. In view of the Ratio Decided of the cases discussed above, against the dismissal options were open to the plaintiff was either to sue in a civil court or to move this Division in writ under Article 102 of the Constitution. The plaintiff opted to sue in a civil court and he is quite entitled to proceed with his suit in the civil court. The impugned decisions of the courts below setting aside the order of returning the plaint therefore do not call any interference. 

21. On the question of limitation, I must say that both the courts below considered the reasons for the delay in making the application for review, and in exercise of their discretion were satisfied in condoning, the delay. Sitting in revision and exercising a limited jurisdiction under Section-115 of the Code, I find it difficult for me to go into the question of exercise of discretion by the courts below and in particular, their satisfaction, in condoning the delay. 


22. So, the submissions in support of the rule have no substance. In the result, the rule is discharged with cost. The impugned judgment and orders are here-by affirmed. The order of stay granted at the time of issue of the rule hereby stands vacated. Let the records be sent down at once so that the suit may be heard and disposed of as early as possible.

End.

full_judgment:
Mr. Mohammad Fazlul Karim, J.:-Returned candidate at an election for the post of Chairman is the appellant in this appeal directed against judgment and order dated 13th March. 2000 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2829 of 1999 discharging the Rule against those dated 28.7.1999 of the Additional District Judge and Election Appellate Tribunal in Election Appellate Tribunal in Appeal No. 4 of 1999 allowing the election petition reversing those dated 10.3.1999 passed by the Election Tribunal and Senior Assistant Judge in Election Tribunal Case No. 8 of 1998 dismissing the election petition. 

2. Facts of the case relevant, in short, are that on 1.12.1997 election for the office of the Chairman, Bandarkhol Union Parishad was held. Petitioner and respondents contested the said election. Petitioner had the symbol of umbrella, respondent No. 1 had pineapple and other respondents had symbols namely chair, swan and deer respectively in the said election. Petitioner was declared elected as the Chairman after the completion of the election as he secured 117 votes more than his nearest rival Respondent No. 1. Thereafter Respondent No. 1 filed the aforesaid election petition before the Election Tribunal alleging that the presiding officers of Ward Nos. 1, 4, 5, 8 and 9 did not properly count the votes and being influenced by the petitioner obtained sig-natures of the election agents of the Respondent No. 1 in blank sheets of papers and illegally rejected scale valid votes cast in f-- our of the petitioner as invalid as thus rejected 61 valid votes of Respondent No. 1 and the Presiding Officers of the said Wards also counted 120 invalid votes with double seals in favour of the returned candidate in spit(' of protest of the election agent.; of the Respondent No. 1 and illegally declared the appellant as elected Chairman by a margin of 117 votes. If the votes are counted by the election tribunal Respondent No. 1 will be elected by a margin of 180/181 votes. 

3. The appellant contested the case filing written objection denying the material allegations stating that the election was held peacefully supervised by two Magistrates and large number of police force. His further case is that after completion of the election Presiding Officers separated the ballots according to symbol and post of candidates in presence of con-testing candidates and their agents and after counting of ballots result sheets were prepared by the presiding officers of the respective centers and the election agents of the respective candidates on being satisfied put their signatures in the result sheets and the allegations that the Presiding Officers of the Ward Nos. 1, 4, 5. 8 and 9 obtained signatures of the election agents of the Respondent No. 1 before the starting of the counting are false and concocted, Presiding Officers duly sent the results to the Returning Officer the same day and on receipt of the same Returning Officer consolidated the same and declared the appellant as elected Chairman on 2.12.1997. Neither the Respondent No. 1 nor his election agents filed any petition before the Presiding Officers or the Returning Officer about aria illegality or irregularity in the counting of votes. 

4. Election Tribunal dismissed the case, the respondent thereupon filed an appeal which was allowed setting aside the election of the appellant whereupon the appellant unsuccessfully moved the .High Court Division. 

5. Mr. Khandaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Counsel appearing for the appellant, submitted that the Election Tribunal on consideration of the nature of double sealing on the ballot papers arrived at definite finding that the double marks on the 120 ballot papers of the returned candidate were not made by the respective voters while casting votes but the same are subsequent post election act of manipulation created by the interested party, the impugned judgment of the High Court Division affirming those of the Court of appeal below are not sustainable in law inasmuch as the sealed packet containing electoral materials inside the gunny bags were not found intact. 

6. Mr. M. Amirul Islam, learned Counsel for the respondents has, submit-ted that the seal on the packet containing ballot papers having found to be intact, the ballot papers containing double seal were invalid votes that were counted in favour of the returned candidate, materially affected the result of the election. The learned Counsel has further submitted with reference to Rule 38 that the seal put on the ballot papers or the seal applied by the presiding officer for marking the ballot papers being the same and as such the ballot papers containing double seal are illegal votes in favour of the returned candidate, for which the result of the election was materially affected. 

7. The matter once came before the High Court Division in Writ Petition No 2549 of 1998 against order dated 29.6.1998 and 11.8.1998 allowing the application under Order 6 Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the direction therein was as under: 
'The tribunal would ascertain as to whether the bag and materials are intact as to seal etc. and upon ascertaining the same the Tribunal may in presence of the President and Secretary of the Bar Association and the learned Advocates of the parties open the bag containing the election materials and count the ballot papers, both valid and invalid of the respective parties in their presence and record the result of the counting in a sheet duly signed by the Tribunal and shall take signature of the President, Secretary and the learned Advocates for the parties, if they so desired and adjudicate of the matter and shall dispose of the election petition taking into account of the result of the counting of ballot papers." 

8. It appears from Order No. 25 dated 7.3.1999, which reads as under: 
“অদ্য মোকদ্দমাটি পুনঃগণনার জন্য দিন ধারয আছে। প্রর্থীপক্ষ হাজিরা দাখিল করিয়াছে। ১নং প্রতিপক্ষ একখানা দরথাস্ত দ্বারা পুনঃগণনার আদেশ বাতিলের  প্রার্থনা করিয়াছে। দরখাস্ত শ্রবনান্তে না মঞ্জুর (ভি ও পি) ১নং প্রতিপক্ষ অতঃপর একখানা দরখাস্ত দ্বারা এক সময়ের প্রার্থনা করিয়াছে। কপি জারি আছে। দরখাস্ত শ্রবনান্তে নামঞ্জুর (ভি ও পি)। পরবর্তীতে ১নং প্রতিপক্ষ দরখাস্তের বর্ণিত কারনে একসময়ে প্রার্থনা করিয়াছেন। কপি জোর আপত্তিতে জারী আছে। দরখাস্ত শ্রবনান্তে না মঞ্জুর (ভি ও পি)। পরবর্তিতে ১নং প্রতিপক্ষ আনিত গানি ব্যাগগুলি অটুট অবস্থায় আছে কিনা তৎমর্মে রিটাণিং অফিসার ও পিজাইডিং অফিসারকে আদালতে উপস্থিত করার আদেশ করিয়াছেন। কপি জোর আপত্তিতে জেলা আদালতে আপিল করিয়াছেন মর্মে একখানা দরখাস্ত  দাখিল করিয়াছেন। কপি জোর আপত্তিতে জারী আছে। নালিশী ১/৪/৫/৮/৯ নং কেন্দ্রের ভোটগুলি প্রতিপক্ষের বিজ্ঞ আইনজীবী বারের সভাপতি ও সেক্রেটারী এবং প্রতিপক্ষের উপস্থিতিতে ব্যাগগুলি উপস্থাপন করা হলো। ব্যাগগুলি উপস্থাপন করা হইলো। ব্যাগগুলির মধ্যে বান্ডিল গুলোর সিল কতক ঢিলা অবস্থায় আছে এবং কতক সিল শক্ত অবস্খায় আছে। সময়ের ব্যবধানে সিলের গালা্ ঢিলা হইয়া যায়। বলিয়া উপস্থিত বারের বিজ্ঞ সভাপতি ও সেক্রেটারী মত ব্যক্ত করেন। এইরুপ অবস্থায় ব্যাগগুলি অটুট অবস্থায় নাই মর্মে সিদ্ধান্ত নেওয়া কষ্টকর। সমস্ত অবস্থায় লিপিবদ্ধ করিয়া ব্যাগগুলি অটুট অবস্থায় আছে বলিয়া সিদ্ধান্তের  পক্ষে একটু মতামত বেশি। প্রতিপদ  সংশ্লিষ্ট ওয়ার্ডের পিজাইডিং অফিসার তলফ করিয়া ব্যাগ পরিক্ষা করার যে দরখাস্ত করিয়াছেন তাহা আইনের আমল যোগ্য নহে   বরং জটিলতা সুষ্টির কারণ ঘটিবে। তাই প্রতিপক্ষের উক্ত মর্মে দাখিলী দরথাস্ত নামঞ্জুর। মাননীয় জেলা জজ আদলতে প্রতিপক্ষ আপিল দায়ের করিয়াছেন। কিন্তু এই আদালেতের কারয়ক্রম স্থগিতে কোন আদেশ দেন নাই। তাই দরখাস্ত নামঞ্জুর। সঠিক অবস্থা বিবেচনায় ব্যাগগুলি অটুট অবস্থায় আছে। ধরিয়া দিয়া ভোট পুন গণনার আদেশ দেওয়া হইল। বারের বিজ্ঞ সভাপতি, সেক্রেটারী ও প্রার্থী ও প্রতিপক্ষের বিজ্ঞ কৌশলীদের (১০ নং পাতা) সম্মুখ্যে গণনা করা হইল। ১,৪,৫,৮ ও ৯নং ভোট কেন্দ্রের গণনারত ব্যালট বাতিল ব্যালট ১-১৪নং পর্যন্ত প্রদর্শিত হইল। আগাম ১০-৩-৯৯ইং তারিখ রায় ঘোষণা।  
And accordingly the trial court arrived at a finding of fact while considering the issue No. 2 is under: 
"I have examined these (48+52+35+25) 160 double sealed votes. I find that all the seals on the symbol of Umbrella is clear. The ink of the seals on the symbol of Umbrella is deep. But the other seal of the two seals i.e. other than Umbrella is not clear and deep inked. The seals on the symbol of Umbrella appears to have been put by a single hand at a single incidence. But the other seals of the exhibits 4,5,9,12 appear to have been put by a single hand at one incidence that is at one seating. Besides there is difference in shape between the two seals. The seal which goes in favour of the petitioner is some-what curved than that of the seal on the symbol. of Umbrella. Besides the seals on the symbol of Umbrella contain round shape dott marks within the seal. But there are no such dott marks on the seals as claimed by the petitioner. In the admit-ted seals I find these round shaper 't marks. So these double sealed votes were really valid votes of the opposite party No.1 and lawfully counted as valid votes against the symbol of Umbrella. Definitely 160 votes have been tampered by putting another seal though they were legally sealed on the symbol of Umbrella. Because if a person seals twice a single rubber stamp on the same ballot paper there should not be any apparent difference between the two impressions. But all the impressions in Exhibits 4,5,9,12 on the symbol of Umbrella have become one set and the other impression becomes another set. Definitely the another set is created later on. The papers of election result are said to have been signed by the candidates or their election agents. But I did not find any result sheet in the gunny bags. It also lends support of forgery and tempering of the ballot papers of Exhibits 4,5,9,12. So the irresistible conclusion is that it is not true that 160 invalid votes illegally counted as valid votes in favour of contesting opposite party No. 1."

 9. The Election Appellate Tribunal, however, without adverting to the said finding of fact arrived at on consideration of materials on record by the Election Tribunal has held that since the seals in the bags are intact, the ballots contain double seals were found illegally counted in favour of the returned candidate and accordingly set aside the election of the return candidate. The High Court Division as well relying on the reasoning of the Appellate Tribunal, in its turn discharged the Rule. 

10. High Court Division in earlier Writ Petition No. 2549 of 1998 in respect of the selfsame election of the Union Parishad cautioned about the sanctity of the election material and held that on receipt of the election material the Tribunal shall ascertain as to whether the bags and material are intact as to seal etc. and upon ascertaining the same the Tribunal may in presence of the President and Secretary of the Bar Association and the learned Advocates of the parties may open the bag containing the election material and count the ballot papers, both valid and invalid of the respective parties in their presence and record the result of the counting in a sheet duly signed by the Tribunal  " 

11. In the instant case it appears from Order No. 24 dated 1.3.99 that:

“ছলার চটের ব্যাগগুলির উপর একটিও সিল নাই। শুধুমাত্র সিলের চিহ্ন  পাওয়া যায়। শিবচরের থানা সহকারী মৎস্য অফিসার জানান যে, টানা হেচরায় ব্যাগের উপরের সীলগুলা সব সময় ভাংগিয়া যায়।”
It further appears from the Order No. 25 dated 7.3.1999 that: 
“ব্যাগগুলির মধ্যের বান্ডিল গুলির সিল কতক ঢিলা অবস্থায় আছে এবং কতক সিল শক্ত অবস্থায় আছে। সময়ের ব্যবুধানে সিলের গালা ঢিলা হইয়া যায় বলিয়া উপস্থিত বারের বিজ্ঞ সভাপতি ও সেক্রেটারী মত বক্তব্য করেন। এইরুপ অবস্থায় ব্যাগগুলি অটুট অবস্থায় নাই মর্মে সিদ্ধান্ত লওয়া কষ্টকর। তবে সমস্ত অবস্থায় আছে বলিয়া সিদ্ধান্তের পক্ষে মতামত একটু বেশি।”

12. The appellant has consistently alleged before the Court as well as in Paragraph 14 of the revisional application that the President of the Local Bar Association was the engaged lawyer on behalf of the opposite party No. 1. Moreover, the President and Secretary of the Local Bar Association were the party men of the Opposite Party No. 1 and as such, they did not allow the learned Tribunal to take decision that the gunny bags were not intact. Since the Presiding Officer has not been examined so as to depose as to the actual position of the ballot paper found inside the bags containing in the ballots and the seal of the same not being intact, and taking out the ballot papers for counting on the opinion of the President and Secretary of the Bar Association without ascertaining intact-ness of the ballot paper inside the bags, no sanctity could be attached to those ballot papers. Under the circumstances, it can-not be said that the gunny bags were intact unless the bandies in the gunny bags do not contain the seal intact. The Election Tribunal found that the gunny bags containing the ballot papers were not intact and that 160 ballot papers cast in favour of the petitioner were double sealed. Learned Additional District Judge on appeal did not advert to the above reasoning of the Election Tribunal and that the ink of the seal in those 160 ballot papers on umbrella was deep and appeared to have been put by a single hand but proceeded on the premises that the gunny bags containing the ballot papers being intact the Tribunal acted illegally in holding the double sealed ballots as invalid. 

13. The High Court Division as well without adverting to the reasoning of the Election Tribunal which has factual basis discharged the rule abruptly holding that "Under the election rules, a double sealed ballot paper shall have to be treated as invalid. We agree with the learned Additional District Judge that there is no scope for deciding as to whether the double seals were put subsequently and not at the time of casting votes by the respective voters in view of the definite finding of the Election Tribunal that the gunny bags containing the ballot papers were found intact and further that these were no convincing material to hold so." 

14. In the case of Nurul Islam V Munsif of the 4th Court at Sadar, Chittagong and others reported in 28 DLR 375 Mr. Justice Shahabuddin Ahmed as his Lordship then was, held inter alia, that; 
"In the instant case, the Tribunal acted with material irregularity when it proceeded to examine the ballot papers ignoring the broad fact that the gunny bags containing the election papers were tampered with having a number of stitched up holes. Again, when, on discovery of apparently tampered ballot papers, so many in number, examination of the Presiding Officers was indispensably necessary in the interest of justice, he arbitrarily refused to examine them and thereby failed to exercise jurisdiction vested in him. Findings arrived at in these circumstances, cannot claim any sanctity nor can they be immune from interference. When the election was held in a peaceful atmosphere and scrutiny and counting of ballot papers were made in an orderly manner, without any objection from any quarter, reports of the Presiding Officers as to due performance of their duties must be accepted. Otherwise, there will be no sanctity of a free election which is a must for running democratic institutions. The facts and circumstances of the case unerringly show that the questioned ballot papers of the petitioner were tampered with by some malicious hand after their dispatch from the local officers. Subsequent act of tampering with the ballot papers cannot be a ground for undoing the election. To do so would be to give premium to corrupt practices." 

15. Admittedly the election was held in a free, fair and congenial atmosphere and the scrutiny of ballots and counting of votes were done in presence of the parties and their agents. The appellant was declared elected as the chairman of the Union Parishad securing 117 votes more than the election petitioner and there was no allegation as to counting of alleged double votes either at the time of counting or before the Presiding or Returning Officers. The election petitioner for the first time in the election petition has made the allegation of double sealing. Election Tribunal on consideration of the nature of double sealing on the ballot papers (48+52+35+25) totaling 160 double sealed ballot papers of the returned candidate (Appellant) arrived at the finding of fact that the double marks on the 160 ballot papers of the returned candidate were not made by the respective voters while casting votes but the same were subsequently post election act of manipulation created by the interested party. The said finding has not been adverted by the Court of appeal below. Moreover, from the order sheet it appears that the seals of the gunny bags containing ballots were not intact and an application to examine the presiding officer by the returned candidate as to the condition of gunny bags and its seals was rejected and the Tribunal in spite of the infirmities of the seals and gunny bags proceeded to count the ballots at the behest of the President and Secretary of the Bar who belonged to the camp of the election petitioner. Furthermore, no result sheet prepared by the Presiding Officer was found inside the gunny bag. From the above, in the facts and circumstances of the case and relying on the aforesaid decision, no reliance could be put on 160 double sealed ballot papers so as to set at naught the election of the returned candidate. 

16. In view of the above, this appeal is accordingly allowed. The impugned judgment and order of the Election Appellate Tribunal duly affirmed by those of the High Court Division are set aside and the election petition is accordingly dismissed restoring those of the Election Tribunal. 

End.

lawyer:

parties:
Grameen Bank ----- Petitioner
Versus
Md. Humayun Kabir & Others ----- opposite parties
full_judgment:
Mr. Syed Mahmud Hossain, J : This Rule at the instance of defendant-petitioner is directed against the order dated 15.10.97 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Islampur, District Jamalpur, in other Class Suit No. 34 of 1997 rejecting an application of the defendant-petitioner filed under Order VII Rule 11 read with Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

2. The Opposite Party as plaintiff instituted Other Class Suit No. 34 of 1997 in the court of Assistant Judge, Islampur. Jamalpur for declaration that the order of dismissal from service by his employer, Grameen Bank, under the signature of the defendant-petitioner was illegal collusive void and not binding upon the plaintiff, impleading the petitioner and others as defendants stating, inter alia, that he joined service of Grameen Bank as an employee in its Head Office on 29.7.1989. Thereafter he was posted to different stations in Grameen Bank branches and eventually he was posted in Kandua branch. While he was working as U.D. Assistant, he was issued with an order of dismissal from service on 1.2.97 on prior issuance of charge sheet on some charges. After obtaining explanation on the same and holding a so-called inquiry the petitioner was illegally, dismissed on false and baseless charge. No proper enquiry was held. With the averments made above the suit was filed. 

3. The defendant-petitioner having entered appearance in the said suit filed an application under Order VII Rae 11 read with Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of plaint stating, inter alia, that the suit was barred by law in as much as an Administrative Tribunal set up under the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 (hereinafter referred to as the Act) had exclusive statutory jurisdiction over the matter in issue relating to dis-missal of the plaintiff opposite party. And moreover the learned court below had no jurisdiction to try the suit. 

4. The learned Assistant Judge after hearing the parties rejected the application by the impugned order dated 15.10.1997. 

5. Mr. Abdur Razzaque Khan, learned Advocate appearing for the defendant petitioner, submits that a service matter relating to dismissal from service of an employee of Grameen Bank, a Statutory Public Authority within the meaning of Section (2aa) of the Act, and a scheduled Bank under the said Act is exclusively made tri-able by the Administrative Tribunal and as such the plaint is liable to be rejected. Section 4 of the Act, he further submits, expressly provides for exclusive jurisdiction of the Administrative Tribunal to try such case excluding the jurisdiction of Civil Court. He lastly, submits that Article 117 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh provides exclusive jurisdiction on the Administrative Tribunal in respect of matters relating to or arising out of the terms and conditions of service and as such the learned Assistant Judge ought to have rejected the plaint. 

6. Mr. S. M. Zillul Hoque, learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff opposite party. on the other hand, submits that the plaintiff opposite party will be subjected to suffer irreparable loss and injury for no fault of him and in fact the time lost for determination of the question of maintain-ability of the suit in the court of the Assistant Judge will restrain the plaintiff-opposite party from seeking appropriate relief against the illegal dismissal order by instituting a case in proper forum. He submits that the rule may be disposed of by an order which will provide efficacious remedy to the plaintiff-opposite party. 

7. Heard the learned Advocates for both the sides, perused the revisional application and - impugned order. It appears from the impugned order that the learned Assistant edge by giving an elaborate finding held that the suit was maintainable before the Civil Court. He relied upon numerous cases, such as The Province of East Bengal Vs. Dewan Abdul Alim Mutwally, 9 DLR-26; Soleman Bibi and another Vs. Administrator. Farajikandi Complex and Ors. 45 DLR-727; Chief Engineer, Roads & Highways Department Vs. Concord Engineers Construction Ltd. 48 DLR-243: Burma Eastern Ltd. Vs. Burma Eastern Employees Union and others 18 DLR-709; A.K.M. Hedayetul Islam Vs. Executive Vice-Chairman, Bangladesh Agricultural Research Council and others, 43 DLR-44; Shudhansu Kumar Barai and others Vs. Abdul Hashem and others, 43 DLR-327; Deputy Secretary: Ministry of Commerce Vs. Nizamuddin Haider- r1LR-103. 

8. The learned Assistant Judge in the impugned order referred to Section 32 of the Grameen Bank Ordinance which is as follows: "No court shall take cognizance of any offence punishable under this Ordinance except upon a complaint in writing by an officer of the Bank authorised in this behalf by the Board." Taking into consideration this section the learned Assistant Judge came to the finding that the jurisdiction of the Civil Court was not expressly barred.

9. The learned Assistant Judge failed to take notice that Grameen Bank was included in the schedule of the Act and to appreciate Section 4 of the Act which is as follows: "4. Jurisdiction of Administrative Tribunals- (1) An Administrative Tribunal shall have exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine applications made by any person in the service of the republic [or of any statutory public authority] in respect of the terms and conditions of his service including pension rights, or in respect of any action taken in relation to him as a person in the service of the republic for of any statutory public authority]." (emphasis supplied). 

10. The learned Advocate for the petitioner referred to a decision in the case of the Managing Director, Rupali Bank Vs. Tafazal Hossain reported in 44 DLR (AD) 260. The relevant portion of the decision in paragraphs 4 and 5 of the said reported case is as follows : "4. The Administrative Tribunals Act, 1980 was made by the Parliament under Article 117 of the Constitution to provide for establishment of Administrative Tribunals to exercise jurisdiction on matters relating to terms and conditions of service of per-sons "in the service of the Republic Qr any statutory authority     Section 4(1) of this Act confers exclusive jurisdiction upon the Administrative Tribunal on certain matters   "5. "Statutory public authority", as defined in Section 2(aa) of the Act. means an authority, corporation or body specified in the Schedule to this Act. The Schedule included, among others. Rupali Bank. This Schedule was brought in by the Administrative Tribunals (Amendment) Ordinance, 1984- Ordinance No. LX of 1984 with effect from 25 September 1984. It is clear that in respect of terms and conditions of service of any person of the Rupali Bank, which is a statutory authority, the Administrative Tribunal got exclusive jurisdiction and that no other court or tribunal shall exercise jurisdiction on such matters. The Civil Court's jurisdiction thus stands totally ousted." 

11. Grameen Bank is also a statutory body within the meaning of Section 2(aa) of the Act and included in the schedule of the Act. From Section 4 of the Act, as well as the decision of the Appellate Division referred to above, it is manifestly clear that the suit filed by the plaintiff-opposite party against his dismissal from service is not maintainable before the Civil Court, being barred by law. Moreover, the Act is a special law. If any legal remedy is ordinarily available under both general law and special law, the remedy prescribed by the special law must be sought to the exclusion of the remedy otherwise available under the general law. 

12. The decisions of the High Court Division referred to and relied upon by the learned Assistant Judge are of no avail as the jurisdiction of Civil Court to try such suits has already been decided by the Appellate Division in 44 DLR (AD)-260 already referred to above. So, the learned Assistant Judge committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of jus-tice in holding that the suit is maintain-able in Civil Court. 

13. The learned Advocate for the plain-tiff-opposite party submits that the learned Assistant Judge committed error of law in holding that the suit was maintainable before him but it was the duty of the learned Assistant Judge to direct the plaintiff-opposite party to file his case in appropriate forum. 

14. With regard to the submission of the learned Advocate for the opposite party it is necessary to mention that the plaintiff of his own accord filed the suit in Civil Court and resisted the application filed under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The learned Advocate for the plaintiff even after filing of the application for rejection of plaint did not file any application for withdrawal of the suit for seeking relief before the appropriate forum. 

15. The learned Advocate for the plain-tiff-opposite party submits that this court can also pass an appropriate order by giving opportunity to the plaintiff-opposite party to seek relief before the appropriate Court. This submission is misconceived because this Court cannot pass any order which may contravene any of the provision of law. Now the plaintiff-opposite party must suffer the consequences. 

16. For the reasons stated herein-above, I find that the suit is not maintain-able before the Civil Court as the same is barred by law in view of Section 4 of the Act and also as per the decision reported in 44 DLR(AD)260 referred to above. Therefore the impugned order calls for interference by this Court in exercise of its revisional power. 

17. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The impugned order dated 15.10.1997 is set aside and the plaint of Other Class Suit No. 34 of 1997 of the Court of Assistant Judge, Islampur Jamalpur is rejected. The circumstances are such that the parties may appropriately be directed to bear their respective costs. This Court directs accordingly. 

18. Let a copy of the judgment be communicated to the learned Assistant Judge concerned. 

End.

lawyer:
