parties:
Md. Habibur Rahman & others ------ Petitioners.
Versus
M.A. Rashid & others ------ Opposite parties.
full_judgment:
Mr. Md. Abdur Rashid. J: This Rule was obtained by the defendant Nos. 1-5 upon making an application under Section 115 of the Code of the Civil Procedure against judgment and order dated 13.03.97 passed by Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Jamalpur in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 10 of 1996 affirming those dated 02.01.96 passed by Senior Assistant Judge at Sadar, Jamalpur in Miscellaneous Case No. 19 of 1994.

2. Opposite Parties Nos. 1-5 as plaintiff instituted Other Class Suit No. 124 of 1986 for perpetual injunction for restraining the said defendants from entering into the suit land measuring 1.38 acre. The suit was decreed ex parte on 29.07.93. The decree was drawn and signed on 01.08.93.

3. The petitioners who are defendants in the suit made an application under Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex parte decree and also restoration of the suit to its file and number arid Miscellaneous Case No. 19 of 1994 was thereupon registered.

4. The case of the defendants in short, is that after the filing of the suit said opposite parties made an application for temporary injunction for restraining the defendants from entering into the suit land Pursuant to the notice of the said application, the petitioners appeared and filed a written objection to the prayer for temporary injunction. Learned Assistant Judge however granted the injunctions. Against the said order of injunction, petitioners preferred an appeal being Miscellaneous Appeal No. 99 of 1986 in the Court of District Judge at Jamalpur. One of the defendants Abdul Malek who used to look after the appeal died on 12.10.1990. On his death, the appeal was dismissed for default for not taking steps in the appeal.

5. After disposal of the appeal, the records of the case was sent clown to the lower court and the lower court on 13.06.93 received the records and fixed 07.07.93 for filing of written statement. On 05.07.93 the learned Advocate of the petitioner appears to have seen the said order but he did not inform the defendants of the arrival of the records and the date fixed for filing written statement. On 07.07.93 the suit was posted for ex parte disposal on 21.07.93. On 21.07.93 the plaintiff got their plaint amended without serving any notice on them. On 21.07.93 the suit was again fixed for ex part disposal on 29.07.93 and on that date, the son was taken up and was decreed ex parte behind the back of the petitioners.

6. On 07.05.94 plaintiffs went to take possession of the suit land being armed with ex parte decree and then the petitioner obtained the certified copy of the order the petitioners became sure that the Suit was decreed ex parte. The defendants on 11.05.94 made the aforesaid application duly supported by an affidavit.

7. Opposite Party No. 5(A) was added as a party in the suit. This opposite party No. 5(A) Only opposed the case of the defendants by filing a written statement oil 16.04.96. His case is that on 11.05.92 her purchased 26 decimals of land out of the stiff land from opposite party No. 1. He also purchased some more lands by other deeds. His case in brief is that after of the record from the appellate court the suit was fixed for filing the written statement on 07.07.93 and the order dated 13.06.93 was shown to the learned Advocate of the defendants. He also that the petitioners had knowledge of the dates but preferred not to appear in the trial of the suit and accordingly the was decreed ex parte.

8. On the said pleadings, defendants examined 2 witnesses while said opposite party No. 5(A) examined himself alone as O.P.W.1.

9. The trial court rejected the application. On appeal the appellate court, also dismissed the appeal and confirmed the decision of the trial court.

10. Mr. Sultan Ahmed the learned Counsel appearing for the Rule, submits that both the courts below failed to consider the case of the petitioner that they had no knowledge about the proceedings of the suit, particularly the date fixed for pre-emptory hearing as their learned Advocate though was shown the order dated 13.06.93 on 05.07.93 but did not inform. And in the absence of any notice or information petitioners had no knowledge and both the courts below acted illegally in rejecting their application.

11. He cited in support of his submission, the cases reported in 44 DLR(AD) 30, 14 DLR(AD) 58, 17 DLR(SC) 487, 16 DLR (SC) 155 and 36 DLR (AD) at page 8 and 88.

12. The learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party No. 5(A) submits that both the courts below found that the petitioner failed to prove their date of knowledge as was stated in their application under Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure and there was no application filed for condonation of delay under Section 5 of the Limitation Act. The suit was decreed on 29.07.93 and application was made only on 11.05.94. In the absence of any application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act the case was correctly found barred by limitation by both courts. Such order of affirmance, does not call for any interference.

13. I have perused both orders passed by the courts below application under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the application under Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, written objection and depositions of P.Ws. 1 and 2 and O.P.W. 1.

<u>14. It appears that after disposal of the Miscellaneous Appeal No. 39 of 1986, the record was received by the Assistant Judge on 13.06.93. On trial date 07.07.93 was fixed for filing of written statement. That order was seen by the learned Advocate for the petitioners on 05.07.93. It is the ease of petitioners that the learned Advocate did not inform them either the date for filing written statements or the date fixed for ex party’s disposal of the suit. It also appears that on 07.07.03 the suit was for the first time fixed for ex parte disposal on 21.07.93. No on 21.07.93 the plaintiff got their plaint amended. On that day, suit was however posted for disposal ex pane on 29.07.93. It is not disputed that no copy of the application for amendment of the plaint was served on the petitioner or on their learned Advocate. When a plaint is amended the suit is generally to be taken out front the list of pre-emptory hearing in order to enable the defendants to file an additional written statement if any they want his this case within 8 days of amendment of the plaint of amendment of the plaint the snit was again posted for ex parte disposal. This hurried action of the trial court to dispose the suit without presence of the petitioners does not appear to be bonafide.</u>

<u>15. Under Order 9 Rule 13 of the code when suit is decreed ex parte the defendant may apply to the court by which he decree was passed for an order to set aside the decree it the court is satisfied either summons was not served or that the defendants were prevented by sufficient cause from appearing when the suit was called on for hearing.</u>

16. In this case pursuant to the notice of the temporary injunction the petitioners appeared and filed objection. The case or petitioners is that one of the defendants, Malek issued to look after the case as tadbirker and he died on 12.10.90. On his death no step could be taken and the appeal was dismissed for default. After arrival of the record to the trial court from the appellate Court the learned Advocate through on 05.07.93 saw the order passed on 13.06.93 but did not inform the defendants and so the defendants could not know about the progress of the suit and be present when the suit was fixed for ex parte disposal.

17. I find that the trial order considered the evidence of P.W 1 who slated that his brother Abdul Malek used to look after the case. But the court took the view that Abdul Malek was not examined as a witness in the case. But this finding is fully misconceived as the whole case of the petitioner is based on the fact that Abdul Malek died on 12.10.90. Appellate Court in considering the evidence of P.Ws. came to a finding that Habibur Rahman used to look after the case on behalf of the petitioners. It also disbelieved the story of the petitioner that the opposite parties went on 07.05.94 to the suit land for taking possession as the suit was for perpetual injunction and there could not be any reason for than to go to take possession of the suit land.

<u>18. In the case of Keramat Ali Bhuivan V Ramizuddin Ahmed. (1991) 43 DLR (AD) 58, an application under Order 9 Rule 9 of the Code for restoration of the suit on the ground that the record of the suit was sent to this Division in connection with a first appeal sometime in 1976 and upon its receipt back no notice was given to either to the plaintiff or his learned Advocate and thus the plaintiff was prevented from appearing in court when the suit was called on for hearing on 03.01.78. The application was resisted on ground of limitation as no application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act was filed for condonation of delay. The trial court allowed the application and restored the suit to its file and number but subject to payment of Taka 300. The order was upheld in revision by this Division. Dismissing the petition for leave to appeal the Appellate Division held that when the direction of the court to inform the learned Advocate of the parties about the receiving of the record from this Division was not complied with and thus. the court had inherent jurisdiction to restore suit under due to any Section 151 of the Code. It was also observed that when an injury is caused to a party due to any mistake or default committed by a court or its officers there are high authorities laying down that in circumstances of this nature, it is not only right and the duty of the court to correct its own mistake.</u>

19. In the case of M.A. Wahab and another V. Abul Kalam and another (1992) 44 DLR(AD) 13 the suit was transferred from the dearth court of Subordinate Judge at Dhaka to the second court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka in implementation of a gazette notification by the fourth court's order dated 28.01.85, which was an off-day for pleader commissioner's report. The second court received the case record on 29.01.84 and fixed 12.03.85 for report of the pleader commissioner and added "inform". This Division found that the defendant never appeared in the new court thereafter and the second court's order never shown to the defendant's Advocate. So the appeal presented by the defendant against judgment and (inter of the trial court rejecting his application under Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code for restoration of the suit after setting aside the ex parte decree was allowed subject to payment of Taka 3000 to the plaintiff by this Division on the ground of non-compliance of Rule 388(2) of the Civil Rides and Orders (Vol-1) in dismissing the petition for leave to appeal, the Appellate Division held that

An order of time court affecting one of the pillers of the suit, namely, place of trial, cannot be meant for communication to the pleader commissioner only. It was not communicated and the course of the suit took an adverse turn to the prejudice of the defendant behind his back and without his knowledge the suit was rightly restored by this Division on terms."

<u>20. In this case, the record of the case was received by the trial court on 13.06.93 and the court on that date fixed 07.07.93 for filing of written statement. On 05.07.93 the learned Advocate of the petitioners was shown the order dated 13.06.93. It is the positive case of the petitioners that the learned Advocate did not inform the petitioners of the receipt of the record or the date fixed for filing of written statement. It is also true that the date of knowledge r on 07.05.94 as alleged by the petitioners was not believed by the courts below. But the assertion of the petitioners that their Advocate did not inform them, it appears, did not receive any consideration by either of the courts below. Moreover, on 07.07.93 the suit was fixed for ex parte disposal on 21.07.93. But on this date, the opposite parties No. 1 to 5 as plaintiffs did not get the suit heard ex parte instead made an application for amendment of their plaint without, serving any notice upon the petitioners or their Advocate. The trial court allowed the application for amendment as prayed for and fixed 29.07.93 just after 8 days, again for ex parte disposal. The petitioners no doubt had a right to a prior notice of hearing of such application for amendment and further right to a date for filing a written statement against such amendment. It is also not disputed that the orders dated 07.07.93 and 21.07.93 were not even shown to the Advocate of the petitioners. The procedure adopted by the trial court is therefore not sanctioned by law.</u>

21. Under Order 9 Rule 13 of the code if the applicant satisfies the court that the summons was not duly served or that he was prevented by any sufficient cause from appearing when the suit was called no for hearing the court shall make order setting aside the decree as it against him upon such terms as to costs, as it thinks fit.

<u>22. In the circumstances of the case, I find that the trial court passed the orders dated 21.07.93 and 29.07.93 behind the back of the petitioners and as a result, when the suit was called on for hearing I he petitioners could not appear as they were not aware of any of the dates. The court of appeal below also missed such vital aspect of the ease. Secondly, when it the duty of a min not to pass any order behind the back of a party which would adversely affect such party and the court is also obliged to correct its own default, if any, by invoking its inherent jurisdiction its was held in the case of Keramat Ali Bhuiyan V Ramizuddin Ahmed. (1991)) 43 DLR (AD) 58, both the courts below erred in law in holding, that the delay in making Application under Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code could not be condoned in the absence of an application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act.</u>

23. For the reasons slated above the court (If appeal below committed an error of law in in dismissing appeal resulting in an error in its decision which has definitely occasioned failure of justice. The application under Order 9 Rule 13 of the order for setting aside the ex parte decree dated 29.07.93 in Title Suit No. 124 of 1986 is therefore liable to be allowed but subject to payment of Taka 5,000.00 only of the opposite parties.

In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The judgment and order of the appellate court affirming those of the trial court are set aside. Other Class Suit 124 of 1986 is accordingly restored to its tile and number subject to deposit of Taka 5,000.00 (five thousand) only in court within two months from the date of receipt of this order by the trial court and the trial court is directed to proceed with the suit from the stage as it was on 07.07.93. If the petitioners- defendants failed to deposit said amount of Taka 5,000.00 (five thousand) only in court in time, the Rule shall stand discharged and this order revoked. After deposit of Taka 5.000.00 (five thousand) only, the plain-tiff-opposite parties would be at liberty to withdraw the amount. The order of stay granted at the time of issue of the above Rule is hereby vacated.

24. Communicate this order to the Senior Assistant Judge at Sadar, Jamalpur at once.

End.

lawyer:
Mr. Abdur Razzaq, Advocate -- for petitioner
Mr. Asad Ullah, Advocate -- for respondents
parties:
Mrs. Tamanna-e-Jahan ----- Petitioner
Versus
The Paper Converting and Packaging Ltd. and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Mr. Justice Bijan Kumar Das, J: This is an application filed under section 241(v) of the Companies Act, 1994 for winding up of Paper Converting and Packaging Ltd. 

2. The case of the petitioner Mrs. Tamanna-e-Jahan, in short, is that she is the Publisher of a Magazine named "Monthly Fulkuri" of 290/1, Free School Street, Sonargaon Road. Dhaka and the respondent No. 1 is a Limited Liability Company registered in Bangladesh under the Companies Act and the company is involved in the business or publishing, printing and packaging. The respondent No. 2 was the Managing Director of the Company at the relevant time in 1991 when the petitioner gave the company a loan of Tk. 2 Lacs. The said respondent No. 2 is the Director of the Company now and very much involved with the subject matter of the application. On 12.10.1991 the petitioner invested/gave a loan of Tk. 2,00,000.00 to the company for a maxi-mum period of 2 years and this investment/loan was authorized by the Board of Directors of the Company which was meant to meet financial requirements of the Company which was in dire need of cash at that time. It was agreed upon between the parties that the profit of investment/loan including that the principal amount would be refunded within 30 September 1993 or on demand by the petitioner, and so long as the principal amount is not fully paid, the Company would publish "Phulkuri" free of cost. It was also agreed upon between the parties that in case of default the company "shall pay a compensation of Tk. 500/- for each day till repayment of the loan in full in addition to Mrs. Tamanna-e-Jahan's right to claim on company's assets. "A deed of undertaking dated 12.10.1991 was executed by the then Managing Director of the Company Mr. Lutfur Rahman, now respondent No. 2 and the Company from the very beginning defaulted in printing "Phulkuri" in time and thereby caused loss to the petitioner. The petitioner was there-fore compelled to buy printing materials, namely, tracing paper, toner, cartridge, plate, film, in and other chemicals to get "Phulkuri" printed in time which was a breach of undertaking on the Company's part. Subsequently by a negotiation the petitioner and the respondent-company agreed that "for the purpose of clear accounts the respondent-company will charge printing cost of the "Phulkuri" and as the profit of Tk. 2 lacs it will pay the petitioner a monthly amount of Tk. 8,000.00 at the rate of Tk. 4%. The company printed certain issues of Phulkuri but after a few months it became irregular in printing Phulkuri. The company for example printed the monthly Phulkuri 15/20 days later then the specified date and delivered lesser number then the pre-scribed number and as a result Phulkuri lost its subscribers and incurred huge loss and the petitioner printed 24 issues of Phulkuri from other press. The petitioner due to such breach of contract, that is. failure to print Phulkuri asked the respondents to pay back the loan with profit but without any result. Thereafter on 1.12.1992 Mr. Sanaullah Nuri, an adviser of the Phulkuri wrote a letter to the Managing Director of the Company requesting him to return Tk. 2 lacks to the petitioner but the company turned a deaf ear to such a request. Thereafter on sever-al occasions the petitioner asked the Company to repay the money but without any result. Subsequently having been pressed by the petitioner the company again started to print "Phulkuri" from December, 1994 and continued the printing till December 1995 and since December 1995 the company printed not a single issue. The company thus printed Phulkuri worth Tk. 1,67,850.00 and till this time the petitioner's profit for that period comes to Tk. 1,68,000.00 which was adjusted with each other. A statement of account for that period which was pre-pared by the company on 16.8.1993 was supplied. Thereafter by a letter dated 15.10.1995 the petitioner asked the Company to repay her debt with profit but without any result. Then on 29.9.1999 the petitioners served a lawyer notice upon the Company under Section 242 of the Companies Act, asking it to repay its debt of Tk. 13,11,000.00' including the principal amount of Tk. 2,00,000/- and compensation of Tk. 500/- for each day was claimed on the basis of the deed of under-taking dated 12.10.1991 failing which winding up proceedings were threatened. The Secretary of the respondent Company sent reply on 16.10.1999 informing the petitioner's lawyer that the management of Paper Converting and Packaging Ltd. has been changed and the papers relating to the petitioner's matter could not be located and asked the petitioner's lawyer to send a statement with relevant papers so that they could settle the matter and accordingly on 9.11.1999 the petitioner's lawyer sent all the relevant papers and documents to the company asking to settle the claim within 15 days but in spite of such letter and documents the petitioner received no reply. On 19.7.2000 the company sent a letter to the petitioner's lawyers admitting the fact of its execution of the deed of undertaking but contending that the said undertaking is merely a piece of paper which was never acted upon and it was further contended that there was difference between the petitioner's representation and her lawyer's legal notice regarding the claim. Then on 12.8.2000 the petitioner's lawyer submitted a revised claim of Tk. 6,99,239.97 and demanded payment to be made within 7 days failing which winding up proceedings were threatened. While the petitioner was waiting for the payment of her debt, the company by a letter dated 23.8.2000 informed her lawyer about Title Suit No. 109 of 2000 filed by the Company in the Court of Sub. Judge, Third Court, Dhaka against the petitioner for declaration that the deed of undertaking dated 12.10.1992 executed by the Company is ineffective, illegal and not binding upon the company. The said Title Suit No. 109 of 2000 was filed on 27.7.2000. It is stated that this petition is based on a genuine bonafide cause of action and has been filed to protect the interest of the petitioner as well as other creditors and the petitioner has come to know from reliable sources that the company is heavily indebted to other creditors and unless the company is immediately wound up, the petitioner and the other creditors will suffer irreparable loss in as much as they will not be in a position to recover their dues and debts. The petitioner also asserted that she learned that the present management of the company has been directing profits for their own personal use and enjoyment instead of paying the company's debts and liabilities and the company has been trying to delay/avoid payment of liabilities from the very beginning and has willfully deceived the petitioner who acted in good faith. It is further alleged that the company is liable to be wound up as it has neglected to pay its debt and that the petitioner's claim is much higher than the statutory sum and a statutory demand has been made more than once and the Company has failed to repay its debt. The petitioner alleged that she has a prima facie case under section 241 and 242 of the Companies Act and in the interest of justice she is entitled to an order of winding up of the company from this court on the ground that the Company is unable to pay its debts and also on the just and just and equitable grounds. 2. This application for winding up of the Company was filed on 1.11.2000 when necessary notices were issued and the matter was ultimately admitted on 19.4.2001 for hearing. 

3. The respondent Company entered appearance and filed an application for summary rejection of winding up application and stay of all further proceedings till the question of debt is decided by the petitioner though process of the competent Civil Court and upon hearing the parties the application for staying the further proceedings was rejected on 18.11.2001.

4. The respondent Nos. 1 and 2 jointly tiled an affidavit-in-opposition denying all the allegations made in the application for winding up of the Company and asserted that the petitioner did not give any loan of Tk. 2,00,000.00 on 19.10.1991 to the Company but paid the amount as advance cost of printing of "Phulkuri " and it was categorically asserted that amount of Tk. 2,00,000.00 taken from the petitioner was not loan or investment but was an advance amount against printing of Magazine Phulkuri . It is also stated that the deed of undertaking dated 12.10.1991 was a paper transaction and was never acted upon. It was further asserted that the petitioner did not deliver the manuscript and other printing materials in time to the respondent company and consequently delay took place in printing Phulkuri which was not a fault of the Company. It was also asserted that if the respondent company defaulted in printing the Magazine "Phulkuri" and if there was a breach of the agreement, legal remedy was available to the petitioner to file a suit for damage against the respondent company but the petitioner can not apply for winding up of the company for the alleged breach. The respondent Company alleged that there was no subsequent negotiation with the petitioner and the respondent Company regarding payment of monthly profit at the rate of 4% or at any rate on the alleged Tk. 2,00,000.00 and that the said amount of Tk. 2,00,000.00 was voluntarily paid by the petitioner to the respondent Company as advance for printing cost of Phulkuri which after adjustment with the bill against printing the Magaine Phulkuri the petitioner is entitled to a sum of Tk. 1,92,816.03 paisa from the petitioner as balance amount of the printing bill. The respondent categorically asserted that the claim as made in the application for winding up of the company involved a bonafide dispute and the remedy available to the petitioner is in a proper forum by an appropriate legal proceeding and not in the winding up proceeding. It is further stated that the printing cost of the Phulkuri up to July, 1993 stood at Tk. 1.67,850 and the printing bill from August, 1993 to October, 1994 stood at Tk. 1,32,341.03 and from December. 1994 to December. 1995 the printing bill of the respondent Company comes to Tk. 92,625.00 and the total printing bill of the respondent company comes to Taka 3,92,816.03. Accordingly the respondent Company asserted that the petitioner did not pay the balance printing bill of the respondent company amounting to Tk. 1,92,816.03 paisa. The respondent Company further alleged that the Company is a Public Limited Company and sharers of the Company are held by the financial institutions and public in general and that the intention of the petitioner is not bonafide and there is no cause of action to file the application for winding up of the company and the application has been filed with malafide intention for causing loss and damage in terms of money and reputation and good will of the respondent company and with ulterior motive of avoiding payment of balance of the printing bill amounting to Tk. 1,92,816.03. The respondent No. 1 is a Public Limited Company having paid up capital of Taka 2,67.80,000.00 and the management of the respondent Company is vested in the Board of Directors and the Chairman of the respondent Company is a representative of Investment Corporation of Bangladesh along with another Director from Investment Corporation of Bangladesh and (ICB) one Director is a representative of Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Shangstha and 4 other Directors are from public share holders and the company is financially solvent enough to meet its any debts. The respondent further alleged that the claim of the petitioner is based of no evidence and the same being malafide the application for winding up is liable to be rejected and the alleged debt shall be decided in Title Suit No. 109 of 2000 which is pending in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Third Court, Dhaka. 

5. The petitioner has filed an affidavit in reply to-day where she reinstated the facts stated in the winding up petition. The application has been filed at the time of delivery of judgment.

6. Mr. Abdur Razzak, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner has invited my attention to the deed of under-taking Annexure A by the Managing Director Mr. Lutfor Rahman on 12.10.1991. Mr. Razzaq submits that the deed of undertaking clearly shows that an amount of Tk. 2,00,000.00 was received as loan by the Company on 12.12.1991 and the Company was to print "Mashik Fulkuri" free of cost but the Company having failed to do the same is liable to repay the debt to the petitioner. Mr. Razzaq also invited my attention to annexure B, a letter written by one Sanaullah Nuri which shows that the petitioner is entitled to Tk. 70,000/- towards advertisement cost published in Phulkuri and the Company is also entitled to about Tk. 70,000/-towards advertisement cost published in Phulkuri and the Company is also entitled to about Tk. 70,000/- towards its bill for printing the Magazine Phulkuri and this should be abducted between the par-ties. In the said letter it has been stated that the petitioner gave load Tk. 2,00,000.00 to the Company with some condition and that the Company should repay the said amount of Tk. 2.00,000.00 without delay so that the management of Phulkuri may arrange printing of the Magazine from other press. Annexure C is a statement of accounts. Annexure 1) is again a letter from the petitioner dated 15.10.1995, asking the respondent Company to repay Tk. 4.15.730.20 paisa within 30th June, 1996. Annexure D I is another letter from the petitioner to the Managing Director of the company dated 24.5.1997 asking the Company to pay Tk. 5,27,730.20 paisa. Annexure E is a notice dated 29.9.1999 under section 241(v) of the Companies Act, 1994 asking the Company to pay her debt of Tk. 13,11,000.00 within 3 weeks. Annexure F is again a letter dated 16.10.1999 from the Secretary in charge of the Company to the petitioner's lawyer informing that the management of the company has been changed and they need the papers to settle the matter with the petitioner. Annexure G is again a notice dated 9.11.1999 under section 241(V) of the Companies Act asking the petitioner to settle their claim of Tk. 13.11.000.00 within next 15 days failing which winding up proceeding was threatened. Annexure H dated 22.6.2000 is another notice under section 241(V) of the Companies Act asking the Company to settle up the claim of Tk. 13,11,000.00 within 15 days in default winding up proceeding was threatened. Annexure I is a letter dated 19.7.2000 from Mr. Lutfor Rahman of the Com;.2.9;- to the petitioner informing that that alleged deed of undertaking dated 12 10.1991 was a more paper transaction and it was never acted upon and that the Advance of Tk. 2,00,000.00 was not a loaning it was ever settled that Tk. 8,000/- would be deposited against the loan of Tk.2,00,000.00 every month in the petitioner's account. Annexure J is again a lawyer notice dated 12.8.2000 under section 241(V) of the Companies Act 1994 informing that after adjustment of the company's bills of Tk. 2,24,966.03 paisa the Company owe to the petitioner an amount of Tk. 6,99.239.97 paisa and this amount should be paid within 7 days failing which an application for winding up of the company shall be filed. Annexure K is a letter from Lutfor Rahman of the Company to the lawyer of the petitioner intimating about the institution of Title Suit. No. 109 of 2000 and asking to a rescind the notice till the decision is given in the said suit. Annexure K1 is a copy of the plaint of Title Suit No. 109 of 2000. These are all the papers filed by the petitioner an Annexure. 

7. The first question needs consideration is whether payment of Tk. 2,00,000.00 by the petitioner to the Company was loan/investment as alleged by the petitioner or an advance for printing the Magazine "Phulkuri " as alleged by the respondent Company. It is not the petitioner's case that the petitioner is a money lender or a financial institution. In the Annexure the petitioner claimed that she had paid Tk. 2,00,000.00 as loan to the company. The respondent Company alleged that the said amount of Tk. 2,00,000.00 was an advance dispute thus is involved as to whether the said amount of Tk. 2,00,000 was given to the company as loan or was an advance for printing the Magazine Phulkuri. On a perusal of the Annexures filed by the petitioner it appears that the petitioner claimed that she paid Tk. 2,00,000.00 to the Company as loan as the company was in need of cash at the relevant time and the said amount was to be repaid within a period of 2 years from the date of the signing of undertaking. The question needs consideration as to whether the petitioner not being a money lender or a financial institution is permitted to grant loan to the company and the company is permitted to accept such loan. The petitioners not being a money lender or a financial institution is not legally permitted to pay loan to any one for deriving interest. On the other hand, the respondent being a company and not a financial institution is also not legally permitted to take any loan and pay interest to any private individual. This view is supported in the case of A.K.M. Abdul Latif Versus M/S. Banani Metal Limited reported in 1999 BLT 258 where it has been held 'The respondent Company not being financial institution cannot take money as loan and give interest. Under Company Law if money is required by the Company it may take it by way of issuing debenture and pay interest etc. The company cannot make payment either by way of interest of otherwise unless sanctioned by law. "Paragraph 6 of Annexure J. runs as follows: 'That from August 1993 to October 1994 your bills for printing Phulkuri comes to Tk. 1,32,341.03, and from December 1994 to December 1995 your bills come to Tk. 92,625.00, making a total of Tk. 2,24,966.03." Paragraph No. 7 of the said Annexure J shows "After adjusting your bill of Tk. 2,24.966.93 you owe to Mrs. Jahan Tk. 6,99,23.97 the details of which is given below : Principal money borrowed by you .... Tk. 2.00.000.00 Profit against the Principal (84 months X 8,000) .... Tk. 6,72,000.00 Cash money paid for printing Phulkuri Tk. 52.206.00  Total amount of Tk. 9,24.206.00 f-I Loss your bill in printing Phulkuri Tk. 2.24.966,03 Balance Taka 6.99,239.97 Since the petitioner is not a money lender or a financial institution she is not permitted to charge any interest or profit on the amount of Tk. 2,00,000.00 and the respondent Company is not legally permit-ted to accept any loan and to pay any interest. Again in Annexure D the petitioner claims Tk. 4,15.730.20 paisa as debt from the respondent and from Annexure D l it appears that the petitioner claimed Tk. 5,27,730.20 as debt from the Company. Annexure E shows an amount of Tk. 13,11,000.00 realisable from the respondent Company as debt. Annexure G shows that the petitioner claimed Tk. 13.11,000.00 as debt from the respondent Company. Annexure H shows the said amount of Tk. 13,11,000.00 as debt and directed to pay the amount within 15 days. Annexure J shows that the petitioner claimed Tk. 6,99,239.97 as debt from the respondent company. In view of the aforesaid annexure it appears a bonafide dispute is involved with regard to the amount of debt and also with regard to the nature of payment of Tk. 2,00,000.00 as to whether the said payment was loan to the company as alleged by the petitioner or an advance made for printing Phulkuri as alleged by the respondent company. On a consideration of the aforesaid materials supplied by the petitioner I am of the view that their exist a bonafide dispute relating to the existence of the debt and the amount of debt and to determine the same winding up proceeding is not available to the petitioner.

8. Mr. Razzaq, the learned Advocate for the petitioner in support of his sub-mission relied on a decision in the case of Agrani Bank versus Bangladesh Tyres Ltd. and reported in 43 DLR (AD) 164. In the said decision their lordships held "The learned Company Judge after hearing the parties and considering the affidavits and counter-affidavits filed in the cases, hold that no prima facie case was made out for winding up of the companies and consequently disposal of the applications for summary rejection of the winding up petitioners and stayed all further proceedings sine die. 'This was not the case here. The learned Advocate also relied on a decision in the case of Bangladesh Road Transport Corporation Vs. M/s. Ashraf Jute Mills Ltd. reported in 43 DLR 240. In the said case it was held that as the affidavit in opposition was not filed within the period allowed by the Court the same was struck off and the learned Advocate for the respondent did not contest the application for winding up of the Company. In the said decision application for winding up of the company was filed for realisation of dues of Tk. 1,85,359.95 towards arrear monthly rents and since the Company Judge found that the respondent company had taken lease of a portion of the promises of the petitioner and that there was out-standing dues of monthly rent amounting to Tk. 1,85,359.95 are not disputed it was held that the respondent company was unable to pay its debt to the petitioner. The facts and the preposition of law laid down in the said decision has no application in the present case. In the decision in the case of Nizamul Haque and other Vs. Singa Bangla Garment Manufacturing Company (Pvt.) Ltd. reported in 4 DLR 603 it has been held that winding up of a company for non-payment of arrear house rent is the liability of a company and if a company is unable to pay such liability it may be wound up. This is again not applicable in the facts of the case before up. Mr. Razzaq relied yet on a decision in the case of M.A. Gaffar and another Vs. Sunjari Garments (Pvt) Ltd. reported in 5BLC 480 where it has been held "Admitted liability of the respondent No. 1to the petitioner is more than Taka eight lacs and no statement in the affidavit-in-opposition was made about the settlement of such liability and the respondent-company is unable to pay its admitted debt and hence the company is liable to be wound up. 'The preposition of law laid down in this decision is not applicable in the facts of the present case in as much as the alleged liability is not admitted. Mr. Razzaq further relied on a decision in the case of K.T.S. (Singapore) PLC. Ltd Vs. Associated Forest Products (Pvt) Ltd. reported in 1996 Company Cases 190. I have perused the said decision and it appears that the proposition of law laid down therein has no manner of application in the case before us. Mr. Razzaq has also relied on a decision in the case of Eastern Bank Limited Vs. Bengal Carpets Limited reported in 48 DLR 392 where it has been held "From the conduct of the respondent company and in the manner promises were made, assurances given new repayment schedule chalked out again and again only to be broken giving the impression that the affairs of the company are not clean and above board, the opinion is that the respondent company is unable to pay its debt and it will be just and equitable if the company is wound up. This is again not applicable in the facts of the case before us here. No promises were made or assurances given or any repayment schedule was checked out by the respondent company to pay the alleged debt. This case is clearly distinguishable and has no manner of application in the facts of the case before us. 

9. Mr. Md. Ashad Ullah, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent company has as relied on a decision in the case of Agrani Bank Vs. Tyres Ltd. and others reported in 43 DLR(AD) 164. In the said decision their Lordships held "Accompany must be found to be commercially insolvent when its existing and probable assets are insufficient to meet the existing liabilities, it is heavily indebted to various creditors, all its assets being in Mortgage or in pledge, and there is no possible chance of a profit being made or its business carried out". In our case the petitioner did not alleged that the respondent Company has no sufficient assets to meet the existing liabilities or it is heavily indebted to various creditors and unable to pay the debts. This decision does not help the learned Advocate for the respondent-company in as such as it as not alleged by the petitioner that the company was insolvent and the basis for an order of winding up of the company on the ground of its insolvency is absent in the present case. On consideration of the materials placed before the court I do find that no case has been made out that the respondent company is unable to pay its debt due to its insolvency. Mr. Md. Ashad Ullah relied on a decision in the case of Abdur Rasheed Vs. Messrs Nippon Robbin Company (Pakistan) Ltd. and 6 others reported in PLD 1982 Lahore 103. In the said decision upon a reference made to AIR 1929 Mad. 265 it has been held that the allegation that the company had failed to pay its debts was not supported by any fact to enable the court to come to the conclusion that the company was unable to pay its statutory demand. The court held "I cannot say that there is no bonafide dispute as to the company's liability to pay this debt. Courts will never allow creditors of a company to invoke the assistance of the Companies Act for getting payment of their debt. If there is genuine dispute with regard to the debt, then the creditors of the company must be referred to a suit. 'The proposition of law laid down in the said decision is applicable in the facts of the case before us. Mr. Md. Ashad Ullah, the learned Advocate for the respondent then relied on a decision in the case of Industrial Development Bank of Pakistan Vs. Sattar & Sons Ltd. reported in 22 DLR Dhaka 170 where it has been held "Where there are bonafide disputes relating to the existence of the debt, there a winding-up order is not called for. A debt in order to be a foundation of the order for winding-up of a company has to be debt which do not suffer and which cannot be disputed on legitimate and bonafide grounds. "The proposition of law laid down in this decision is also applicable in the facts of the case before us. On a perusal of the Annexure I find that there is bonafide dispute relating to the existence of the debt and accordingly winding up proceeding was not available to the petitioner. The petitioner has her remedy in other forum by an appropriate proceeding and not by an application for winding up of the Company. We have noticed that the petitioner herself is confused with regard to the alleged debt inasmuch as in some annexures claim has been made for Tk. 4,15,730.20, in another claim has been made for Tk. 5,27,730.20 paisa and then in Annexure-E a claim for an amount of Tk. 13,11,000.00 has been made while in Annexure J a claim of Tk. 6,99,239.97 paisa has been made towards debt from the respondent company and in the said Annexure J the petitioner has admitted that an amount of Tk. 2,24,966.03 was adjusted towards printing cost of the Magazine 'Phulkuri'. According to the own statements made in the aforesaid annexures it appears that a bonafide dispute is involved with regard to the debt and amount of debt and unless this dispute involving the amount of debt is settled 
before appropriate forum and also the dispute with regard to the nature of the payment of Tk. 2 lacs, whether a loan or an advance of printing cost of Phulkuri is resolved by competent court in an appropriate proceeding the petitioner is not entitled to claim winding up of the respondent company. 

10. Mr. Md. Ashad Ullah has also relied on a decision in the case of Mulla Abdullahbhai and 9 others Vs. Saria Rope Mills Ltd. reported in YID 197 Karachi 597 where it has been held that 'The reason why an application for winding up is not a substitute for a suit, is that in a suit for the recovery of a debt the creditor has to prove what is due to him, whereas in winding up proceedings he has also to establish that the company is unable to pay its debts. The words "unable" does not mean "unwilling" and the word "debts" refers to all the creditors as a class and not separately to the interest of each individual creditor. There should, firstly, exist a debt, secondly, it should not be the subject of an honest dispute and, thirdly, the company should be unable to pay its debts. In the aforesaid 1971 Karachi case it has been held "If a debtor is merely unwilling to pay his debts, then the nor-mal remedy is a suit. If a creditor instead of instituting a suit against debtor-company, files on application for winding it up, one asks himself why has he done so, instead of following the straight forward course of proving his claim directly and then executing the decree? If his del-.t is undisputed, then the decree will fallow easily. If he simply desires to save Court-fee, then the consideration of less to the State revenue may not be in his way, but he involves himself in the problem of proving insolvency of the company which is different from a temporary misfortune of a company. "It is further held "It is wrong to unnecessarily resort to winding up proceedings because there is an implied threat in them to bring disaster to the company and because an odium is also attached to such proceedings. "I respect-fully agree with view expressed in the said decision and I find that bonafide dispute is involved with regard to the amount of debt and the nature debt. I am thus con-strained to hold that the application filed for winding up of the respondent company is not a proper forum for the petitioner. I do not, therefore, find any substance in the winding up petition. 

11. Accordingly this winding up application is rejected. 

End.

lawyer: Mr. Rafiq-Ul Hoque with Mr. Ahsanul Karim and Mr. Aneek  R Hoque, Advocates -- For the Petitioners. Mr. Mahmudul Islam with Mr. Akhter Imam, Mr. Syed Mamun Mahbub and Mr. Chowdhury, Md. Jinnat Ali, Advocates -- For Opposite Party Nos. 2 and 3

Mr. S I Khan and others ----- Petitioners
Versus

full_judgment:
Md. Abdur Rashid, J: This Rule was obtained by the defendants upon making a revision application under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure against judgment and order dated 11.03.2001 passed by the District Judge at Dhaka in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 308 of 1999 affirming those dated 31.10.99 passed by Subordinate Judge, First Court at Dhaka in Title Suit No. 198 of 1999 which granted temporary injunction.

2. Opposite parties No. 1 to 8 as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 150 of 1999 in the First Court of Senior Assistant Judge at Dhaka for declarations that the Extraordinary General Meeting of the company (EGM) dated 22.02.98 was illegal and void, and the resolutions passed therein were not valid, and that the 68th  meeting of the board of directors of the company held on 15.04.99 and 28.04.99 is valid and the resolutions passed therein were valid and binding upon the company and also for perpetual injunction for restraining the defendants from interfering with and/or disturbing, in any way, the smooth function of the business administration and management of the company.

3. Short facts for disposal of the Rule are that the plaintiff No. 1 is a private limited company registered in 1993 under the Companies Act, 1913. Plaintiff No. 2 is the chairman and plaintiff No. 3 is the new managing director, and plaintiff Nos. 2 to 8 are all directors of the company holding 79.05% of the shares. Defendant No. 1 Is former managing director, defendant No. 2 is former company secretary and defendant No. 3 is a director while defendant No. 4 is another company, Kranti Associates Ltd. holding together 20.5% of the total shares.

4. Defendant Nos. 2 and 3 are also the nominee directors of said Kranti Associates in the board of directors of the plaintiff company. Defendant No. 1 owns 0.5% only of the shares of the company.

5. Plaintiffs entered into a joint venture with a Malaysian company called Technology Resources Industries (TRI) and established a registered company in Bangladesh in the name and style, "Sheba Telecom (Pvt.) Ltd. (STL). Originally, in Sheba Telecom the plaintiff company had 51% and the TRI 49% of the shareholding but subsequently, plaintiff transferred 2% of its shares raising the share holding of the TRI to 51% of the total shares. As per provisions of the articles plaintiff company was represented in the board of directors of the STL through its three directors, namely, plaintiff No. 2, defendant Nos. 1

and 3, and in the management committee of the STL by defendant No. 1. All decisions in the meeting of board of directors as well as the annual general meeting of the STL were required to be taken through consensus and consent of at least of two directors of representing each of the two companies was necessary to pass a resolution.

6. Then plaintiff company by a decision restrained its nominee directors from attending the 9th board meeting of the directors of said STL. But defendant Nos. 1 to 3 started working in league with each other and taking decisions in the meetings of the STL in collusion with the TRI people against the interest of the ISL.

7. They also held an EGM of the ISL on 22.02.98 without service of any notice upon the majority shareholders of the company. In the meeting only two share-holders were present, yet, without any valid quorum, they took various decisions in order to bind the company.

8. Thereafter, plaintiff No. 2 chairman of the ISL asked twice the company secretary, defendant No. 2 to call a meeting of the board of directors which he declined. Consequently the chairman himself had to call the meeting of the board on 15.04.99 after due service of notice upon all directors on 08.04.99 followed by supporting letters dated 12.04.99. But the defendants by letter dated 13.04.99 informed that they would not come to the meeting.

9. On 15.04.99 the meeting was usually held and the business was transacted in accordance with the agenda. In order to secure the presence of the defendant Nos. 1 to 3, the meeting was adjourned to 28.04.99 with a request to the chairman to request the defendants to attend the adjourned meeting. Again, on 27-04.99 the defendants in writing informed that they would not come to the meeting.

<u>10. On 28.04.99 the adjourned meeting of the board was held and number of decisions including termination of service of the defendant No. 1 as managing director and that of defendant No. 2 as company secretary, withdrawing the nomination of defendant No. 3 from the board, and that of defendant No. 1 from the managing committee of the STL.</u>

11. Even after the decision the defendants started acting against the interest of the plaintiff company, ISL Hence the suit. The suit was then on transfer to the First Court of Subordinate Judge at Dhaka renumbered as Title Suit No. 198 of 1999.

12. On the above averments, the plaintiffs also made an application under order XXXIX Rules 1 and 2 for temporary injunction for restraining the defendants from disturbing and/or interfering, in any way, with the smooth business and management of the affairs of the plaintiff company.

13. Defendant Nos. 1 to 4 opposed the application by filing a written objection. They also tiled an additional written objection. Their main objections, in short, are that the application was filed with the objective to oust the defendants, who are minority shareholders in the company. Sheba invested more than 50 Lac in the plaintiff company. In order to secure their rights, they had informal discussions with the shareholders in the 57th board meeting held on 01.04.98, it was resolved that no decision would be taken in any meeting of the company without consensus of the minority shareholders. To further secure rights of the minority shareholders, an EGM was held on 22.02.98 wherein number of decisions were taken to safeguard their interest. The EGM was validly called after service of the notice upon all the shareholders, the plaintiff No. 2 chairman of the company preside over the meeting and the decisions were validly taken. It was also resolved that no decision would be taken without consensus of the Krant Associates.

14. Further case is that defendant No. 2, company secretary informed that plaintiff Nos. 3, 7 and 8 ceased to be directors of the company for their failure to attend three consecutive board meetings. They also informed by letter dated 14.04.99 that they could not attend the 68th meeting of the board since the notice was circulated even to those directors who ceased to be directors. Notice of the adjourned meeting of the board was served very late and in such meeting series of resolutions were adopted, which were derogatory to the interest of the company.

15. They also claimed that the plaintiffs had no prima facie case for temporary injunction on mere apprehension, and the balance of convenience and inconvenience was clearly in favour of the defendants.

16. On hearing the application, learned Subordinate Judge has found that the plaintiffs have got a prima facie and arguable case, and the balance of convenience and inconvenience is also in favour of them, and that there is likelihood to encounter irreparable loss if injunction as prayed for be not granted. Upon such view, learned Subordinate Judge allowed the application for temporary injunction and granted a temporary injunction till the disposal of the suit to the following effect,

a. the defendants are restrained from interfering with and/or disturbing the smooth functioning of the business, administration and management of the company;

b. the defendant No. 1 from acting as managing director of the company and as a nominee director in the board and managing committee of the STL;

c. defendant No. 2 from acting as the company secretary of the company; and

d. defendant No. 3 from acting as a nominee director in the STL.

17. On appeal therefrom, the appellate Court below also by independent consideration of the materials on record concurred the findings of the trial Court and affirmed the order of temporary injunction and dismissed the appeal by impugned judgment and order.

18. Mr. Rafiq-ul Huq, learned Senior Counsel seriously challenged the order of temporary injunction on number of counts. Firstly, he submitted that the EGM held on 22.02.98 was presided over by the chairman of the company, plaintiff No. 2, and attended by the managing director of the company with others. The chairman confirmed the minutes of the meeting by his own signature. The members present in meeting also waived the question of short notice in writing. Such meeting and the decisions taken therein must be presumed under the provisions of Section 89 (3) of the Act to be duly called and held, and valid. He relied the view of a single Bench of this Division in the case of Shamsul Huda v Alauddin, 36 DLR 316,

"When a company produces the minutes of proceedings of its annual general meeting or of its Board of Directors signed by the Chairman of the meeting at which the meetings were held or by the Chairman of the next succeeding meeting the minutes shall be evidence of the proceeding, under Section 83(2) of the Companies Act (of 1913). Under Section 83(3) of the Companies Act, until the contrary is proved, every general meeting of the company or meeting of the Board of Directors in respect of the proceedings whereof minutes have been so made shall be deemed to have been duly called and held, and all proceedings had thereat to have duly had. The onus is on the petitioners to show that the minutes of proceedings are not correct and until the petitioners so prove this Court shall take the minutes of proceedings to be evidence of the same."

Secondly, he submitted that the defendant Nos. 1 to 3 were most illegally removed in the so-called meeting of the board dated 15.04.99 and 28.04.99 without any notice upon them and any agenda for such removal. He cited the authority in the case of Shamsul Huda v Jalaluddin Ahmed, 31 DLR 5 and submitted that no director could validly be removed without an agenda for that. Next, he submitted that the adjourned meeting held on 28.04.99 in the absence of any notice upon the defendants and they were removed from the office of managing director and directors in violation of Section 95 of the Act. He relied upon the authority in the case of Mohibul Ahsan v Ittefaq Group and others, (1998) 50 DLR (AD) 138,

"It is now a well settled principle that the Courts are generally reluctant to interfere with the decisions taken at company meetings unless there is almost a manifest breach of the Articles or the Statute, because it is the company and not the Court which is responsible for its management. The High Court was well aware of the legal position and having found, among others, that here was an apparent breach of Section 95 of the Companies Act, 1994 in holding the meeting on 07.01.95 granted the temporary injunction."

and the decision in the case of Ittefaq Group v Arab Bangladesh Bank, (1998) 50 DLR 597,

"It is true that this is an internal affair of a company but the law provides that in all companies either of private or public for holding a board meeting a written notice shall be given to every director and civil Court may not interfere when there is a valid meeting. The prima facie non issuance of notice of the meeting to be held on 07.01.95 made this resolution an invalid resolution and when there is prima facie an invalid resolution the Civil Court can interfere."

Finally he submitted that as the board meeting in question was held in violation of the provision of Section 95 of the Act, such meeting and the resolutions adopted therein have no legal effect in the eye of law. The plaintiffs must therefore be found to have no prima facie or any arguable case for temporary injunction. On granting injunction affecting the internal management of the affairs of a company, he cited the decisions in the case of Mrs. Shahnaz Chowdhury v Mr. Elthem B Kabir, (2001) 21 BLD (AD) 57 and Mainul Hosein v Anwar Hossain of 1996 BLT (AD) 76. The Appellate Division in the latter case held,

"... we think that in the matter of a company, it is advisable that the Court should not interfere by granting injunction where in the internal management and functioning of the company may be affected."

19. The plaintiffs opposite parties opposed the Rule by filing an affidavit-in-opposition. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, learned Senior Counsel for the plaintiffs first drew my attention to the notice issued on 07.02.98 and the minutes of the EGM taken on 22.02.98 and read the provisos to Section 85(1)(a) and 87(2) of the Act, and submitted that neither the calling and holding of said EGM nor resolutions taken therein could be said to be valid. In the meeting 6 persons were present and two of them were shareholders representing 39.4% of total shareholding only. Resolutions annexed also evidenced that it was intended to be a board meeting of the directors.

20. He also read the statements made in paragraph No. 6(c) and (h) of the affidavit-in-opposition that a few directors attended the meeting; that 60.6 share-holders were not notified; that ex facie there was no quorum as per article 39; that representation on behalf of Kranti Associates Ltd. was also not represented as per provision of Section 86 of the Act; that two different versions of the minutes one signed by the Chairman and the other by the Managing Director were submitted to the Registrar, defendant No. 5 and the Registrar by his letter dated 10.05.99 asked for an explanation from the Managing Director, defendant No. 1 who did not comply with the request. He submitted that the statements should be taken as correct since the petitioners did not controvert any of them. No book containing any minutes could also be produced. In the circumstances, when the contrary was proved that there was no valid EGM was called and held there was no scope for any presumption under Section 89(3) of the Act.

21. Opposing the contentions of Mr. Huq, he submitted that the 68th meeting of the board of directors dated 15.04.99 and 28.04.99 and the resolutions adopted therein were all valid and lawful with regard to notice, agenda, quorum etc. Elaborating, he submitted that when by writing letters dated 14.04.99 and 27.04.99 the defendants informed that they would not come to the meeting, now they could not validly raise any question against service of notice. Secondly, he submitted that no notice is required for an adjourned meeting of the board. He read the following from 'the Principles of Modern Company Law' by L C B Gower at page 495 on notice,

"An adjourned meeting is deemed to be a resumption of the original meeting and no further notice is needed unless the regulations otherwise provide, and no business can be transacted except left over."

He then relied the decision in the case of Promode Kumar Mittal and others v Southern Steel Ltd. and others, (1980) 50 Company Cases 555, at page 559,

"Thereafter, the meeting scheduled to be held on the 14th of May, 1976 could not be held due to lack of quorum and it was adjourned till 16th of May, 1976. The whole dispute in this application turns on the question whether any fresh notice of the adjourned meeting was necessary to be given to the directors and it appears to me from the provisions of the Companies Act, 1956, and the articles of association of the company that for an adjourned meeting no fresh notice is necessary and, therefore, in my view, the meeting held on the 16th of May, 1976, appears to be legal, valid and according to law and it is not ultra vires or illegal as alleged by the petitioners."

22. He also submitted that the articles of the association of the company do not require any fresh notice for an adjourned meeting. Regulations of the Act also do not require such notice. Alternatively he submitted that even if it were found that such notice was required that would at best be an irregularity, which was cured by ratification in the subsequent 69th meeting of the board. He relied upon the authority on ratification in the case of Ittefaq Group v Arab Bangladesh Bank, (1998) 50 DLR 597,

"If this is as such as submitted by Mr. Ahmed then the Board of Director, in a fresh legally constituted meeting can now, ratify, the resolution dated 07.01.95. The Indian Supreme Court has propounded in the case of Parmeshwari Prasad Gupta v Union of India reported in AIR 1973 (VI 60) 2389 that it was open to a regularly constituted meeting of the board of directors to ratify the action which, though unauthorized, was taken by the chairman on behalf of the company. The ratification would always relate back to the date of the act ratified. So, if every thing is going on smoothly the Board of Directors, if necessary, may again meet in a properly constituted meeting and ratify the resolution which is prima facie found to be invalid.

23. Similarly, he submitted that no agenda was required for such meeting either under the regulations of the Act or the articles of association. Even for removal of a managing director. He read article 52 of the company and submitted that in the meeting, the board can elect a director from amongst the directors pre sent, and equally can remove one. Law does not require an agenda for such removal. He cited the decision in the case of Sreemati Abnash Kaur v Lord Krishna Sugar Mills Ltd. and others, (1974) 44 Company Cases 390.

He read therefrom, "under Section 288 only notice of the meeting of the board of directors is required to be given in writing to every director; the law does not require an agenda for a meeting of the board of directors and any business whatsoever can be transacted at the board meeting.

" He also relied upon the rule as laid down in the case of La Compagnie De Mayville v Whitley, L R (1896) Chancery Division 788 CA at page 197,

"The great point is whether, when a directors' meeting is to be held, it is necessary to give a notice not only of the meeting, but of the business to be transacted at the meeting. I am not prepared to say as a matter of law that it is necessary there is an immense difference between meetings of share-holders or cooperators and meetings of those whose business it is to attend to the transaction of the affairs of the company or corporation. It is not uncommon for directors conducting a company's business to meet on stated days without any previous notice being given either of the day or of what they are going to do .........................

I can not now say for the first time that as a matter of law the business conducted at a directors' meeting is invalid if the directors have had no notice of the kind of business which is to come before them. Such a rule would be extremely embarrassing in the transaction of the business of companies."

He also submitted that the decision as was relied upon by Mr. Huq in the case of Shamsul Huda v Jalaluddin Ahmed, 31 DLR 5 is not applicable in the facts and circumstances of the case.

24. As a matter of facts, Mr. Islam also submitted that the petitioners instituted Title Suit No. 116 of 1999 against the plaintiffs challenging the holding of the 68th board meeting and the resolutions taken therein. They also prayed for a temporary injunction against said resolutions to take effect till disposal of their suit, which they failed to obtain up to this Division.

25. In reply, Mr. Ahsanul Karim submitted that the decisions relied upon by Mr. Islam might be good under the relevant laws at the relevant time and place but not applicable in our law and the facts of the case. He submitted that in view of Section 95 of the Act, notice for both fresh and adjourned meeting of the board is necessary for a valid board meeting. In the 68th board meeting, admittedly three of the directors were found to be disqualified they were asked to take them out of the meeting but most illegally in the same meeting they were reelected directors and allowed them to attend the meeting and resolutions were passed with their concurrence in violation of the provisions of Section 91(c) of the Act. Such meeting cannot be termed as valid under the law. But he was very candid and polite, which must be appreciated, to say, in disowning Mr. Huq that they should not insist that the EGM was validly called and held.

26. I have perused the plaint, the application for temporary injunction, objection thereto and number of papers and documents produced by the parties. I have heard at length the learned Counsels. In their submissions, they have left no point untouched in their deliberations. But the issue that calls for my determination in this revision is whether the District Judge is well founded in his judgment affirming the order of temporary injunction as granted by the trial court. I cannot go deep into the merit of the case which would be finally decided in the suit.

27. Plaintiff No. 1, Integrated Services Limited, in short, ISL is a private limited company comprising of six shareholders. Of the shareholders, defendant No. 1 former managing director holds 0.5% and defendant No. 4 Kranti Associates Limited 20% of the shares. Of the shareholders, plaintiff No. 2, defendant No. 1 and others on behalf of defendant No. 4 representing 40.4% of the share only attended the Extraordinary General Meeting (EGM) held on 22.02.98. All of them appear to have attended the meeting as directors. Notice of the meeting was issued on 07.02.98 and in view of provision of Section 85(1)(a) of the Act the same was a short notice. Of course, in view of the proviso (ii) to Section 85(1)(a) of the Act such meeting could be called by a shorter notice only by agreement in writing by members of the company holding not less than 95 percent shares and in view of proviso to Section 87(2) of the Act by a resolution to be proposed and passed by the requisite number of members under Section 87(1) shorter notice could be waived. Having regard to the uncontroverted facts as stated in paragraph 6(c) to (h) of the affidavit-in-opposition, there is hardly any scope under Section 89(3) of the Act to presume that the EGM was duly called and held, and consequently, the minutes were deemed to be valid. Ultimately, it became difficult for the defendants to defend such EGM as validly called and held.

28. Then, it appears from the plaint that the chairman of the company twice asked the defendant No. 2, company secretary to call a meeting of board of directors on 05.04.99 and then, on 08.04.99 but he did not comply with any. Thereafter the chairman himself called the 68th meeting of the board of directors on 15.04.99 after service of notice dated 08.04.99 but defendants by their letter dated 14.04.99 informed of their unwillingness to attend the meeting. The notice dated 08.04.99 contains various agenda of which agenda No. 3 is ISL affairs, No. 3.2 attending the 9th Board meeting of Sheba Telecom and 3.3 performance of MD. The meeting was adjourned to 28.04.99 and the chairman was requested to request defendant Nos. 1 and 3 to attend the meeting. But they again refused to attend the adjourned meeting in writing a letter dated 27.04.99. After such refusal, it does not fit the mouths of the defendants that the meeting was held without the statutory notice. In the adjourned meeting, resolutions were adopted withdrawing nomination of defendant Nos. 1 and 3 to represent the ISL in the STL board, and also the nomination of defendant No. 1 to represent as member in the managing committee of the STL. Defendant No. 1 was also removed from the office of managing director and defendant No. 2 company secretary on various considerations. Such holding of the meeting of the board cannot be deemed to be not duly called and held and the decisions taken therein are not valid for want of fresh notice under Section 95 of the Act. I also could not find any valid reason for the defendants to abstain from the meeting and/or withhold their cooperation in the transacting of important business of the company.

29. Section 95 of the Act of course makes it obligatory to issue a notice in writing to every director. Such requirement does not appear to extend the obligation to give fresh notice for an adjourned meeting for transaction of the unfinished business of the last meeting. Business to be transacted in the adjourned meeting also appears to be notified in the notice dated 08.04.99. It is difficult to say on the agenda decisions taken could not validly be taken. Such meeting and the decisions taken therefore cannot be said to be invalid for violation of any law or the article of the company. Even re-election of the three directors in question in the same meeting also cannot invalidate the whole proceedings of the board meeting.

30. In such view of the matter, it is very difficult for me to say that the plaintiffs had no prima facie case or no arguable case for going to trial. The term of the office of defendant No. 1 as managing director already expired in 31.12.2000 before the impugned order was passed. In view of the loss of confidence of the majority shareholders in the defendants and the non-cooperation of the defendants, it will not be correct to say that the steps taken in the 68th meeting of the board of directors for smooth conduct of the business of the company were not necessary or not taken in the interest of the company. The courts below therefore rightly found the balance of convenience and inconvenience is clearly in favour of the plaintiffs.

<u>31. The impugned judgment and order affirming the order of the trial Court granting temporary injunction do not suffer from any error or illegality, and therefore do not call for any interference by this Division. No failure of justice has occasioned thereby.</u>

32. The result therefore is that the Rule is discharged with costs. Order of stay granted at the time of issue of the Rule is hereby recalled and vacated. Order of temporary injunction as granted by the trial Court is hereby confirmed. The trial Court is directed to take steps for speedy disposal of the suit. Communicate.

End.
