case_source:
In the matter of:
Application under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh
full_judgment:
Mr. Mainur Reza Chowdhury, J: On application made by the petitioners in the above writ petitions under Article 102 of the Constitution Rules Nisi were issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned notices in the writ petition passed by the respective respondents should not be declared illegal, without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect. 

	2. As the impugned orders relate to enquiry under the Anti-Corruption Act, 1957 issued by the same department that is the Bureau of Anti-Corruption the writ petitions are being disposed of by a single judgment. 

	3. In Writ Petition Nos. 5383 of 1996, 3963 of 1996, 4863 of 1996, 4864 of 1996, 2043 of 1994 and 4702 of 1996, the impugned notices are purportedly issued under Sections 94/160 of the Criminal Procedure Code. Writ Petitions No. 4154 of 1992, 1413 of 1996, 1414 of 1996, 1415 of 1996, 1416 of 1996, 867 of 1994 and 1323 of 1993 the impugned notices do not refer to any authority under which the notices were issued by the notices asked for similar information from the petitioners as mentioned in the impugned notices of the aforesaid writ petitions. By the respective impugned notices the petitioners were directed to appear before an officer of Bureau of Anti-Corruption connection with enquiry in respect of complaint received by the department and in some cases to produce documents as mentioned in the notices. 

	4. It has been argued by the learned Counsels for the petitioners that the issuance of such notices under Sections 94 and 160 of the Code of Criminal Procedure are illegal and without lawful authority. In the absence of initiation of cases against the petitioners the Bureau of Anti- Corruption cannot issue any notice under Sections 94 and 160 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Section 4 of the Anti- Corruption Act, 1957 gives power to the authorised department to make enquiry and exercise power under Sections 94 and 160 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and this power can be exercised by the Police. Officer only after initiation of a case Therefore the impugned notices without initiation of any case are illegal. It has been further submitted that the impugned notices did not disclose the nature of complaint which has been received and therefore the notices are vague and the petitioners are not bound to comply with the notices as they are illegal on that ground. 

	5. We will first take up the question whether the respondent being an officer of the Bureau of Anti-Corruption has the power to issue the impugned notices under Sections 94 and 160 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. 

	6. The learned Assistant Attorney-General has submitted that Section 3(2) of the Anti-Corruption Act, 1957 has vested officers of the Bureau for the purpose of carrying out enquiry with all the powers of a police officer of Bangladesh connection with the investigation. Sections 94 and 160 Cr.P.C. provides for such power to the50police officers of Bangladesh and therefore may be exercised by the officers of the Bureau for making enquiry. Section 3 of the Anti-Corruption Act concerns the constitution of the power of the Bureau. For our purpose it may be convenient to quite the relevant portion of the Section. 

	Sub-Section (1) of Section 3 says "Notwithstanding anything contained in the Police Act, 1861 (V of 1861), the Government may constitute a Bureau to be called the Bangladesh Bureau of Anti-Corruption for enquiry into and investigation in Bangladesh of the offences specified in the schedule and offences notified by the Government." 

	Sub-Section (3) of Section 3 reads as follows: 

	"Subject to any orders which the Government may make in this behalf, officers of the Bureau shall have throughout the Bangladesh in relation to the enquiry into, and investigation of, such offences all powers of seizure, search and arrest of persons concerned in such offences and all other powers, duties, privileges and liabilities which the police officers of Bangladesh have in connection with the investigation of such offences." 

	(our emphasis)
	7. It was argued by the learned Counsels for the petitioners that the power under Sections 94 and 160 Cr.P.C. could be exercised by the police only for the purpose of investigation where cases had been recorded, and an enquiry not being an investigation, the officer of the Bureau cannot exercise power under Sections 94 arid 160 Cr.P.C. at the enquiry st age. If we closely examine Section 3(2) to the Act we find that it says that the Bureau shall have throughout Bangladesh in relation to the enquiry into, and investigation of such offences all powers of seizure, search and arrest of persons concerned in such offences and all other powers, duties, privileges and liabilities which the police officers of Bangladesh have in connection with the investigation of such offences. By this we understand that the officers of the Bureau while making an enquiry as different from investigation made under the Code of Criminal Procedure can exercise all powers of the police in connection with the investigation of offences. The Anti-Corruption Act has empowered the officers of the Bureau for the purpose of enquiry all the powers which police have in connection with the investigation of an office. The learned Assistant Attorney-General submitted that by section 3 of the Act the Bureau of Anti-Corruption even at the stage of enquiry shall have all the powers of a police officers or officers in charge of police station. In this connection he has referred to the case of Hamida Oil Mills Vs. District Anti-Corruption. Officer, Chittagong and another reported in 2 BLC (AD) 1997) page 78. In that case the District Anti-Corruption Officer, Chittagong filed an application before the Sessions Judge, Chittagong being Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 27 of 1995 (Permission) with a prayer for directing the Laldhigi Purpapra Branch of Agrani Bank, where the petitioner had an account, for furnishing all connected bank records in connection with an enquiry into an alleged allegation of defalcation of Government money of Taka 30 crore. The learned Counsel for the petitioner in that case had submitted that the High Court Division failed to consider that in terms of Section 94 Cr.P.C. a police officer or an Anti-Corruption officer in competent to apply for permission of the Sessions Judge for production of any document from the custody of a Bank only when it is necessary for the purpose of investigating an offence under Sections 403, 408, 409, and 421 to 424 (both inclusive) and sections 465 to 477A of the Penal Code. Ile submitted that unless there is any pending proceeding by way of lodging any FIR under any of the said sections the Anti-Corruption officer is not competent to apply for permission from the Sessions Judge. To this submission the Appellate Division in the said case made the following observation: 

	"It is riot necessary for the purpose of enquiry into a complaint that a formal case upon lodging an FIR will have to be filed before a police officer or an Anti-Corruption Officer can apply for permission to the Sessions Judge the production and seizure of any document. It is necessary for the Sessions Judge before according permission. to satisfy himself that the police officer or Anti-Corruption officer is investigating on an alleged crime and is not merely fishing for information to harass, intimidate or coerce innocent persons." 

	8. It is submitted by the learned Assistant Attorney General that this case shows that for the purpose of exercising power under Section 94 Cr.P.C. no formal case of lodging on FIR is required to be filed before a police officer. The Bureau of Anti-Corruption will exercise the power of officer-in-charge of Police Station even when he is carrying out an inquiry on receipt of a complaint. It was however submitted by the learned Counsel for the petitioners that the above mentioned case had not manner of application in the present cases. The case decided by the Appellate Division related to an application for direction from the Court to a bank to furnish all connected bank records in connection with an enquiry by the Bureau. The Bankers' Books Evidence Act 1891 provides for inspection of Bank records by an order of a Judge or Court. 

	9. Section 6(1) of the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891 specifically provides that on the application of any party to a legal proceeding the Court or a Judge may order that such party be at liberty to inspect and take copies of any entries in a bankers' book for any of the purposes of such proceeding, or may order the bank to prepare and produce, within a time to be specified in the order, certified copies of all such entries, accompanied by a further certificate that no other entries are to be found in the books or the bank relevant to the matters in issue in such proceeding, and such further certificate shall be dated and subscribed in manner directed in reference to certified copies. 

	10. Section 2(4) of the said Act provides that legal proceeding means any proceeding or inquiry in which evidence is or may be given, and includes arbitration. It was submitted that in the said case the inquiry proceeding come within the meaning of legal preceding under the said Act and so the Appellate Division held that for the purpose of enquiry in a bank case it was not necessary for any case to be pending. It was argued that since Section 6(1) of the Bankers' Books Evidence Act relates only to a Banks case the observation of the Appellate Division was not applicable in the present case. However we do not find any reference to Section 6 of the Bankers' Book Evidence Act, in the judgment of the Appellate Division. The observation of the Appellate Division which we have quoted above was made in reference to sub-mission made by the learned Counsel for the petitioners in that case was that High Court Division had failed to consider that in terms or section 94 Cr.P.C. a police officer of Anti-Corruption Officer was competent to apply for permission of the Sessions Judge for production of any document from the custody of a Bank only when it was necessary for the purpose of investigating an offence under sections mentioned. Unless there were any pending proceeding by way of lodging an FIR under any of the said sections the Anti-Corruption officer was not competent to apply for permission from the Sessions Judge. We are therefore unable to accept that the observation of the Appellate Division was only in respect of documents in possession of the Bank. The observation was made in respect of the power exercised under Section 94 of the Criminal Procedure Code by an officer of the Anti-Corruption Department while making an inquiry on receipt of complaint. 

	11. The learned Assistant Attorney General also referred to the case of Emperor Vs, Khawaja Nazir Ahmed reported in AIR (32) 1945 Privy Council 18 in which it was held that in respect of cognizable offence-receipt and a recording of first information report is not condition precedent to criminal investigation. 

	It was held: 
	"In the case of cognizable offences receipt and recording of a first information report is not a condition precedent to the setting in motion of a criminal investigation. No doubt in the greed majority of cases, criminal prosecutions are undertaken as a result of information received and recorded in this way, but there is not reason why the police, if in possession through their own knowledge or by means of credible though informal intelligence which genuinely leads them to the belief that a cognizable offence has been committed, should not of their own motion undertake an investigation the truth of the matters alleged. Section 157 when directing that a police officer, who has reason to suspect from information or otherwise that an offence which he is empowered to investigate under S. 156 has been committed shall proceed to investigate the facts and circumstances supports this view. 

	The object of the provisions as to an information report (Commonly called a first information report) is to obtain early information of alleged criminal activity, to record the circumstances before there is time for them to be forgotten or embellished, and the report can be put in evidence when the informant is examined if it is desired to do so." 

	12. It was then argued that the power of making inquiry by the Bureau of Anti-Corruption under the Anti-Corruption Act. 1957 was not available against private person. It was argued that the definition of corruption would show that the private citizen cannot be involved in such an offence and in support of their contention referred to the decision of a division bench of the High Court. in the case of Abul Basher Vs. State that a private person cannot be tried under Sections 4(2) and 5(1) of the Anti- Corruption Act, 1957. It was observed that the alleged offence committed by the present petitioner may be tried under normal law but not under the Anti-Corruption Act. However in a criminal petitioner for leave to Appeal No. 153 of 1995 in the case of Sontosh Bhusan Das & Anr vs. The State and ors reported in 4 BLT (AD) (1996) 58 the Appellate Division took a different view. In considering the question whether an officer of Bureau of Anti-Corruption is competent to hold the investigation as the alleged offences under Sections 406/420/109 of the Penal Code are said to have been committed by private persons and not by public servants the Appellate Division held "there is nothing either in Section 3 or in the schedule from where it can be said that on investigation to be made by an officer of the Bureau of Anti-Corruption in respect of the aforesaid offences must be alleged to have been committed by a public servant-this is not an authority for the proposition that the Bureau of Anti- Corruption has no authority to investigate the offences mentioned in the schedule of the Act unless they are committed by a public servant." 

	13. In the case of Abdul Kabir vs. State reported in 50 DLR (1998) 306 a Division Bench of the High Court held as follows: 

	"From the preamble we have not iced that the Bureau was constituted not only for enquiry into and investigation of offence relating to corruption but also relating to certain other offences. This has been elaborated in Section 3(1) of the Act which provides that the Bureau of Anti-Corruption is for inquiry into and investigation of offences specified in the schedule and offences notified by the Government. We have no doubt that corruption is not confined only to public servants. Other persons may also resort to corruption to Ames wealth. From the statement of the objects and reasons of the bill as quoted above it is also clear to us that the purpose of the bill were to check the persistent tendency to amass property by dishonest means on the part of public servants and other persons." Corrupt and dishonest means may be adopted by a private person such as a businessman to amass property. 

	It further observed that: 
	“The new law was introduced to try any person who has amassed property disproportionate to his known sources of income by improper means. It cannot be conceived of that the legislature will be powerless where there is no question of violation of the fundamental rights in enacting a law for taking penal action against persons who have amassed property by improper means and such persons will go unpunished only because they are not public servants and in our view to give such power, the Act of 1957 was enacted by the Legislature to prevent growing tendency to amass property by such improper means. 

	14. The learned Assistant Attorney -General in the present cases also drew our attention to the offences included in the schedule which he said were offences concerning the community at large. The offences which are included in the schedule are not confined to public servant. These offences are liable to be committed by any person. We find strength in the submission made by the learned Assistant Attorney General. Further this also finds supports in the above mentioned cases decided by the Appellate Division and a Division Bench of the High Court Division. We are therefore unable to accept the second submission made by the learned Counsels for the petitioners that the powers under Sections 94 and 160 Cr.P.C. are not available against private persons and are meant only to deal with cases of abuse of power and corruption by public servants. 

	15. The third submission was that the petitioners cannot be asked to make statement or produce evidence which would incriminate them. The impugned notices are violative of Article 35(4) of the Constitution. Sub-Article 4 of Article 35 provides that no person accused of any offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself. 

	16. In the present cases the petitioners are apprehensive that by making abatement or providing documents as directed by the impugned notices they would by providing evidence against themselves. On the other hand it was contended on behalf of the respondents that the said Article of the Constitution has no manner of application in the present cases as the petitioners arc not accused of any offence. They being not accused persons they are not entitled to get the protection of article 35 as a fundamental right. The purpose of the impugned notices is to verify and inquire into the complaint or information received by them. It is" merely a fact finding commission. Further the statement made and document to be examined in the enquiry stage cannot be used as evidence of an accused if and when there is a trial. It is submitted that sub-article 40 of Article 35 is only relevant when evidence is sought from an accused which lead to his conviction and punishment. In the instant cases the enquiry being of a preliminary nature the statements or documents produced by the petitioners will not lead to their conviction and punishment. The counsels for the petitioners have submitted that the word accused (in sub-article-4 of Article-35 is not defined in the Constitution. The word has a much wider meaning than the accused charged with an offence. The mere complaint received and enquiry started on the basis of complaint by the Bureau of Anti- Corruption makes him an accused and therefore he has full protection of the Article. We find that there is a side note to Article 35 of the Constitution which says "protection in respect of trial and punishment." The side note gives the impression that Article 35 essentially gives protection to accused person faced with trial and punishment and therefore in over view the word accused in sub- Article 4 means a person facing trial and punishment. It is only an accused in a trial who cannot be compelled to be witness against himself. Therefore it is our considered view that a person cannot seek the protection of Article 35(4) when a notice is sent by the Bureau of Anti- Corruption under Sections 94 and 160 Cr.P.C. Section 3 of Anti-Corruption Act which empowered an officer of Bureau of Anti-Corruption to serve notice under Sections 94 and 160 Cr.P.C. in only for the purpose of enquiry to determine the truth of the information received or has about offences connected with community interest, that is offences in the schedule to the Anti-Corruption Act. We therefore do not accept the submission of the petitioners that the impugned notices are violative of Article 35(4) of the Constitution. 

	17. In the light of our above observation we hold that the officer of this Bureau of Anti-Corruption has the power to order and summon under Sections 94 and 160 Cr.P.C. for the purpose of making a preliminary enquiry. But as we hold that an officer of the Bureau of Anti-Corruption can exercise all the powers which the Police Officer has in connection with the investigation of offences under the Criminal Procedure Code for the purpose of enquiry under the Anti-Corruption Act we feel that the person asked to make statement or produce documents ought to enjoy the save-guard provided by the Code of Criminal Procedure. Section 161 Cr.P.C. provides for examination of witness by police. Sub-Section (1) of the said section says that "any police officer making an investigation under this chapter or any police- Officer not below such rang as the Government may by general or special order, prescribe in this behalf, acting on the requisition of such officer) may examine orally any person supposed to be accounted with the facts and circumstances of the case." Sub-Section (2) of the said section provides that ''Such person shall be bound to answer all questions relating to such case put to him by such officer, other than questions the answers to which would have a tendency to expose him to a criminal charge of to a penalty or forfeiture." 

	In the present cases the persons on whom the notices are served under Sections 94 and 160 should at least have the right to know the nature of information and complaint the Bureau of Anti-Corruption has received so that he unknowingly does not make a statement to a question which might have a tendency to expose him to a criminal charge. So although an officer of the Anti- Corruption Department is armed with power of a police officer under different sections of the Criminal Procedure Code the person against whom an enquiry, is being made ought to have protection provided by the Criminal Procedure Code, Having found that the Bureau of Anti-Corruption has the power to issue orders and summons under Sections 94 and 160 Cr.P.C. We can now move on the next question to see whether the notices have been issued in accordance with law or not. 

	18. In writ petition No. 5383 of 1996, 3963 of 1996, 4863 of 1996, 4864 of 1996, 4702 of 1996, we find that the notices were issued under Sections 94 and 160 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and Clause 31/50 of the Anti- Corruption Manual. In all the impugned notices the petitioners have been directed to appear before the relevant officer at a given time for their statements and to produce certain documents as the notices have been issued under Sections 94 and 160 Cr.P.C. Section 94 of the Code of Criminal Procedure reads as follows : 

	"94. Summons to produce document or other thing (1) Whenever any court or, any officer in charge of a police- Station consider that the production of any document or other thing is necessary or desirable for the purposes of any investigation, inquiry, trial or other proceeding under this Code by or before such Court of Officer, such court may issue a summons, or such officer a written order, to the person in shoes possession or power such document or thing is believed to be, requiring him to attend and produce it or to produce it, at the time and place stated in the summons or order. 

	Provided that no such officer shall issue any such order requiring the production of any document or other thing which is in the custody of a bank or banker as defined in the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891 (XVII of 1891), and relates, or might disclose any information which relates, to the bank account of any person except :-

	(a) for the purpose of investigating an offence under Sections 403, 406. 408, and 409 and Section 421 to 424 both inclusive) and Sections 465 to 477A (both inclusive) of the Pakistan Penal Code, with the prior permission in writing of a Sessions Judge, and

	(b) in other cases, with the prior permission in writing of the High Court. 

	Section 160 Cr.P.C. reads as follows: 
	"Police Officer's power to require attendance of witnesses, any police-Officer making an investigation under this Chapter may, by order in writing, require the attendance before himself of any person being within the limits of his own or any adjoining station who, from the information given or otherwise, appears to be acquainted with the circumstances of the case, and such person shall attend as so required." 

	19. We do not Sind any illegality in the impugned notices which have been issued under the above aforementioned sections requiring I he m to produce certain documents and 1.0 appear before the relevant authority of the Bureau of Anti-Corruption. 

	20. In that view of the matter the Rules issued in these writ petition cannot be sustained and therefore are discharged. 

	21. In the Writ Petitions No. 1413 of 1996. 1414 of 1996, 1415 of 1996, 1416 of 1996, 867 of 1994 and 1323 of 1993 we find in these writ petitions that the impugned notices have been sent from the Anti-Corruption Bureau without mentioning under what authority the notices were being sent. To take a typical example we may quote the impugned order in writ petition No. 1414 of 1996 which reads as follows:

	“অত্র ব্যুরোতে পরিচালিত একটি অভিযোগ অনুসন্ধান সংক্রান্ত আপনার জবানবন্দী গ্রহণ একান্ত প্রয়োজন। এমতাবস্থায় আপনাকে আগামী ১০/৪/৯৬ইং তারিখ ০৯ টার সময় দূর্ণীতি দমন ব্যুরোর ব্যাংক শাখা, ১১৯/১, গেগুন বাগিচা, ঢাকাতে এই বিষয়ের অনুসন্ধানকারী অফিসার অত্র ব্যুরোর পরিদর্শক জনাব মবিনুল ইসলামের নিকট উপস্থিত হইয়া জবানবন্দি প্রদানের জন্য অনুরোধ করা হইল।”

	22. In these cases the respondents have been asked to produce certain documents that being no mention under what authority or power the notice has been issued. The petitioners who have received the notices have a right to be satisfied that the impugned notices have been issued under due process of law and unless the source of power and authority is mentioned the petitioners has no means of knowing that the notices are authorized by law. The notices suffer from inadequacy making them no notice under law, therefore find that the notices in these Writ Petitions to be not being in accordance with law. The Petitioners are not under obligation to comply with the direction given by the impugned notices. 

	23. In the result the Rules in these Writ Petitions are made absolute. 

	24. In Writ Petition No. 2043 of 1994 that although notice has been served under Section 160 Cr.P.C. asking the petitioner to appear before the relevant authority for making statement and examination of documents the notice does not disclose what documents are to be produced. The words “সংশ্লিষ্ট কাগজপত্রের বিবরণ” has been penned through. The notice therefore suffers from serious defect which cannot be complied with by the petitioner in its present form. The notices is also vague and indefinite. We therefore hold the impugned notice Annexure- A is illegal and without lawful authority. 

	In the result, the Rule is made absolute. 

	25. In Writ Petition No. 4154 of 1992 the impugned notices, Annexures A and B have been served under Sections 94 and 160 Cr.P.C. which reads as follows: 

	“অত্র ব্যুরো কর্তৃক পরিচালিত একটি অনুসন্ধানের স্বার্থে নিম্নলিখিত কাগজপত্র গুলি সহ আগামী ১৪/১২/৯২ইং তারিখে সকাল ০৯.০০ ঘটিকায় দুর্ণীতি দমন ব্যুরো, প্রধান কার্য্যালয়, ১নং সেগুন বাগিচা, ঢাকাস্থ ব্যুরোর পরিদর্শক জনাব মোঃ মোসলেহ উদ্দিন এর নিকট হাজির হইয়া বক্তব্য পেশ করার জন্য অনুরোধ করা গেল।
	গত ১২/১২/৯২ইং তারিখে স্মারক নং- ১৫৯৯৩ মাধ্যমে আপনাকে দেয়া চিঠির প্রেক্ষিতে পুনরায় আপনাকে আগামী ২১/১২/৯২ইং তারিখে সকাল ০৯.০০ ঘটিকায় পরিদর্শক মোঃ মোসলেহ উদ্দিনের নিকট ব্যুরোর প্রধান কার্য্যালয়, ১ নং সেগুন বাগিচায় হাজির হইয়া বক্তব্য কাগজপত্রের সরবরাহ করার জন্য অনুরোধ করা হইল।”

	But the notices also direct the petitioner to submit the following documents:

	কাগজপত্রের বর্ণনাঃ
	১। আপনি যে সকল ব্যবসায়িক প্রতিষ্ঠানের মালিক/অংশীদার সেই সকল প্রতিষ্ঠানের নাম ও কি পরিমান শেয়ারের মালিক তাহার বিবরণ সহ কাগজপত্র।
	২। আপনার ও আপনার উপর নির্ভরশীল স্বনামে বেনামে থাকা সমুদয় সম্পদের বিবরণ (স্থাবর/অস্থাবর)।
	৩। আপনার বাৎসরিক আয়ের একটি বিবরণ।

	26. It would appear from the impugned notice that although it is supposed to be under Sections 94 and 160 Cr.P.C. the respondents have asked for list of documents relating to this property in his name. Such statements of property can only be asked for under Section 4(1) of the Anti-Corruption Act. To serve a notice under Section 4 (1) of the Anti- Corruption Act it necessary for the Government to be satisfied that the petitioner has property disproportionate to his known source of income. The learned Assistant Attorney-General submits that so far as the notice itself' is concerned the Bureau has the power to ask for documents and things under Section 94 Cr.P.C. and so the impugned order Annexure-A has been issued with lawful authority. However we observe that the notice has not only asked for documents and things but has also asked for statement of moveable and immovable properties in the name of the petitioner and his benamders. This statement obviously can be only asked under Section 4(1) of the Anti-Corruption Act, which requires the satisfaction of the Government. In the instant case the Annexure-A does not say that the Government or the Anti-Corruption is satisfied that the petitioner has property disproportionate to the known source of income. Therefore the impugned notice Annexure-A is illegal and without lawful Authority. 

	27. In the result, the Rule is made absolute.

End.

12. Before entering into the merit of these cases we would examine the validity and enforceability of the impugned circular from its legal perspectives. 

13. In the book named 'THE CONSTRUCTION OF DEEDS AND STATUTES', 5th Edition, the author ODGER has examined the legal position of a "circular" at page 420-425 as follows:-'Ministerial circulars and memoranda', "Apart from departmental and office communications, Government departments issue to persons and bodies charged with the duty of carrying out statutory functions numerous circulars and memoranda of the most varied character. There are circulars simply drawing attention to recent Legislation including delegated Legislation reminding people that something has to be done, giving advice or giving information on what has been decided departmentally. In some circulars the Minister gives his views upon the meaning to be given to a statutory provision. Such an opinion has no binding effect in law and when the Court has occasion to decide in a contrary sense a fresh statement is issued. Another type of circular which is purely executive contains a model of order such as a tree-preservation order to be made by a local planning authority."

 14. Thus according to Odger, Circulars are of three kinds, i-e, simply drawing attention to recent legislation and delegated Legislation, giving advice or information and the third is purely executive containing a model form of Order to be made by a Local authority. 
15. The impugned Circular was issued to the Deputy Commissioners from the Ministry of Forest and Environment comes under the nature of the third category which contains a model form of Order to be made by the Deputy Commissioners in issuing and renewing Brick Kilning Licenses and steps to be taken and the procedure to be followed in doing so. 

16. In the case of Blackpool Corporation Vs Locker 1948, I. K. B. 349 their Lordships held that "this type of circular are also called sub-delegated Legislation" and in discussing the nature of Circulars their Lordships further held that 'the regulations made under the power then confer upon a Minister to make Orders, in which case the exercise of the power is made known by means of a Circular to which the direction is appended'. According to Scott L. J. "Minister's "Circulars" were not mere executive directions but delegated Legislation with statutory force. conferring powers on the Corporation which they would not otherwise have possessed." 

17. ODGER has cited the following portion of the Judgment delivered by Lord Greene M. R. in the case of Carltona Limited Vs. Commissioner of Works, 1943, 1 ALL. ER 560 as to the role of Courts: "All that the court can do is to sec whether the power which it is claimed to exercise is one which falls within four corners of the powers given by the Legislature and to see that the powers are exercised in good faith. Apart from that the Court have no power at all to enquire into reasonableness, the policy, the sense or any other aspect of the transaction." It was further held that "if the delegated Legislation is ultra vires, the Court will strike it down." (Construction of Deeds and Statutes, 5th Edition, page-424). It is profitable to cite few lines from the case of Sparks Vs. Edward Ash. reported in 1943, K. B. 223 from Scott L. J. in this respect: "A bye-law, of the class we are here considering, I take to be an Ordinance affecting the public, or some portion of the public, imposed by some authority clothed with statutory powers ordering some things to be done or not to by done, and accompanied by some sanction or penalty for its non-observance. It necessarily involves restriction of liberty of action by persons who come under its operation as to acts, which, but for the bye-law they would be free to do or not to do as they pleased. Further, it involves the consequence- that, if validly made, it has the force of law within the sphere of its legitimate operation." "When the Court is called upon to consider the bye-laws of public representative bodies clothed with the ample authority which 1 have described, and exercising that authority accompanied by the checks and safeguards which have been mentioned, 1 think the consideration of such bye-laws ought to be approached from a different standpoint. They ought -to be supported if-possible. They ought to be, as has been said, 'benevolently' interpreted and credit ought to be given to those who have to administer them that they will be reasonably administered." "I think Courts of justice ought to be slow to condemn as invalid any bye-law so made under such conditions, on the ground of supposed unreasonableness." 

18. From perusal of the impugned Circular No. পবম-৪/৭/১২৩/২০০২/৯১২ dated 20.10.2002 it appears from its recital portion that the circular was issued under the Brick Kilning (Control) Act. 1989 as amended upto 2001 and also under Environment Conservation Act, 1995 and Rules framed thereunder with a view to implement the provisions of those Acts more effectively in practice. In its concluding portion, it has also recalled the circulars No. পবম(শা-৩)২১/৯৯/৯৮৭-dated 21.11.1999 and No. পবম(শা-৩)২১/৯৯/২৯১dated 07.04.2001 substituted by the present circular. In its paragraph-1, the Circular has stated that nobody can establish or run a brick field without prior obtaining a "No Objection Certificate" from the Director General, Environment Directorate and in making such an application the applicant shall furnish an undertaking to the effect that he has already started to raise the Chimney to the height of 120 feet and shall complete it within 4(four) months. The 2nd paragraph states that whenever any person apply to the Deputy Commissioner for a licence for Brick-Kilning, the Deputy Commissioner must examine whether such person has in the meantime obtained a "No Objection Certificate" from the Environment Directorate and that the Deputy Commissioner shall ensure that sub-section (3) of Section 4 of Act VIII of 1989 as amended upto 2001 has been strictly complied with. In paragraph 4 the circular also states that in renewing the brick Kilning Licence the Deputy Commissioner must satisfy himself that the height of the Chimney has already been raised to the prescribed height i-e, 120 feet and certificate required has been appended. 

19. Considering these directives with reference to the nature of a circular as has been examined by Order. we find that the directives were issued under the impugned circular were to the local authority to be followed by them at the time of issuing new licence and renewing old licenses for Brick Kilning and thus, we are of the opinion that they have been issued under certain Legislations with specific reference to those Legislations and the same derive its force and validity from the Legislations themselves namely, the .Brick Kilning (Control) Act, 1989 and the Conservation of Environment Act, 1995.

Articles 31 and 32 guarantee a right to life. This expression 'life' does not mean merely an elementary life or sub-human life but connotes the life of greatest creation of the Lord-A right to a decent and healthy way of life in a hygienic condition- It also means a qualitative life free from environment hazards".

24. The impugned circular states that it has been issued under those provisions of law for the purpose of conservation of environment. It is apparent that the scope of Section GA is very 
wide. Not only polythene but any commodity which may appear to be hazardous for environment, the Government may interfere under this Section in respect of production etc. and may impose conditions which the concern person(s) must obey. 

25. Mr. Muhammad Nawshad Zamir argued that in the absence of Rules the circular cannot 
be effective. The question of enforceability of a circular also came up for consideration 
in the case of Philips Electrical Company Vs. Commissioner of Taxes. reported in 45 DLR 190 and their lordships held that "if the circular do not refer any law on the strength of which it 
was made, the Circular cannot be equated with the statutory law as it was not made by the Parliament or by a competent law making authority." In the case of Muzaffar Ali and another. 
reported in 43 DLR (AD) 137 it was held that "All the Circulars beginning from 15.11.68 relating to exchange cases are relevant and could not be said had no authority to execute the 
document in question on behalf of the Government." It cannot be said that the impugned 
Circular has no nexus with the statutes it has referred to The Brick Kilning (Control) Rules, 1989 was issued under S.R.O. No. 421-Law/89 and published in the Bangladesh Gazette on 24.12.1989 containing only three rules which, under no circumstances, can be said exhaustive. 

26. The Brick Kilning (Control) (Amendment) Act, 2001 was published in the Bangladesh Gazettee on 11.4.2001 substituting sub-section (1) of Section 4 of Act VIII of 1989 as follows:-
“(১) লাইসেন্স ব্যতীত কোন ব্যক্তি ইটের ভাটা স্থাপন করিতে পারিৰেন না বা ইট প্রস্তুত বা ইটপোড়াইতে পারিৰেন না।
Section 4 of the Act VIII of 1989 made a Licence mandatory for Kilning bricks but the amendment made the Licence also compulsory for establishing a brick-field. By Section 3 of Act XXII of 1992 the Deputy Commissioner of each District was made the Licensing Authority and by Section 3(3B) of Act XVII of 2001 it was provided that on receipt of a report as provided under -Section 3A the Deputy Commissioner shall issue Licence in the manner prescribed by rules, as the case may be. Section 9 of Act VIII of 1989 provided that the Government may frame rules by Notification in the Gazettee for the purpose of the Act. 

27. After Amendment of Act VIII of 1989 by the Act XVII of 2001 the powers of the Government under Section 9 of the Act VIII of 1989 for framing exhaustive rules by Government Notification in the Gazettee remained unaffected and thus the government is authorized to issue Circular or Memoranda to give effect to the provisions of the statutes. 

28. According to Order, "Rules and Orders are called statutory instruments, when made under the authority of an Act. Under the British "Statutory Instruments Act, 1946, a "Statutory Instruments' means (i) any document by which is exercised a statutory power conferred on her 
majesty to be exercised by Order in Council or a Minister of the Crown to be exercised by statutory instrument, and (ii) any document which would have fallen within the definition of "statutory rules" in Section 4 of the Rules publication Act, 1893 and (iii) Certain confirmatory Orders required to be laid before Parliament." (Construction of Deeds and Statutes, Supra, P-314, 418). A Circular as such, contain both rules and Orders issued by the sub-ordinate Legislating authority which is also the rule making authority under the Law. Rules contain specific and prescribed procedure in detail but the Circular contain directives and while Rules are included within the ambit of the term 'law' the Circular is included within the term 'bye-law'. But a Circular cannot substitute chalked out, well-drawn and exhaustive rules. Though the Circular is enforceable in law but the Government is under obligation under Section 9 of the Brick Kilning (Control) Act, 1989 to frame rules containing specific and prescribed procedure in detail in .accordance with the terms of the Act. 

29. A licensee enjoys such rights that have been conferred upon him under the licence issued or granted by the statutory competent authority and therefore a licence is subject to terms and conditions of the provisions of the Statute, sub-ordinate legislation or bye-laws, rules made thereunder. 

30. Under Article 152 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh "law" means any act, ordinance, order, rule, regulations, bye-law notification or other legal instrument and customs of having the force of law in Bangladesh (Underlining is mine). As such, it cannot be said that the impugned circular is not having any legal force or lacking enforceability or suffers from invalidity.

 31. Mr. Maqbul Ahmed, Learned Advocate appearing in Writ Petition No. 6941 of 2003 submits that sub-section (5) of Section 3 introduced by Act XVII of 2001 is an absurdity 
in the context of density of population existing pattern of villages and plantation in the rural area. The sub-section provides as follows: 

“(৫ ) এই ধারায় যাহা কিছু থাকুক না কেন, উপজেলা সদরের সীমানা হইতে তিন কিলোমিটার, সংরক্ষিত, রক্ষিত, হুকুম দখল বা অধিগ্রহণকৃত বা সরকারের নিকট ন্যস্ত বনাঞ্চল, সিটি কর্পোরেশন, নিঊনিসিপ্যালিটি, আবাসিক এলাকা ও ফলের বাগান হইতে তিন কিলোমিটার দূরত্বের মধ্যে কোন ইটের ভাটা স্থাপন করার লাইসেন্স প্রদান করা যাইবে না এবং এই ধারা কার্যকর হইবার অব্যবহিত পূর্বে উক্ত সীমানার মধ্যে কোন ইটের ভাটা স্থাপিত হইয়া থাকিলে সংশ্লিষ্ট লাইসেন্স গ্রহীতা, সরকার কর্তৃক সরকারী গেজেট প্ৰজ্ঞাপন দ্বারা এতদুদ্দেশ্যে নির্ধারিত সময় সীমার মধ্যে, এই উপ-ধারার বিধান মোতাবেক উহা যথাযথ স্থানে স্থানান্তর করিবেন, অন্যথায় সংশ্লিষ্ট লাইসেন্স বাতিল হইয়া যাইবে। ব্যাখ্যা।-এই উপ-ধারা “আবাসিক এলাকা" অর্থ অন্যুন পঞ্চাশটি পরিবার বসবাস করে এমন এলাকা এবং “ফলের বাগান” অর্থ অন্যূন পঞ্চাশঢি ফলজ বা বনজ গাছ আছে এমন বাগানকে বুঝাইবে ৷"
32. In view of Section 3 of Brick Kilning (Control) Act, 1989 that 'notwithstanding anything contrary contained in any other law time being in force, the provisions of this Act shall be applicable' and paragraph 5 of the impugned Circular that "the Deputy Commissioners must inspire the intending manufactures to manufacture Block-Brick with new technology", we find that though sub-section (5) of section 3 of the Brick Kilning (Control) Act, 1989 as amended upto 2001 has imposed certain conditions on establishing new Brick fields and also on existing Brick-fields engaged in Kilning bricks in issuing or renewing Licenses, but they are the Act of the Parliament and it also appears from consecutive enactments/amendments on this subject that the Parliament has taken a tough turn to the Brick Kilning to the best of their wisdom having 
regard to the public health. The Government by issuing the impugned Circular has only translated the intention and purpose of the Acts of Parliament. 

33. In the case of Bangladesh Soya-Protein Project Limited Vs. Ministry of Disaster 
Management, reported in 22 BLD 378 the role of the Court has been underlined as follows: "The Courts are always alive to the paramount public interest, either in upholding the decision 
of the Government even to the prejudice of an individual or in the case of striking down as arbitrary or unreasonable, the public interest element is always, the criteria for doing so. The 
Courts all over the World in deciding an issue give importance always to the overall interest of 
the people at large which commensurate with the sense of social justice." 

34. The grievances of the Petitioners may have some foundations but that to be considered by the Parliament. Courts duty is defined and in the case of Madmnchi Ramappa and another Vs Muthaluru Bojjappa, reported in AIR 1963 (SC) 1633 (1637) their Lordships held that "What is administered in Courts is Justice according to law and considerations of fair play and equity however important they may be must yield to clear and express provision of law". 

35. We find nothing arbitrary in the impugned Circular or in the Act of Parliament. 
None can carry on Brick Kilning business without obtaining a Licence under the law and 
on the basis of a Trade Licence. Similarly a Licensee can not violate a condition embodied on the Licence or an undertaking which they themselves have executed and that "The concept of Legitimate expectation can not be given such wide interpretation so as to allow any wishful hope without lawful root" (MD. Hafizul Islam Vs. Government of Bangladesh, 11 BLT 65). 

36. We therefore find no substance in the arguments that the impugned Circular is 
violative to Articles 31 and 42 of the Constitution. The rest of arguments are for complete justice, "according to law, according to fairness, equity, good conscience, nature of arbitration, tempered with mercy" (Secretary. Internal Resources Division and another Vs. Nasrin Banu and 5 other, 48 DLR (AD) 171). 

37. In the result, all the rules issued in Writ Petition Nos. 7068 of 2003, 7073 of 2003, 7074 of 2003, 6941 of 2003 and 7189 of 2003 are discharged without any order as to costs. Orders of stay granted at the time of issuance of the rules stand vacated. 

End.
