full_judgment:
A.B.M. Khairul Haque, J: This Rule Nisi was issued at the instance of one Mr. Kazi Farooque Ahmed, calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the order as contained in Memo No. এস বি পি সি সি/০২/০৩ dated 22.8.2003 issued by respondent nos.2 and 4 with the approval of respondent nos.1 and 5 (Annexure-I-1), removing the petitioner from the post of principal, Shaikh Burhanuddin Post Graduate College, should not be declared to have been passed without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

The case of the petitioner:

2. The facts of the case, in brief, are that the petitioner was appointed as the principal of Shaikh Burhanuddin College (the 'collage' in short) by a letter of  appointment dated 22.10.1993 (Annexure-A) and while he was continuing as such principal, a notice to show cause containing charges was issued to the petitioner on 1.2.2003 and the petitioner replied to those charges on 3.2.2003 but ultimately this petitioner was removed from the post of the principal of the college, by an order dated 22.8.2003 (Annexure-I-1). Being aggrieved, the petitioner issued a notice demanding justice on 24.8.2003 (Annexure-K), through his learned Advocate but without any response, as such, this petitioner obtained the present rule on 27.8.2003.

The case of the respondent no.2

3.  Mr. Wakil Ahmed, Chairman, Governing Body of the College, respondent no.2, made his appearance through his learned Advocate on 7.10.2003. In due course, an affidavit-in-opposition was sworn on 11.1.2004. In the said affidavit-in-opposition the allegations raised in the petition was denied. In reply to the statement made in paragraph 4 of the petition it is stated that the enquiry committee found the petitioner guilty of corruption forgery, deceit and defalcation of the college funds and as such, he was removed from the post of principal of the college after due approval by the National University in accordance with the provisions of the Regulations. In reply to the statements made in para-6, it is stated that although the Regulations do not so require, yet the enquiry committee wrote several letters to the petitioner offering him the opportunity of being heard but the petitioner refused to receive such letters. A copy of the letter dated 27.3.2003 (Annexure-1) written by Professor Lutfunnahar Nizam, convener of the enquiry committee was enclosed with the said affidavit.

4. In reply to the statements made in the said affidavit-in-opposition, the petitioner in his affidavit sworn on 13.4.2004, stated that the petitioner was not aware of the formation of any enquiry committee against him and he was not given any notice to appear before the enquiry committee or to show cause as to why he should not be removed from service, that the letter dated. 27.3.2003 (Annexure-1) was never offered to the petitioner.

5. Another supplementary affidavit, sworn by the petitioner on 19.4.2003, was filed in Court.

6. A supplementary affidavit to the affidavit-in-opposition, sworn on 18.4.2004, on behalf of the respondent no.2 was filed. It is further stated in reply to the statements made in paragraph-6 of the affidavit-in-reply of the petitioner that not only one letter but as many as three letters dated 22.3.2003, 27.3.2003 and 24.4.2003 were issued by the enquiry committee asking the petitioner to appear before them offering him the opportunity of being heard but the petitioner refused to receive those letters. The copies of the letters dated 22.3.2003 and 24.4.2003 were annexed with the said affidavit (Annexures 3 and 4).

7. Another supplementary affidavit-in-opposition sworn on 19.4.2004 was filed in Court on behalf of the respondent no.2 annexing a copy of the enquiry report dated 6.7.2003 (Annexure-6) and also the report of a Courier Service and a G.D. entry, etc. (Annexure-7 series).

8. Mr. Mustafa Niaz Mohammad, Advocate, appears with Mr. Aftab Uddin Ahmed, Advocate, on behalf of the petitioner while Mr. Mainul Hosein, Advocate, appears with Mr. Md. Shamim-ul Alam, Advocate, on behalf of the respondent no.2.

Submissions on behalf of the petitioner

9. Mr. Mustafa Niaz Mohammad, the learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that since his joining the college on 22.10.1993, the petitioner worked to the best of his ability and because of his honest endeavours, as many as 11(eleven) new disciplines including Environmental Science. B.B.A. Computer Science, etc. could be introduced in the college and because of his untiring efforts the college was upgraded to a post graduate college, but in spite of all his contributions towards the uplift and improvement of the college, the petitioner was deliberately victimized, for no fault of his own, in removing him from the post of principal of the college in the garb of taking disciplinary action against him on vague and nonexistent charges. The learned Advocate submits that at the behest of some interested persons in the Government, a deep conspiracy was engineered against him through the former and the present Chairman of the Governing Body of the College along with others and on the basis of a sham enquiry report he was ultimately removed from the college in a most high handed and illegal manner for which the petitioner was constrained to take shelter of this Court under the provisions of the Constitution. The learned Advocate thereafter argued elaborately his different grounds for declaring the order of removal of the petitioner as illegal which are as follows:

I. The charges are vague,

II. Violations of the principles of natural justice in initiating the enquiry behind his back without affording him any chance of personal hearing in his defence before the enquiry committee.

III. The enquiry committee was not properly constituted.

IV. Violations of reg. 16(kha) of the Regulations,

V. Bias on the part of a member of the Syndicate.

VI. Malafide,

Submissions on behalf of the respondent no.2

10. On the other hand, Mr. Mainul Hosein, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent no.2, denies all the allegations raised on behalf of the petitioner and submitted that a charge-sheet containing specific charges were brought against the petitioner and on receipt of his reply, in accordance with the provisions of the regulations, a most impartial enquiry committee with highly educated and dignified members, was formed. The enquiry committee after giving the petitioner all opportunities of being heard in person conducted its enquiry and found him guilty of all the charges. Thereafter, with prior approval from the Syndicate of the National University, following the provisions of the Regulations, the Governing Body of the College duly removed the petitioner from the post of the principal of the college, as such, the writ petition itself is not maintainable. Besides replying to the allegations raised on behalf of the petitioner, the contentions of the learned Advocate on behalf of the respondent no.2 are as follows:

I) The writ petition is not maintainable since the petitioner did not avail the opportunity to file the appeal as provided for in the Regulations,

II) Disputed questions of fact are raised, as such the writ petition is not maintainable,

III) Rules of natural justice and the provisions of the Regulations were meticulously followed, in imposing the penalty of removal of the petitioner,

IV) Enquiry was conducted by a number of highly educated and impartial set of persons,

V) The allegation of bias on the part of the member of the syndicate is not correct.

Facts

11. We have heard the learned Advocates of both the sides and also perused the petition, the affidavit-in-opposition, the further affidavits filed on behalf of both the parties.

12. It appears that the Chairman of the Governing Body of Shaikh Burhanuddin Post-Graduate College, by his Memo No.- মপবি/এমডিপিপিএডিপিএ/১৯(১)/২০০২-১০২২ dated  1.2.2003 (Annexure-E), asked the petitioner to show-cause within 3(three) working days from the date of receipt of the said letter, as to why penal action would not be taken against him because of the charges stated therein. The petitioner duly replied to the said notice to show-cause on 3.2.2003 (Annexure-E-1) denying all allegations raised in the notice to show-cause. He also stated in his reply that the 2nd, 3rd and 5th charge in the notice to show-cause were vague and prayed for making those charges specific so that he can reply properly. On receipt of the reply of the petitioner, the Chairman of the Governing Body by his letter dated 5.2.2003 (Annexure-F), asked him to convene an emergency meeting on 6.2.2003. In his reply dated 6.2.2003 (Annexure-F-1), he stated inter alia that he received the said letter dated 5.2.2003 at about 10 O'clock in the evening, that he did not receive the specific charges as mentioned in his reply dated 3.2.2003 so as to entitle him to give a proper reply in support of his defence, that some of the charges are similar to those contained in the letter dated 4.1.2003, issued by the Assistant  Secretary, Ministry of Education, which is related to an action pending, before the Court, besides, he proposed to the Governing Body to hold the said meeting in the third week of February, subject to the decision of the Court, instead of holding it just before the Eid holidays.

13. It may be recalled that a Senior Assistant Secretary. Ministry of Education, section-4, Government of Bangladesh, by his Memo no.- শা৪/৭সি-৩/২০০১/৪৬৪ dated 10.11.2002 (Annexure-C), brought a number of charges against the petitioner and asked him to show-cause within 10(ten) working days, as to why action in accordance with law would not be taken against him because of the allegations contained therein. The petitioner duly responded to the said notice to show-cause by his reply dated 19.11.2002(Annexure-C-1) and also prayed to be heard in person in support of his defence which was renewed by another letter dated 17.12.2002 (Annexure-C-2). However, the Ministry of Education, by its memo dated 4.1.2003 (Annexure-D) requested the Chairman of the Governing Body of the College, to take action against the petitioner, in accordance with law including his removal from the post of principal of the College because of his involvement in the 7(seven) charges contained in the said memorandum. The memorandum dated 4.1.2003, issued by the Senior Assistant Secretary„ Ministry of Education, to the Chairman of the governing Body of the College, was challenged in Writ Petition no.313 of 2003 and a rule was issued on 7.1.2003 and the operation of the said memorandum was stayed. The Chairman of the Governing Body was the respondent no.3 in the said writ petition. But thereafter the Chairman of the Governing Body of the College, issued the impugned notice to show-cause dated 1.2.2003, upon the petitioner to which he replied on 3.2.2003.

14. However, it appears from the Memo no.- মপবি/এমডিপিপিএ/ডিপিএ/বিবিধ১/২০০২- dated  10.2.2003, that an emergency meeting of the Governing Body was held on 10.2.2003 (Annexure-F-2). In the said meeting, the majority members were of the opinion that the reply of the petitioner to the notice to show-cause is not acceptable. It was resolved in the said meeting that an enquiry on the allegations is required to be made, that in the interest of a proper enquiry, it was resolved to put the petitioner under suspension with effect from 10.2.2003, that it was further resolved that Begum Kamrun Nahar Ahmed, Chairman, Department of Political Science, would act as the principal-in-charge.

15. According to these decisions of the Governing Body of the college, the petitioner was put under suspension with effect from 10.2.2003.

16. In the meantime, after hearing, the rule in Writ Petition no.313 of 2003 was made absolute by the judgment dated 12.3.2003 (Annexure-G).

17. It appears that on the conclusion of the enquiry, an emergency meeting of the enquiry committee was held on 6.7.2003 in the chamber of the principal and the convener of the enquiry committee handed over their enquiry report dated 6.7.2003 (Annexure-6) to the principal-in-charge of the college (Annexure-8).

18. The petitioner, however, by his letter dated 16.8.2003 addressed to the present Chairman of the Governing Body of the College, the respondent no.2 (Annexure-H) informed him that none of the members of the enquiry committee ever contacted him, as such, he prayed for allowing him a personal hearing before the Governing Body of the College in his defence on 18.8.2003 when the report of the enquiry committee would be considered.

19. However, the principal-in-charge of the college, the respondent no.4 by her letter no. এস বি পি জি সি dated 22.8.2003(Annexure-I-1) informed the petitioner that he has been removed from the post of principal of Shaikh Burhanuddin Post-Graduate College, in accordance with the decision of the Governing Body, the respondent no.3 and as approved by the Syndicate of the National University, the respondent no.5. It appears from the said letter that the respondent no.3 on due consideration of the recommendations of the enquiry committee on the charges raised against the petitioner in its meeting held on 18.8.2003, resolved to remove the petitioner from his service and the decision was duly approved by the respondent no.5, in its meeting held on 22.8.2003.

The Disciplinary Proceedings: Legal Position:

20. Let us first consider the legal provisions in this respect.

21. This Shaikh Burhanuddin Post Graduate College is affiliated with the National University. The National University came into being by the Jatio Bishwabiddalay Ain, 1992 (Act XXXVII of 1992) (the 'Act' in short). Section 45 of the Act enables the University to frame necessary regulations to carry out its purposes. In pursuance to the said provision, Jatio Bishwabiddalaya (Adhivukta College Shamuher Governing Body) Shangbidhi, 1993 (the 'Statute' in short), was made. Similarly, in pursuance to various provisions of the Act, Besharkari College Shikkhakder Chakurir Shartabali Regulations, 1994 (the 'Regulations' in short), was made.

22. Section 13 of the Statute described the powers and the responsibilities of the Governing Bodies of a non-government college. Sub-section 2(uma) of section 13 empowers a Governing Body to impose punishment on the teachers and others. Section 13(2)(uma) reads as follows:

“১৩ বেসরকারী কলেজের গভর্নিং বডির ক্ষমতা ও দায়িত্বঃ

(১)-----------------

(২)-----------------

(ঙ)শিক্ষক কর্মকর্তা ও কর্মচারীর নিয়োগ, ছুটি, শাস্তিমূলক ব্যবস্থা, বেতনক্রম, ভাতা, অবসরভাতা ও গ্রাচুইটির ক্ষেত্রে বিশ্ববিদ্যালয় কর্তৃক অনুমোদিত চাকুরী বিধি অনুযায়ী কাজ করিবে।  তবে শর্ত থাকে যে, অধিভূক্ত বেসরকারী কলেজের কোন শিক্ষককে সাময়িক বরখাস্ত বা অব্যাহতি প্রদানের পূর্বে অভিযুক্ত শিক্ষককে তাহার বিরুদ্ধে আনীত অভিযোগ খন্ডন করিবার এবং বক্তব্য থাকিলে তাহা পেশ করিবার সুযোগ দান করিতে হইবে। (চ)------------------।”

23. It may be noted in this connection that although the word অব্যাহতি was stated in the above provision but the word 'accused' (অভিযুক্ত) was used before the word teacher opportunity with the provision for allowing to refute allegations (আনীত অভিযোগ খন্ডন করিবার) as such, this provision is obviously made empowering the Governing Body of a college to impose a penalty.

24. Regulation 16 of the Regulations provides for disciplinary proceedings against a teacher in the college on the grounds of professional misconduct or moral turpitude. Sub-regulation Ka, as amended (Annexure-2) provides for enquiry by a five member enquiry committee while sub-regulation Kha provides that reasonable opportunity for being heard in person has to be afforded to the concerned teacher in his defence. Sub-regulation Kha reads as follows:

“১৬।শাস্তিমূলক ব্যবস্থাঃ

একজন শিক্ষকের বিরুদ্ধে গভনিং বডি পেশাগত অসদাচরণ অথবা নৈতিক পদস্থলনের জন্য শাস্তিমূলক ব্যবস্থা গ্রহণ করিতে পারিবেঃ  তবে শর্ত থাকে যে,

(ক) -----------------

(খ) যে শিক্ষকের বিরুদ্ধে অভিযোগ আনা হবে তাহাকে আত্নপক্ষ সমর্থনের জন্য যুক্তিসঙ্গত সুযোগ প্রদান করিতে হইবে।

(গ)------

25. But the above provision does not elaborate the extent of reasonable opportunity to be afforded to a delinquent teacher in his defence. But this far at least is understood that such an opportunity must not only be an empty formality or an apology of opportunity but must be a fair one in the circumstances, with a right of an impartial hearing in his defence on the charge(s).

26. In order to understand what are those rights and its extent, I would first consider the decision in the case of Ridge V. Baldwin 1964AC 40.

27. In Ridge V. Baldwin 1964 AC 40, Mr. Ridge, the chief constable of Brighton, was dismissed by the watch committee under the relevant provisions of law which provides 'the watch committee may at any time dismiss, any borough constable whom they think negligent in the discharge of his duty, or otherwise unfit for the same.' The order of dismissal was also affirmed by the Home Secretary. Lord Reid in the House of Lords, held at:

".....the power of dismissal in the Act of 1882 could not then have been exercised and cannot now be exercised until the watch committee have informed the constable of the grounds on which they propose to proceed and have given him a proper opportunity to present his case in defence."

28. The principle of natural justice has by now ingrained in the legal systems of all civilized societies. Our Supreme Court also in the case of Bangladesh Small Industries Corporation V. Mahbub Hossain, 29 DLR (SC) (1977) 41, upheld the principle adumbrated in Ridge V. Baldwin. In that case, the dismissal of an employee of the corporation was declared illegal by the High Court. Upholding the said decision, A.B. Mahmud Husain, C.J. held:

"91. -----------------------------

(a) If an employee is dismissed or his service is terminated in contravention of a mandatory statutory provision, the employee has a right of action either in a superior Court in its writ jurisdiction or a Civil Court.

(b) If the service of its employee is terminated in violation of the principle of natural justice, the employee has a similar right of action as in (a).

(c) If the office is a statutory one, the holder of the office has similar right of action as in (a) in case of termination of the said office not in accordance with the law, under which the said office has been created.

(d) In spite of the office being a statutory one or of public character, terms and conditions of the office may be regulated by contract, and termination of service in contravention of such contract, but otherwise than in the manner mentioned in (a) and (b) is not actionable for the purpose of reinstatement in the office,

(e) Terms and conditions of service prescribed by rules, regulations or any other form of delegated legislation made by a body under statutory powers are not contractual, but have statutory force and the dismissal or termination of service in substantial disregard of them will entitle the employee to a right of action as in (a).

94. Again an employee of a statutory Corporation of public character, who does not hold any statutory post or status can nevertheless maintain an action in a Court of law, on a limited ground, that of violation of any mandatory statutory provision as to the kind of contract or the statutory ground of dismissal, or on the doctrine of ultra vires or the violation of the rule of natural justice."

29. Having settled this way the question of right to a hearing, the next question is what procedure has to be followed if the relevant provision is silent as to such procedure as in the present case. Neither sub-section 2(uma) of section 13 of the Statute nor sub-regulation 16(Kha) elaborate as to whether a notice to show-cause with a charge-sheet has to be given, if so, what it should contain, whether an enquiry has to be conducted, whether a second notice is required to be given, whether the enquiry report has also to be forwarded and the like questions to satisfy the requirements of fairness in holding a disciplinary proceeding, are not answered. But these questions are of fundamental importance otherwise, the provisions as to the right to a fair hearing will be meaningless.

30. In these context, Mr. Mainul Hosein, the learned Advocate for the respondent no.2 submitted that since the Regulation does neither provide for giving a second notice to show-cause nor for giving a copy of the enquiry report, the instant disciplinary proceeding would not be vitiated for not issuing such a second notice or for not allowing a copy of the report. In support of his argument he relied on in the case of Sk. Ali Ahmed V. The Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs 40 DLR (AD)(1988)170 and also on the case of Md. Torah Ali V. Bangladesh Textile Mills Corporation 41DLR(1989)138.

31. In the case reported in 40 DLR (AD)170, it was held that in canceling the licence of a fire arm under section 18 of the Arms Act 1879, there is no requirement to inform the reasons of cancellation to the licensees, still in the facts of the said case, the order of the Government in canceling the licence was declared illegal as the said order was made in violation of the principles of natural justice. As such, this decision has got no manner of application to the facts and circumstances of this case.

32. In the case reported in 41 DLR 138, although it is said that a second opportunity to show-cause cannot be claimed as a matter of right unless the relevant service regulation provides such an opportunity but in the instant case section 13(2)(uma) of the Statute requires that opportunity to refute the allegations must be afforded to the accused teacher with a right of hearing before he is removed. Similarly, regulation 16(Kha) requires that the accused teacher must be afforded reasonable opportunity to show-cause in support of his defence. The legal position has to be considered in the back ground of these two provisions along with the relevant decisions. Let us consider some of the decisions in this context.

33. Even as far back as in 1885 in the case of Spackman V. Plumstead Board of Works (1885)10AC 229, Earl of Selborne L.C. said at page 240:

"No doubt, in the absence of special provisions as to how the person who is to decide is to proceed, the law will simply no more than that the substantial requirements of justice shall not be violated. He is not a judge in the proper sense of the word; but he must give the parties an opportunity of being heard before him and stating their case and their view. He must give notice when he will proceed with the matter, and he must act honestly and impartially and not under the dictation of some other person or persons to whom the authority is not given by law. There must be no malversation of any kind. There would be no decision within the meaning of the statute if there were anything of that sort done contrary to the essence of justice.

34. In the case of R V. Archbishop of Canterbury (1944)1 All ER 179(CA), in upholding the fundamental principle of natural justice, Lord Greene, M.R. held at page-181 H:

“If this had been a matter in which the Archbishop was exercising quasi-judicial functions and had to act in accordance with the rules of what is commonly and loosely called natural justice, it would be open to the comment and, I am disposed to think, successful comment, that a tribunal or an authority exercising such functions cannot perform its duty unless it  gives the person concerned a real and  effective opportunity of meeting any relevant allegations which may be made  against him. Merely to show a letter of that kind under the seal of secrecy to counsel or the friend of the person concerned obviously does not enable that person, who is precluded from seeing it, effectively to deal with its contents.

35. In the case of R V. Architects' Registration Tribunal Ex parte Jaggar (1945)2 All ER  131(KBD), in upholding the fairness of the proceeding, Lewis, J. held at page-I39 A, C-D:

"The tribunal had before them, and used, documents which should have been disclosed, or documents which the applicant was entitled to see if they were going to be used by the. Tribunal----- I am extremely doubtful whether anything short of telling the litigant what the information is and what source it came from would be giving him a real and effective opportunity of dealing with it. When that is not done, as it was not done in this case, and the tribunal have before it correspondence of this nature which is not disclosed, and the tribunal look at that correspondence and base what they call relevant questions upon that correspondence, it seems to me, as I view it, that is not doing what this tribunal in its position should have done, namely, if they looked at the letters at all, to inform the litigant what they contained and the source from which they came.

36. In the case of The High Commissioner for India V.I.M. Lall AIR 1948 PC 121, I.M. Lall challenged the order of his removal from the Indian Civil Service on the proved charge of nepotism and victimization. His challenge was on the ground, inter alia, that the order of his removal was not passed in due process of law. The relevant portion of section 240, Government of India Act, 1935, reads as follows:

"240.-(1) Except as expressly provided by this Act, every person who is a member of a civil service of the Grown in India, or holds any civil post under the Crown in India, holds office during His Majesty's pleasure,

(2)------

(3) No such person as aforesaid shall be dismissed or reduced in rank until he has been given a reasonable opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him."

The Privy Council addressed itself on the following questions for its decision:

"14. Three important questions of construction arise for decision, viz, first, is sub.s.(1) of S.240 qualified by sub-s.(3)?; secondly, is sub-s.(3) mandatory, or permissive? and thirdly, What is the proper construction of the words in sub-s.(3) "the action proposed to be taken in regard to him?

The first question above is not necessary for our purpose.

In respect of the second question, it was held at para-19:

“----the provision as to a reasonable opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed is now put on the same footing as to provision now in sub-s.(2) of S.240--- is mandatory, and necessarily qualifies the right of the Crown recognized in sub-s.(1) of S.240 of 1935."

In respect of the third question on the construction of the phrase 'A reasonable opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him', the observation of the Lahore High Court, as quoted at para-20 of the judgment of the Privy Council was as follows:

“20-------- The plaintiff's contention that there should be two enquiries the first to establish that he had been guilty and the second to determine what should be the appropriate punishment, and that in each stage be should have reasonable and independent opportunities to defend and show cause does not appear to be correct or intended by the Legislature."

In contradistinction to what was held by the High Court, the position of I.M. Lall was correctly found by the learned Chief Justice of the Federal Court, as quoted from the judgment of the Privy Council at para-11:

"He had received the general invitation to show cause against possible dismissal (amongst other possible punishments) included at the end of the charges originally served on him. But no opportunity to show cause against dismissal was given to him, after dismissal had passed from being a possible punishment to the punishment proposed and recommended. At no time, was he given an opportunity, before dismissal, of making representations against the accuracy of facts found by Mr. Anderson or Mr. Brayne in their reports or against he adverse deductions drawn against him, particularly by Mr. Brayne.

In this regard, the majority view of the Federal Court, as expressed by the learned Chief Justice, as quoted in the judgment of the Privy Council, is as follows at para-20:

"....but the real point of the sub-section is in our judgment that the person who is to be  dismissed or reduced must know that that  punishment is proposed as the punishment for certain acts or omissions on his part and must he told the grounds on which it is proposed to take such action and must be  given a reasonable opportunity of showing cause why such punishment should not be imposed."

On appeal, the Privy Council disagreed with the views of the High Court and upheld the majority view of the Federal Court. Lord Thankerton on behalf' of the Council held at para-21-22:

"21.In the opinion of their Lordships, no action is proposed within the meaning of the sub-section until a definite conclusion has been come to on the charges and the actual punishment to follow is provisionally determined on. Prior to that stage, the charges are unproved and the suggested punishments are merely hypothetical. It is on that stage being reached that the statute gives the civil servant the opportunity for which sub-s.(3) makes provision. Their Lordships would only add that they see no difficulty in the statutory opportunity being reasonably afforded at more than one stage.  If the civil servant has been through an enquiry under R.55, it would not be reasonable that he should ask for a repetition of that stage, if duly carried out but that would not exhaust his statutory right, and he would still be entitled to represent against the punishment proposed as the result of the findings of the enquiry.

22. On this view of the proper construction of sub-s.(3) of S.240. it is not disputed that the respondent has not been given the opportunity to which he is entitled thereunder, and the purported removal of the respondent on 10th August 1940, did not  conform to the mandatory requirements of sub-s.(3) of S.240, and was void and  inoperative.

It would appear from analysis of the judgment of the Privy Council that although sub-section 3 of section 240 of the Government of India Act, did not in so many words provide for show-cause at two stages, still, on the interpretation of the said provision found that the initial show-cause speaks about the punishment only provisionally and was mere hypothetical but only when a definite opinion on the charges has been reached, the employee is entitled to another opportunity to represent which is the second notice.

37. It may be noted that section 13(2)(uma) of the Jatio Bishwabiddalay Statute, 1993 and regulation 16(Kha), read together, are similar to the provision of section 240(3) of the Act of 1935.

38. In the case of Suwarn Transport Co. Ltd, V. Appellate Authority, Madhya Pradesh, Nagpur etc. AIR 1956 Nagpur 235, where it was found that in refusing the route permit to the appellant, the appellate authority considered another report, as such, quashing the order of the Appellate Authority, Hidayatullah C.J. and Kotwal J. in stressing the .utmost need of a fair hearing and a proper opportunity for being heard, held:

“13. --------

The requirement is not fulfilled where there is mere lip service done to the principles of natural justice and an audience allowed which amounts to nothing. There must be always a substantial opportunity and proper latitude to meet everything which is likely to be considered against a party."   In the case of M/S. Kharavela Industries Pvt. Ltd. V. Orissa State Financial Corporation AIR 1985 Orissa 153, in connection with declaring the taking over of an industrial concern as illegal for not complying with the principles of natural justice, G.B. Patnaik, J. held at para-11:

"Where a statute authorizing interference with property or civil rights was silent on the question of notice and hearing, the Court, drawing upon the authority of the older cases, invoked "the justice of the common law" to "supply the omission of the legislature"

40. In the case of Fazlul Huq Chowdhury V. Govt. of Bangladesh 30 DLR (1978)144, although there was no provision for issuing a second notice to show-cause under the Government Servant (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1976, still upholding the decision of the I.M.Lall’s case, it was held that the petitioner was entitled to the second notice to show-cause.

41. In the similar context, Lord Morris of Borth-y-Gest, in the case of Ridge V. Baldwin quoting Byles J. dealt with the matter thus at:

"If it be assumed that no regulations had been made then the fact that section 191(4) is silent as to any procedure for a hearing does not involve that there could be a dismissal without a hearing. The "justice of the common law" would require it, for, as Byles J. said in Cooper V. Wandsworth Board of Works, "a long course of decisions, beginning with Dr. Bentley's case and ending with some very recent cases, establish, that although there are no positive words in a statute requiring that the party shall be heard, yet the justice of the common law will supply the omission of the legislature.

42. Professor Sir William Wade, in his celebrated works, Administrative Law, Eighth Edition, 2000, narrated Dr. Bentley's case thus at page-470:

"According to one picturesque judicial dictum, the first hearing in human history was given in the Garden of Eden:

I remember to have heard it observed by a very learned man upon such an occasion that even God himself did not pass sentence upon Adam before he was called upon to make his defence. 'Adam says God, where art thou? Hast thou not eaten of the tree, whereof I commanded thee that thou shouldst not eat? And the same question was put to Eve also.

This was in Bentley's case, in which the University of Cambridge had deprived that recalcitrant scholar of his degrees on account of his misconduct in insulting the Vice-Chancellor's court; but he was reinstated on a mandamus from the Court of the Kung's Bench on the ground that deprivation was unjustifiable and that, in any case he should have received notice so that he could make his defence as required by the laws of God and man. This is a nice example of the old conception of natural justice as divine and eternal law."

43. The above noted decisions would Show that the Superior Courts all over the Globe insist in the fairness of the proceedings. Generally the procedures as spelt out in the written instruments, such as, the Constitution of a country or the statutes made there-under, or the Rules or Regulations made in pursuance to such statutes, ensure that principles of natural justice are followed and the fairness in the proceedings are sought to be strictly maintained. Even in case, if the relevant statute in some way tends to curtail the right to a fair hearing or the principles of natural justice. Chief Justice Coke and Chief Justice Hobart went so far to say that such an Act of parliament is void, in itself.

44. Rather, principles of natural justice, reasonability and overall fairness in the entire disciplinary proceeding must he read into the Rules and Regulations.

45. Under such circumstances, in view of the provisions of section 13(2)(uma) of the Statute, regulation 16(kha) of the Regulations and the decisions discussed above we are of the view that the fairness in the disciplinary proceedings require that a second opportunity must be afforded to the accused teacher with a copy of the enquiry report, because, in the language of Mustafa Kama, J (as his Lordships then was) in the case of Md. Torab Ali V. Bangladesh Textile Mills Corporation 41 DLR 138 at page 142 pars 10:

"A second show cause notice is, in fact the accused employee's last opportunity to place his side of the case heave the appointing authority who is about to take the last decision against the accused employee armed with the report of the enquiry officer. The accused employee has the burden of disabusing the mind of the appointing authority from the impression created by the report of the enquiry officer. If he does not get a copy of the report, he has no means of knowing what finding or findings of the enquiry officer have gone against him and what have weighed with the appointing authority in coming to a decision as to the punishment proposed to be inflicted upon him. He does not know on what point or points he should address himself to the appointing authority. Without the report he is groping in the dark. The second show cause notice no doubt requires him only to show cause why the proposed punishment shall not be inflicted upon him. But upon perusal of his reply the appointing, authority may still take any view of his guilt. The second show cause notice therefore is not an idle formality. In order to be meaningful it has to be accompanied or followed by the report of the enquiry officer. So whether or not rules or regulations provide a copy of the report to be given to the accused employee, the rules of natural justice require that along with the second show cause notice that accused employee should be finished with the same. Failure to do so will be a failure to comply with the principles of natural justice which will be read into the Rules or Regulations.

46. In this connection, another matter of great importance requires due attention. The principle of proportionality. This is the latest innovation again to achieve ultimate fairness in any situation where the authorities are required to take a decision which may adversely affect a person or a body. In simple language this principle invokes scrutiny by Courts in respect of the severity of the penalties unduly imposed by the concerned Authorities, although within its powers, so that the Authorities act reasonably within the meaning of Wedenesbury principle propounded by Lord Green. M. R. (1948)1 KB 223 (1947)2 All ER 680 CA. Hower, Lord Slynn of Hadley in R V. Chief Constable of Sussex (1999)1 All ER 129 HL= (1999)2 AC 418 considering in the Wednesbury reasonableness and the principle of proportionality observed (at page 145 h) that though those are different in some ways but whichever lest is adopted the result is same. Lord Cooke of Thorndon in the same case approved (at page 157 (d) a simpler test "whether the decision in question was one which a reasonable authority could reach."

47. This principle of proportionality has also been accepted in our jurisprudence which would be evident from the decisions reported in 14 BLD (AD)(1994)171 and 55 DLR (AD)(2003)65.

48. In the area of disciplinary proceedings’, even if the charges are established the principle of proportionality ordains that the administrative measures must not be disproportionate to the proved guilt and be more drastic than is necessary. After all the purpose of the disciplinary proceedings are not to victimize any body but to dispense justice even in imposing a penalty which is just.

49. Under the circumstances, it would appear that in cases of drawing up of disciplinary proceedings against a person in the service of the Republic of Bangladesh or of any other public authority, the procedures as spelt out in the provision of the relevant service rules or regulations, as applicable to him, shall have to be meticulously followed.

50. But where the relevant Rules or Regulations of a public authority do not provide or ensure actual adherence to the principles of natural justice, fairness in the disciplinary proceedings and proportionality in imposing penalty or is silent about the procedure to be followed in case of disciplinary proceedings against an employee then also such procedure ought to be followed which satisfy the requirements of nano judex in re sua and aude alteram partem and guarantee an overall fairness in the entire disciplinary proceeding against the said employee and also the principle of proportionality. These requirements are summed up as follows:

I) A notice containing a brief statement of facts with specific charge(s), spelt out with sufficient clarity, giving date, time and manner of occurrence, enclosing relevant papers, if any, which will he considered by the enquiry committee or the concerned authority, with direction to show-cause within a reasonable period of time such as 10 (ten) working days as provided in the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1985. The notice must also state the punishment proposed to be imposed, in case the delinquent employee is found guilty of the charge(s).

A notice must satisfy the above noted all the requirements even the proposed punishment has also to be stated, so that the concerned employee can understand the nature and the gravity of the charge(s) leveled against him in order to allow him to reply properly in his defence.

II) if the reply is not satisfactory to the concerned authorities an enquiry officer or committee has to be formed in order to find out the truth or otherwise of the charge(s). In the instant case, this is provided for in sub-regulation Ka in regulation 16 of the Beshrkari College Shikkhakder Chakurir Shartabali Regulations 1994. An opportunity for being heard in person, is to be afforded, if so prayed for by the delinquent employee.

III) The enquiry has to be conducted in presence of the delinquent employee including examination of witnesses, if any with the right to cross-examine them.

IV) If the enquiry committee finds the charge(s) as proved and the authority decides to impose a major penalty a second notice, enclosing a copy of the enquiry report ought to be forwarded to the delinquent employee to show-cause as to why such a major penalty should not he imposed upon him.

V) On receipt of the reply to the second notice to show-cause, the authority would then decide as to whether a penalty has to be imposed upon him and if so, what kind of penalty. The recommendations of the Public Service Commission may be required in case of Government servants while approval of the University will he required under regulation 18(3) of the Regulations in case of teachers in the non-government Degree Colleges.

VI) The penalty must not be unduly harsh but should be proportionate to the proved charge(s).

51. These are not mere empty words but are gifts of centuries of intellectual exercises by the legal sages of the enlightened societies and save and except in the case of master and servant as noted in the case of B.S.I. Corporation V. Mahbub Hussain 29 DLR (SC) 41, the above provisions ought to be followed by all public authorities in order to ensure overall fairness in their actions.

52. Adherence to and meticulous compliance of the above noted procedure would ensure the compliance of ideals of the principles of natural justice and a right to a fair hearing. Any departure of any of the procedures mentioned above would surely curtail the rights of the delinquent teacher but compliance of these procedures would not prejudice the rights of a public body or authority including a University or an educational institution, in any manner, rather, ensure an overall sense of fairness in its dealings with its employees or teachers who are its the most valuable and precious assets in a modern welfare state.

Disciplinary proceedings against the petitioner:

53. Keeping these principles in view, let us examine the different stares of the disciplinary proceedings taken against the petitioner.

54. It started with the notice to show-cause dated 1.2.2003 (Annexure-E). It allowed only 3(three) working days to reply. This is too inadequate a time to reply. Even the notice to show-cause dated 10.11.2002 (Annexure-C) issued by the Senior Assistant Secretary, Ministry of Education allowed 10(Ten) working days to reply. But since the petitioner did not raise any objection to that effect, rather, replied within the given time such requirement of allowing adequate time would be deemed to be waived. But the notice does not contain the statement of facts based on which the charges were made. It does not either state the punishment proposed to be imposed upon the petitioner he is found guilty. These are not mere technical errors but go to the root of reasonability and fairness in issuing a notice to the petitioner.

55. It appears that the reply of the petitioner was not found satisfactory to the majority members of the respondent no. 3 as such a five member enquiry committee was formed on 26.2.2003. The convener of the committee by her letters dated 22.3.2003. 27.3.2003 and 24.4.2003 asked the petitioner to appear before the enquiry committee.

56. On behalf of the petitioner it was contended that none of those letters were actually sent to the petitioner and the enquiry was conducted behind his back.

57. On the other hand, Mr. Mainul Hosein, Advocate, strenuously argued that in order to ensure proper delivery of those notices, not one but two special messengers were assigned to serve those notices (Annexures- 1.3 and 4) but the petitioner refused to accept as such, those special messengers put their endorsements on those notices with their signatures that those were not received. When asked as to why those letters were not sent through registered post, the learned Advocate replied, firstly because the petitioner earlier did not receive any letter sent through courier service or even through by registered post, as such, in order to ensure delivery the convener of the enquiry committee thought it prudent to serve those notices by two special messengers. In support of his contention another supplementary affidavit was sworn on 19.4.2004 annexing Annexure-7 series.

58. Annexure-7 is the photostat copy of the face of an envelope which was sent by the principal in-charge to the petitioner through registered post on 30.4.2003 in his residential address but was returned on 12.5.2003 with the endorsement 'refused' but the said letter written by the principal in charge to the petitioner was not however annexed. The contents of the said letter was not stated in the affidavit either.

59. Annexure-7A is a photostat copy of the receipt dated 11.2.2003 of a courier service, namely, Dolphin Courier. It shows that a letter was sent to the petitioner on 11.2.2003 but the name of the sender was not written on it. Annexure 7B is the report of the messenger. It stated that on 10.2.2003 he carried a letter to the address of the petitioner but the security guards did not allow him to hand it over to the petitioner and reported that he was not there, (his flat) was under lock and key and nobody was available. This report does not, however, inspire much confidence as the receipt (Annexure-7A) shows that it was sent on 11.2.2003 but the report (Annexure-7B) shows that the said letter was sought to be delivered on an earlier date on 10.2.2003, but which letter was sought to be delivered on that occasion was not mentioned in the affidavit sworn by the respondent no. 2 on 19.4.2004.Annexure-7C is a copy of an information lodged on 13.2.2003 with the Kotwali Police Station, Dhaka, alleging that the petitioner not only refused to receive the letter of his suspension which was made on 10.2.2003 on the allegations of defalcation but threatened the messengers of the letter with dire consequence but the said information to the police did not mention as to the date when the said letter was sought to be delivered to the petitioner and by whom and where, was it at his residence or in the college, nothing has been mentioned in the said information to the police, these facts were not even stated in the affidavit dated 19.4.2004, save and except that it was sought to be delivered on 13.2.2003 however in paragraph 8 of the writ petition it is stated that the petitioner received the said letter of suspension on 15.2.2003. It also transpires from Annexure-7C that the college was on holidays at the relevant time. It is not understood who lodged the information with the police and why he stated therein that the petitioner was put under suspension on the allegations of defalcation, among others against him although no such allegation of defalcation (তহবিল তসরুফ) was mentioned either in the notice to show-cause dated 1.2.2003 (Annexure-E) or in the letter of suspension dated 10.2.2003 (Annexure-F-2).

60. Referring to the papers annexed as Annexure-7 series Mr. Mainul Hosein sought to justify the reasons as to why the subsequent notices dated 22.3.2003, 27.3.2003 and 14.4.2003 were not sent through post.

61. He also submitted that whether the petitioner refused to accept the concerned letters or not is a disputed question of fact, as such, outside the ambit of the jurisdiction of the Court under Article 102 of the Constitution.

Disputed questions of fact:

62. It is a settled principle that in a summary proceeding under Article 102 of the Constitution, the Court will not embark on an investigation on the disputed questions of fact which requires examination of evidence in depth. There are numerous such examples. In the case of Shamsunnahar Salam V. Mohammad Wahidur Rahman 51 DLR AD 232, the question of title and possession in the disputed lands arose. The decision of the High Court Division was set aside to that extent but the declaration in respect of illegal demolition of the structure was maintained. In the case of Bangladesh V. Habib Zamil 52 DLR (AD)174, the questions of transactions like exchange, partition etc arose which was not dealt with by the High Court Division. In the case of Director, Housing and Building Research Institute V. Darus Salm, 54 DLR(AD)111 there was unresolved serious dispute as to possession, which even does not come within the ground of exceptional cases where it could be disposed of by calling one to give his testimony but required adjudication on the basis of evidence of detail nature.

63. In this writ petition, the relevant letters are presented before us as annexures on behalf of the respondent no.2, to show that adequate opportunity was afforded to the petitioner for his presence before the enquiry committee and we are considering the legality of such an opportunity through such service of those notices which is a question of law and not of any disputed questions of fact. As such, we shall presently consider the objection raised by Mr. Hosein,  Advocate in juxta position to the facts and circumstances of this case.

64. The principles of natural Justice require that reasonable opportunity for being heard in person has to be afforded to the person about whom a decision is going to be taken which may adversely affect his interest. This opportunity is only reasonable and not absolute. Nobody would expect that the concerned authority would hunt down the delinquent employee in order to give him a personal hearing. But the principle of natural justice and the relevant provisions of law, in this case section 13(2)(uma) of the Statute and regulation 16(Kha) require that the concerned authority would take necessary steps to allow the petitioner such an opportunity which is fair and reasonable under the circumstances. A properly addressed letter sent through registered post would normally satisfy such a requirement. If it is returned without service with an endorsement 'not found' or 'refused', even then there will be a presumption of service under the law, provided it was correctly addressed and however, not rebutted.

65. In the instant case, the relevant three notices were not sent through registered post, as such whatever explanation Mr. Hosein may have, for not sending those letters through registered post there shall be no such presumption of service.

66. Besides, all three letters were addressed to the petitioner in the college. But it is not expected that the petitioner would be so available after his suspension specially when the letter of his suspension dated 10.2.2003 (Annexure-F-2) did not require his such presence in the college. Even the proceedings of the meeting of the enquiry committee held on 6.7.2003 in the chamber of the principal of the college (Annexure-8) duly signed by the convener would show that the petitioner never came to the college after his suspension. It was not stated in any of the three affidavits filed on behalf of the respondent no.2 that those notices, though addressed to the college, were also sought to be served in the residence of the petitioner.

67. In such Circumstances, the service of notices upon the petitioner in respect of holding of the enquiry, could not be established on behalf of the contesting respondent no. 2.

Enquiry

68. Let us no consider the enquiry report dated 6.7.2003 (Annexure-6).

69. In the instant case, the enquiry committee proceeded with their enquiry on the basis of the resolution of the Governing Body of the college taken on 10.2.2003. The exact resolution was not made available to us but the letter of suspension dated 10.2.2003 (Annexure-F-2) of the petitioner gives us an idea of the resolution of the Governing body which was taken on that date. In the first paragraph of the said letter it is stated that the replies of the petitioner to the notice to show-cause dated 1.2.2003 was not satisfactory. In the second paragraph it is state that the Governing Body also discussed the financial aspects of the college, considered the report of Dr. Nurul Islam in this regard and resolved that a full fledged enquiry on the financial irregularities pointed out in the said report is necessary. In the third paragraph it is stated that a resolution was taken to form a five member enquiry committee under regulation 16 or the Regulations presumably to enquiry into the charges brought against the petitioner in the notice to show-cause dated 10.2.2003. The following charges were stated in the notice to show-cause dated 1.2.2003(Annexure-E):

১) শিক্ষা মন্ত্রণালয়ের সিদ্ধান্ত অনুযায়ী বেসরকারী ডিগ্রী কলেজের অধ্যক্ষের সপ্তাহের নূন্যতম ৬টি ক্লাশ গ্রহনের নিয়ম থাকলেও কলেজের সার্বিক ক্লাশ রুঢিন পর্যালোচনা করে দেখা যায় রুটিনে আপনার কোন ফ্লাশ নেই যা ঐ আদেশকে অবমাননার শামিল।

২ ) আপনি কলেজ পরিচালনা পরিষদের নির্বাচিত শিক্ষক প্রতিনিধিদের মেয়াদ শেষ হবার পরেও বিধি বর্হিভূতভাবে তাদের কার্যক্রম অব্যাহত রেখেছেন এবং অভিভাবক প্রতিনিধি নির্বাচনের ক্ষেত্রে ব্যাপক অংশ গ্রহণের সুযোগ দেননি, যা শিক্ষক ও অভিভাবকদের অধিকার হরনের শামিল।

৩) আপনি নীতিমালা বর্হিভূতভাবে ৩(তিন) জন সহকারী অধ্যাপককে উপাধ্যক্ষ পদে নিয়োগ প্রদান করে আর্থিক ও অনাধিক সুবিধাদি প্রদান করতঃ তাদের ও ক্লাশ রুটিনে কোন ক্লাশ না রেখে শিক্ষা সংক্রান্ত নয় এমন কাজে তাদের ব্যবহার করেছেন যা কলেজের স্বাভাবিক কার্য্যক্রমকে ব্যাহত করেছে।

৪) আপনি সরকারী নির্দেশ মোতাবেক কলেজের আয় ব্যরের যাবতীয় হিসাব সংরক্ষণ করেননি। তাছাড়া আপনার নির্দোশ কলেজের সংরক্ষিত ও ভবিষ্যৎ তহবিল ছাড়াও একাধিক ব্যাংক হিসাব খোলা হয়েছে যা কলেজের স্বচ্ছতাকে প্রশ্নের সম্মুখীন করেছে ৷

৫) আপনি যথা সময়ে কলেজে আসেন না । বিগত কয়েক দিন কলেজ সংক্রান্ত জরুরী কাজে আপনাকে কলেজে খুঁজে পাওয়া যায়নি । আপনার অবস্থান সম্পর্কে কোন সদত্তর কোন কলেজ ষ্টাফ দিতে পারেনি ৷ কতিপয় অধ্যাপক অভিযোগ করেছেন যে আপনি যখন ইচ্ছা কলেজে আসেন যখন ইচ্ছা কলেজ ত্যাগ করেন। যার ফলে দৈনন্দিন প্রশাসনিক ক��জকর্ম সম্পাদনে যথেষ্ট অসুবিধার সৃষ্টি হচ্ছে৷

In the forwarding letter or the enquiry report dated 6.7.2003 (Annexure-6) the summary of all the above 5 (five) charges were mentioned. But it appears from their forwarding letter that they sub-divided the charges in I 8(eighteen) sections.

70. The first charge considered by the enquiry committee is as follows:

“অভিযোগ-১: শেখ বোরহানুদ্দীন পোস্ট গ্রাজুয়েট কলেজের সাময়িকভাবে সাময়িক বরখাস্তকৃত অধ্যক্ষ জনাব কাজী ফারুক আহমেদের অধ্যক্ষ পদে নিয়োগ অনিয়ম ৷”

There is no such charge in the notice to show-cause, still the enquiry committee found the petitioner guilty of the said charge because he did not hand over his personal file to the management of the college. The enquiry committee also made recommendations to take action against him under the provisions of civil and criminal law including taking of disciplinary proceedings against him. Such a finding is perverse in the eye of law when there is no such charge against the petitioner anywhere in the notice to show-cause dated 1.2.2003 (Annexure-E).

71. The second charge is as follows:

“অভিযোগ-২: ১ ৯৯8 সাল থেকে ২০০ ২ পর্যন্ত শিক্ষক ও কর্মচারী নিয়োগে অনিয়ম।”

72. We do not find any such charge in the notice to show-cause, so also most of  the 18(eighteen) charges which has got no nexus with the charges mentioned in the notice to show-cause. Let us mention the charges considered by the enquiry committee which are as follows:

“অভিযোগ ৩: অধ্যক্ষ উপাধ্যক্ষবৃন্সের ও শিক্ষক কর্মচারীদের বেতন ভাতা নির্ধারণে অনিয়ম৷

অভিযোগ 8: শিক্ষকদের পদোন্নতি প্রদানে অনিয়ম ৷

অভিযোগ ৫: কলেজের সাধারন ব্যয়জণিত অনিয়ম ।

অভিযোগ ৬: নির্মাণ ও সংস্কারে কাজে অনিয়ম ।

অভিযোগ ৭: অধিক সংখ্যক ব্যাংক হিসাবের মাধ্যমে আর্থিক অনিয়ম ।

অভিযোগ ৮: প্রশাসনিক অনিয়ম প্রসঙ্গ ৷

অভিযোগ ৯: কর্তব্য কাজে অবহেলা ও অনিয়ম।

অভিযোগ ১0: আর্থিক অনিয়ম ৷

অভিযোগ ১১: সাধারণ শিক্ষকদের অর্থ প্রদানে অনিয়ম।

অভিযোগ ১২: বিভাগীয় শিক্ষকদের অভিযোগ।

অভিযোগ ১৩: কলেজ শিক্ষক সমিতির কাজে, সকল অনুষ্ঠানে শিক্ষকদের বাধ্যতামূলক উপস্থিতি।

অভিযোগ ১৪: পরিচালনা পরিষদের শিক্ষক প্রতিনিধি নির্বাচন না করা প্রসঙ্গে এবং অভিভাবক প্রতিনিধি নির্বাচনে অনিয়ম।

অভিযোগ ১৫: হিউম্যান রিসোর্স ডেভেলপমেন্ট নামে পাঠ্যক্রম সূচী বহির্ভূত প্রোগ্রামখানী জাতীয় বিশ্ববিদ্যালয়ের আওতা বহির্ভূত  একটি প্রোগ্রাম। উক্ত প্রোগ্রামের পিছনে কলেজ কর্তৃক বিপুল পরিমান অর্থ ব্যয় করা হয়েছে ৷ যাহা অবশ্যই অপচয়ের সামিল। উক্ত প্রোগ্রামের উদ্দেশ্য মূল ক্যাম্পাস থেকে অর্থ যোগান দিয়ে আলাদা একাঊন্টের মাধ্যমে বিপুল পরিমান টাকা খরচ করা; যে জন্যে কাজী ফারুক সাহেবকে এককভাবে দায়ী করা যায়৷ তবে এ ক্ষেত্রে পরিচালনা পরিষদের ও গাফিলতি রয়েছে।
