অভিযোগ ১৮: ব্যবস্থাপনা বিভাগের চূক্তি ভিত্তিক শিক্ষক জনাব মোহাম্মদ আলীকে চুক্তির মেয়াদ শেষ হলেও পরিচালনা পরিষদের অনুমোদন ছাড়া চাকুরীতে বহাল রাখা।

73. Out of the above mentioned charges only the charge nos.5 and 7 and the charge no.14 may have some relevance with the charge no.4 and the charge no.2 respectively as stated in the notice but the rest of the other charges have got no relevance or nexus with the charges mentioned in the notice.

74. Besides, it appears that the enquiry report did not refer either to the charges mentioned in the notice to show-cause dated 1.2.2003 (Annexure-E) or to the reply dated 3.2.2003 of the petitioner (Annexure-E-1). It is very surprising that no where in their entire report extending to 16(sixteen) typed pages, the enquiry committee considered or referred to the replies given by the petitioner. Evidently, the members of the Enquiry Committee did not at all apply their minds either on the charges stated in the notice or the replies given by the petitioner. Apparently, they conducted an enquiry on the affairs and running of the college as a whole as stated in the second paragraph of the letter of suspension dated 10.2.2003 (Annexure-F-2) and not on the charges against the petitioner. In doing so, they addressed to the 18(eighteen) charges framed by themselves and found the petitioner guilty of almost all the charges. Those charges had hardly any nexus with the charges against the petitioner in the notice. As such, this was no enquiry as contemplated under regulation 16(Ka) and (Kha) of the Regulations and the report is a perverse one. Besides, as many as 16(sixteen) general comments were made in the report with recommendations which were uncalled for.

75. In exercising jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution generally enquiry report are not assessed but the enquiry report in this case is so illogical and perverse that we could not help commenting on it in the interest of justice, without actually assessing it in details.  After all fiat justicia, ruat coelum. In this connection reliance is made on the observations of A.T.M. Afzal., J (as his Lordship then was) in the case of Sk. Ali Ahmed V. secretary, Ministry of Home affairs 40 DLR( AD)(1988) 170 at para-20 page 175.

76. The members of the enquiry committee are no doubt highly educated, well experienced and distinguished persons but they may have had only a lurking and quite undefined impression about a domestic enquiry. Apparently they lack any idea about an enquiry in respect of a disciplinary proceeding. But as a matter of fact this is rather simple. As members of the enquiry committee, they were only required to find out the truth based on facts in respect of the allegations made in the notice to show-cause and nothing else but they miserably failed to do so.

77. It should be noted that the function of an enquiry officer or an enquiry committee is to find out the truth or otherwise of the allegations or charges contained in the notice to show-cause. They must confine themselves within the four corners of the notice to show-cause Containing the charges and is not permitted to travel beyond it. Their function is to make their own findings on the charges but are not permitted to make any recommendations and even if they do, it should be ignored. It is the concerned authority who would take their own decision based on the findings of the enquiry committee and not on its recommendations.

78. In this connection we could not help quoting what Lord Loreburn LC. said about the enquiries because it is quoted in numerous occasions by the learned Judges all over the Globe. In the case or Board of Education V. Rice 1911 AC 179 Lord Loreburn L.C. said at page 182:

"Comparatively recent statutes have extended, if they have not originated, the practice of imposing upon departments or officers of State the duty of deciding or determining questions of various kinds. In the present instance as in many others, what comes for determination is sometimes a matter to be settled by discretion, involving no law. It will, I suppose, usually he of an administrative kind; but sometimes it will involve matter of law as well as matter of fact or even depend upon matter of' law alone. In such cases the Board of Education will have to ascertain the law and also to ascertain the facts. I need not add that in doing either they must act in good faith and listen fairly to both sides, for that is a duty lying upon everyone who decides anything. But I do not think they are bound to treat such a question as though it were a trial. They have no power to administer an oath and need not examine witnesses. They can obtain information in any way they think best, always living a fair opportunity to those who are parties in the controversy for correcting or contradicting any relevant statement prejudicial to their view.

79. Under the circumstances, since the enquiry report has got no nexus or relevance with the charges mentioned in the notice to show-cause, it is no enquiry in the eye of law and it is to be disregarded.

80. It appears that this enquiry report dated 6.7.2003 was placed before the Governing Bode of the college on 18.8.2003 and their recommendations were also placed before the Syndicate of the National University for its approval on 22.8.2003. The distinguished members of both those dignified bodies were also expected to apply their minds judiciously on the charges stated in the notice, the replies thereon of the petitioner and the findings, if any on those very charges in the enquiry report. But apparently the distinguished members of both the Governing Body and the Syndicate did not at all apply their minds on those materials. It is only unfortunate that they failed to do so. Had they done so, they could themselves find out that the enquiry report was no where near the charges.

81. We are constrained to observe this because the interest of justice requires that we say so. The persons, whoever, they may be, if charged with a duty to perform such functions in respect of a person whose late will depend on their such exercise of discretion must to do so meticulously cautiously and with due seriousness, otherwise, injustice would follow and if challenged they shall also be answerable and their such decision will be liable to be set aside.

82. Mr. Mainul Hosein, the learned Advocate, next contended that even if the service of notices upon the petitioner about holding of the enquiry could not he proved but the petitioner knew that an enquiry would be held, as such, he also had an obligation to make necessary enquiries about holding of such an enquiry and he having failed to make such an enquiry cannot now take advantage of his own latches.

83. We know of no such provision which puts an obligation upon a delinquent employee to find out himself about holding of an enquiry and Mr. Hosein could not refer to any such provision or decision in support of his such contention. The obligation to notify is always upon the concerned authorities but to the extent of reasonability and nothing further.

84. Mr. Mainul Hosein, the learned Advocate, next contended that after his suspension, the petitioner was virtually absconding and could not be contacted inspite of their best efforts, as such, the enquiry will not be vitiated only because of his absence from appearing before the enquiry committee. In support of his contention he relied upon a decision in the case of U.P. Singh V. Board of Governors, MACT, Bhopal.

85. In the case of U.P. Singh V. Board of Governors, MACF, Bhopal AIR 1982 MP 59, a group of students in a college hostel, assaulted others so much so that the right hand of one of the students was practically severed and it had to be amputed and some other students were grievously hurt, as such, the Proctorial Committee of the college expelled the petitioners from the college holding that there was no denial of natural justice on the special facts of the case. G.O. Singh, C.J. held at pars-8:

"8 .----The situation after the incident in the college campus was tense and immediate  action was needed. A search for the petitioners was made but none of them was available in the college campus. The petitioners were absconding. The Committee had with it the first information report and the two statements in the form of letters of Bharil and Shastri and acting upon them the Committee recommended the expulsion of four of the petitioners. In our opinion,  having regard to the situation that was created by the incident and the fact that the petitioners were not available for being heard it cannot be said that the expulsion  order suffers from denial of natural  justice. --Notices were pasted on the notice hoard and thereafter final decision was taken to expel them also. The petitioners were obviously absconding: they were not found in the college campus. They cannot complain of failure to follow the requirements of natural justice as their own act of absconding from the college campus made it impracticable for the authorities to notice them before taking final action. It cannot be lost sight of that the power of a Principal, which in the instant case was exercised on the recommendations made by the Proctorial Committee is a power of summary expulsion. It is so mentioned in the prospectus. No detailed enquiry is required by the prospectus before any punishment for indiscipline is inflicted by the Principal. Having regard to all the circumstances of the case, in our opinion the power of expulsion was fairly and honestly exercised and no case is made out for interference under Art. 226 of the Constitution.

The allegations raked against the petitioners of the said case have got no near nexus with the facts of the present case.

86. But even in the said case the learned Judge upheld the principles of natural justice in his decision at para-10:

"10. Before parting with the case we must state that we have assumed that a student  can file a petition under Art.226 of the  Constitution for quashing of an order of expulsion for acts of indiscipline if rules of natural justice have not been followed even though there is no statute or statutory rule on the subject. Cases of use of unfair means in examinations stand on a different footing for examinations and punishment for use of unfair means in them are regulated by statutes and ordinances made under the universities Act.

87. Mr. Hosein next argued that even if, for argument's sake assuming but not admitting that personal hearing could not be afforded to the petitioner, still he had under regulation 18, a right of appeal before the Syndicate where his such rights could have been vindicated and even if any lacuna was left in the decision of the Governing Body, this could have been cured at the hearing before the Syndicate in appeal. In support of his argument he relies on the decision in the case of Lloyd V. Mc Mohan where inspite of apparent defect in the procedure the decision of the auditor was upheld by the house of Lords. But before we consider the said decision we would like to refer to an earlier decision on this point, the case of Calvin V. Carr where most of the earlier decisions were considered. The question how far a procedural Failure at the first instance can be cured at the appellate stage was considered by the Privy Council in Calvin V. Carr (1979)1 All ER 440 PC = 1980 AC 574, in which an appeal was held to cure an initial decision of the stewards in disqualifying the owner of a horse. After considering all relevant authorities Lord Wilberforce held at page 449 f.g:

“Their Lordships regard this as a decision that in the context namely one of regulations concerning establishments procedures, justice can be held to be done if, after all these procedures had been gone through the dismissed person has had a fair hearing and put his case. It is thus an authority in favouring the existence of the intermediate category but not necessarily one in favour of a general rule that first instance defects are cured by an appeal. Their Lordships are also of opinion that the phrase 'hearing of evidence de novo'. Though useful in that case does not provide a universal solvent. What is required is examination of the hearing process original and appeal as a whole, and a decision on the question whether after it has been gone through the complainant has had a Lair deal of the kind that he bargained for"

His Lordships Further held at page 451 c:

"Their Lordships agree and have given their reasons for concluding that in this field there is no automatic rule. But they do not understand the Court of Appeal to be subscribing to a view that cases of 'insulation' of 'curing' alter a full hearing by an appellate body may not exist: on the contrary Cooke J expresses the opinion that the court in the exercise of its discretion, when reviewing the domestic or statutory decision should take into account all the proceedings which let to it, the conduct of the complaining party and the gravity of any breach of natural justice which may have occurred. This, though perhaps with some difference in emphasis, is their Lordships' approach.

Now we would like to consider the decision in the case of Lloyd V. Mc Mohan (1987)1 All ER 1118 HL= 1987 AC 625.

88. This case raises a question of considerable importance as such. I intend to discuss it a little elaborately.

89. This is the case of the Liverpool Councilors. They failed to make a valid rate, as such, the district auditor surcharged them consequent on the failure to make a rate or the delay in making the rate as due from the appellants on the ground that a loss had been incurred due to the willful misconduct of the appellants. The district auditor in his notice to the appellants enclosed the documents giving them the full particulars of allegations against them allowing them the right to make written representations which the appellants did but none of them prayed for an oral hearing. In due course, the district auditor issued certificates against the appellants. The dispute went before the House of Lords, mainly on procedural grounds. The question among others was as to whether there was an absolute obligation on a district auditor to give a personal hearing before issuing a certificate. On the question of procedural fairness, Lord Bridge of Harwich held at page-1161 d e:

"My Lords the so-called rules of natural justice are not engraved on tablets of stone. To use the phrase which better expresses the underlying concept what the requirements of fairness demand when anybody, domestic, administrative or judicial has to make a decision which will affect the rights  of individuals depends on the character of the decision-making body the kind of decision it has to make and the statutory or other framework in which it operates. In particular it is well established that when a statute has conferred on anybody the power to make decisions affecting individuals the courts will not only require the procedure prescribed by the statute to be followed but will readily imply so much and no more to be introduced by way of additional procedural safeguards as will ensure the attainment of fairness.

His Lordships found that the auditor's certificate will be effective only if no appeal is filed but the ultimate power to control the issue of certificates are entrusted to regular Courts. Whatever way the auditor decides, an unfettered right of appeal to the Courts lies both on facts as well as on law and if the court falls into error, the error can be corrected by the Court of Appeal or if necessary by the House of Lords.

90. In considering the procedure, his Lordship also "did not find--- what, in particular is required to provide such an opportunity in the circumstances of any particular case---“ It appears that the relevant provision does not require the district auditor to invite oral representations as a matter of law. On the question of unfairness in not allowing personal hearing his Lordship held at page- 1164 b c:

"If any had asked to be heard orally and the auditor had refused, there would have been clear ground for a complaint of unfairness. It has never been suggested that it was unfair that the auditor did not invite the appellants to address arguments to him through solicitor or counsel. The proposition that it was per se, in breach of the rules of natural justice not to invite oral representations in this case is quite untenable.

Lord Bridge next addressed to the Following question at page-1165 f:

“----whether, if there had been any unfairness in the procedure followed by the auditor, this would necessarily have led, as the Divisional Court thought to the quashing of the certificate or whether, as the Court of Appeal concluded, the full hearing of the appeal to the court on the merits was in law able to make good any deficiency in the auditor's procedure."

This is the very question which relates to the submission of Mr. Hosein.

Lord Bridge answered his own question at page-1166 b:

"Whether the auditor has decided to certify or not to certify, the court is empowered to Confirm or quash the decision to vary the decision if a certificate has been issued by the auditor, and in any case to give any certificate which the auditor could have given. The language describing the court's powers could not possibly be any wider. Procedurally there is nothing either in the statute or in the relevant rules of court to limit in any way the evidence which may be put before the court on either side."

91. The above noted case of Lloyd V. Mc Mahon, relied on by Mr. Hosein, shows that although the district auditor failed to allow oral representation, his decision in issuing the certificate was allowed to stand because of the following reasons:

I) there was no right of oral representation under any provision of law.

II) none of the appellants prayed for personal hearing.

III) the provision for statutory right of appeal both on law as well as on facts, with the  right to examine witnesses before the trial Court, then to the Court of Appeal and also to the House of Lords.

IV) the certificate issued by the district auditor is effective only where no appeal has  been filed, that is certificate has been accepted without any objection.

But even in this case the House of Lords recognized that "if any had asked to be heard orally and the auditor had refused, there would have been clear ground for a complaint of unfairness" (Lord Bridge at page-1164 b).

92. The question as to whether personal hearing in the forum of appeal, can cure the initial detects Lord Templeman in the same case gives the Following reasoning’s at page-1171 j - 1172 a, b:

"My. Lords, when by statute an appeal lies from a tribunal to a court of law, the statute must be construed to determine whether the court is Free to determine the appeal on the basis of the evidence before the court or is hound by the evidence or information laid before the tribunal. In the present case I have no doubt that it was for the court of law to consider whether 'willful misconduct' was proved and for that purpose to consider the evidence laid before the court. The task of the court was to 'give any certificate which the auditor could have given' (s. 20(3) of the 1982 Act). The court was not concerned with any defects in the procedure adopted by the auditor because those defects (if any) did not hamper the prosecution or conduct of the appeal. Different considerations apply if a statute only allows an appeal to a court of law on a question of law, or entitles or obliges the court of law to reply on the facts found by the tribunal. And  the detects in the inquiry conducted by the tribunal may be so prejudicial to the  aggrieved person that the court in its discretion may decide to quash  the decision and not to proceed with an appeal  on the merits in the absence of the views of the tribunal after a proper inquiry. In the present case the Divisional Court was entitled to consider the appeal on its merits and on the basis of the evidence presented to the court.

93. In the instant case the right of appeal is before the Syndicate, the same body which approved the removal of the petitioner but in the case of Lloyd V. Mc Mahon, the statutory appellate authority is not only a separate forum but the Court itself with very wide powers and which can issue a certificate just like the district auditor. That makes a great difference between an appellant in the case of Lloyd V. Mc Mahon and the petitioner in the instant case.

94. Under the circumstances, the decision in the case of Lloyd V. Mc Mahon is of no help to Mr. Hosein.

95. Professor Sir William Wade in his celebrated works 'Administrative Law' Eighth Edition 2000 at page 520, approached the problem thus:

"Whether a hearing given on appeal is an acceptable substitute for a hearing not given or not properly given before the initial decision is in some cases an arguable question. In principle there ought to be an observance of natural justice equally at both stages; and accordingly natural justice is violated if the true charge is put forward only at the appeal state. If natural justice is violated at the first stage, the right of appeal is not so much a true right of appeal as a corrected initial hearing; instead of a fair trial followed by appeal the procedure is reduced to unfair trial followed by fair trial.

96. On the basis of the discussions made above it would appear that only in exceptional circumstances, an appeal may be accepted as a substitute for the failure of procedure at the initial stage which may be of trivial or of mere technical in nature and can be cured by the appellate authority but otherwise not.

97. In the instant case the notice to show-cause itself being defective and the failure of the enquiry committee to give opportunity to the petitioner to he heard in person went to the root of the proceedings which could not be cured in appeal. Besides, the Syndicate which approved the removal of the petitioner, is itself the appellate authority, as such, do not satisfy the requirements of law as lucidly adumbrated by both Lord Bridge and Lord Temple man in the case of Lloyd V. Mc Mahon.

Alternative remedy

98. Mr. Mainul Hosein, Advocate, next contended that since alternative remedy has been specifically provided for in regulation 18 of the Regulation to an aggrieved teacher, the petitioner ought to have exhausted his such remedy before coming to the Court under its writ jurisdiction, as such, this petition under Article 102 is misconceived.

99. It is very true that one has to exhaust all available remedy before he avails this extraordinary remedy under Article 102 of the Constitution. But this is not of universal application. There are many situations where an aggrieved person can successfully maintain a petition under Article 102 of the Constitution inspite of other available remedies but found to be not adequate and effective or equally efficacious. Reliance in this respect can be made in the decisions reported in 27 DLR 476, 40 DLR(AD)206, 42 DLR (AD) 167. 52 DLR (AD)17.

100. In the instant case, there was gross violation of the principles of natural justice and the provisions contained in section 13(2)(uma) and regulation 16(Kha), in not allowing reasonable opportunity of being heard in person, the total failure of the enquiry committee to consider the charges in the notice to show-cause, even a copy of the said report was not given to the petitioner, besides, the Syndicate which is the appellate authority itself, approved the recommendation of the Governing Body in imposing the punishment of removal without considering the above noted facts and circumstances. Under such circumstances, an appeal before the said Syndicate would neither be adequate nor efficacious or effective.

BIAS

101. Let us now deal with the allegations of bias raised on behalf of the petitioner. It was stated in ground V of the writ petition.

102. It appears that earlier the Ministry of Education by the Memorandum No. Sha-4/7C-3/2001/464 dated 4.1.2003, directed the Chairman of the Governing Body to take action against the petitioner (Annexure-C), including his removal from the post of principal of the college. The said memorandum was challenged in writ Petition no.313 of 2003. After hearing by a judgment dated 12.3.2003 (Annexure-G), the said notice was declared illegal and struck off. In the said writ petition, Mr. Mainul Hosein, Advocate, appeared on behalf of the Chairman of the Governing Body of the College and on its behalf Conducted the hearing of the said writ petition. He is also a member of the Syndicate of the National University. It is alleged that Mr.Hosein participated in the meeting of the Syndicate dated 22.8.2003 where the recommendations of the Governing Body of College to remove the petitioner was approved. On these facts, Mr. Mostafa Niaz Mohammed, Advocate strenuously argued that since admittedly Mr. Hosein appeared on behalf' of Chairman of the Governing Body again the petitioner, the approval of the Syndicate to remove the petitioner has been vitiated on the principle that no man can be judge of his own cause.

103. In reply, Mr. Mainul Hosein, Advocate, did not deny any of the above noted facts. He submitted that he is an Advocate and in due discharge of his professional duties to his clients, he appears in various Courts on their behalf that in its normal course, he appeared in Writ Petition no.313 of 2003 on behalf of the Chairman of the Governing Body, nobody can question his such right to perform his professional duty, again, he is also a member of the Syndicate of the National University and in due discharge of his such calling. He participated in the deliberations in the meeting of the Syndicate on 22.8.2003, in its usual course in respect of the recommendations of the Governing Body of the College, for removal of the petitioner and since he was performing his such functions as a member of the Syndicate and not as an Advocate at that time in the meeting of the Syndicate its decision cannot he termed as illegal. He further disclosed that in the said meeting of the Syndicate, He said nothing ill about the petitioner, rather, he clarified the legal position. In this connection he relies on the decision in the case of Porter V. Magill (2002)1 All ER 465 H.L and submitted that the decision in the case of R.V. Sussex Justices (1924)1 K.B. 256, had already been overruled by the said decision of the House of Lords and is no longer a good law. Under such circumstances, he submitted that there is no scope for the application of the principle of bias and neither he acted illegally in participating in the deliberations of the meeting nor the decision of the Syndicate in approving the removal of the petitioner, has been vitiated because of his presence in the said meeting.

104. We have heard the learned Advocates of' both the sides on this point.

105. Now let us consider the legal position in this respect. It is well settled for the last 500 (five hundred) years, if not earlier that Nemo judex in re Sua, no man a judge in his own cause.

106. In Dr. Bonham's Case (1610), the concerned statute entitled the College of Physicians to impose imprisonment and fines for practicing without the licence of the College, half of which would go to the King and half to the college. On this ground, Chief Justice Coke disallowed the claims of the College of Physicians to fine and imprison Dr. Bonham for practicing in the City of London without such licence of the College because it itself had a financial interest in the cause.

107. Professor Sir William Wade in his Rook 'Administrative Law' Eighth Edition, 2000 at page 439 commented that Chief Justice Coke went so far as to say that court could declare an Act of Parliament void if it made a man judge in his own cause, or was otherwise against common right and reason. His such view was approved by Hobbart C,J in Day V. Savadge (1614) who said “even an Act of Parliament made against natural equity, as to make a man judge in his own case is void itself, for jura naturae sunt immutabilia and they are leges legum." Professor Wade further observed at page 439:

"It was also commended by another great judge, Chief Justice Holt, in 1701. Holt said that it was 'far from any extravagancy, for it is a very reasonable and true saying, that if an Act of Parliament should ordain that the same person should be party and Judge it would be a void Act of Parliament."

108. In the case of Dimes V. Proprietors of Grand Junction Canal (1852) the order of injunction and the ancillary order sought for by the Canal company which was an incorporated body against the defendant, were allowed by Shadwell V.C, whose orders were affirmed in appeal by Lord Cottenham, I.C. Subsequently on the discovery that Lord Cottenham owned a substantial shareholding in the canal company, the defendant sought to discharge the order passed by him. The House of Lords set aside the decree passed by the Lord Chancellor and the House Itself dealt with the appeal on merit and affirmed the decrees passed by the Vice-Chancellor. It was not shown any where that Lord Cottenham's decision was affected in any way by his interest in the company. His decision was set aside not because he himself was a shareholder of a company which was a party to the litigation but because he had by virtue of his shareholding an interest in the cause. Lord Campbell said as quoted from the speeches of Lord Hutton in Ex p Pinochet Ugarte (no.2) (1999)1 All ER 577 at page-596 g h j:

"No one can suppose that Lord  Cottenham could be, in the remotest degree influenced by the interest that he had in this  concern; but, my Lords, it is of the last importance that the maxim that no man is to be a judge in his own cause should be held sacred. And that is not to be confined to a cause in which he is a party, but applies to a cause in which he has an interest. Since I have had the honour to be Chief Justice of the Court of Queen's Bench, we have again and again set aside proceedings in inferior tribunals because an individual, who had an interest in a cause, took a part in the decision. And it will have a most salutary influence on these tribunals when it is known that this high Court of last resort, in a case in which the Lord Chancellor of England had an interest, considered that his decree was on that account a decree not according to law, and was set aside. This will be a lesson to all inferior tribunals to take care not only that in their decrees they are not influenced by their personal interest but to avoid the appearance of labouring under such an influence."

109. In the case of The Queen V. Meyer (1875)1 QBD 173, there was a dispute between one Harrison an owner of a farm and Enfield Local Board of which Mr. Janees Meyer was the Chairman. He sat with three other justices on the bench in the proceedings taken by Lee Conservancy Board against Harrison. Meyer swore that he did not directly or indirectly exercise any influence on the proceedings except so far as to recommend after the other justices had unanimously resolved to convict a mitigation of the penalties that he did not sign the convictions still Blackburn. J. held at page 177:

"The question is, was he so interested in the matter as that he ought not have sat '? Formerly, any amount of pecuniary interest however small used ipso facto to disqualify a justice. But statutes have in a great many, cases removed this disability. But the disqualification in the present instance is not on the ground of pecuniary interest. The question is was Mr. Meyer substantially interested though not in a pecuniary sense in the proceedings as to which these information’s were one step so as to be likely to have a real bias in the matter? In the present case there is such a real bias. Mr. Meyer was sitting as a judge in an information arising out of a matter in which he was a litigant party with the defendant: and although he states he took no part in the conviction yet he clearly ought not to have been on the bench.

110. In the case of R.V. Justices of Great Yarmouth (1882)8 QBD 525. Mr. Aldred, the Mayor who was himself appellant in one of the cases acted as Chairman with other magistrates to hear the appeals against poor-rate. After disposal of several cases when the case of the Chairman was taken up, he left the bench went into the body of the court and himself conducted his appeal. Field, J. in deploring and condemning the course adopted, quashed all the orders. Held at pages 527-8:

"The administration of justice ought not only to be pure in itself, and capable of being demonstrated to be so, but noting should be done by those who are administering it to throw on it a substantial doubt. It is not enough that the conclusion arrived at was right, and that it has been arrived at on right principles, for every person having a personal interest in any litigation, or having a direct or indirect motive for desiring a particular decision to be come to, should abstain from putting himself in such a position as that unconsciously to himself, a bias adverse to the due administration of justice might take possession of his mind. This principle is acted on in a case of less importance than that of the administration of justice, namely, the relation of principal and agent. Nothing is clearer than that where an agent takes a reward from the other side, or puts himself in the position of having a personal benefit out of the matter in which he is acting for his employer, it is not necessary to show any damage resulting, nor any bias in point of fact, it is enough to show that he has put himself in a position that is inconsistent with the fair and unbiased discharge of his duties.  The reason for this is plain, for it is impossible to measure the effect, great or little, that such a bias may produce.

111. In the case of Frome United Breweries Company Ltd. V. Bath Justices 1926 AC 586, the application for renewal of an on-licence of a hotel known as the Seven Dials Hotel in the county of Bath was refused by the compensation authority subject to compensation but three of the justices who sat as the members of the said authority, earlier instructed a solicitor to oppose the renewal which he did before the said authority. Objection was taken to these justices sitting and adjudicating with the compensation committee.

112. In the House of Lords, the minority view of Atkin L.J. in the Court of Appeal was accepted. Viscount Cave L.C, held at page-590:

"My Lords, if there is one principle which forms an integral part of the English law, it is that every member of a body engaged in a judicial proceeding must be able to act judicially; and it has been held over and over again that if a member of such a body is subject to a bias (whether financial or other) in favour of or against either party to the dispute or is in such a position that a bias must be assumed, he ought not to take part in the decision or even to sit upon the tribunal. This rule has been asserted, not only in the case of Courts of justice and other judicial tribunals, but in the case of authorities which, though in no sense to be called Courts have to act as judges of the rights of others. From the above rule it necessarily follows that a member of such a body as I have described cannot be both a party and a judge in the same dispute, and that if he has made himself a party he cannot sit or act as a judge and if he does so the decision of the whole body will be vitiated. My Lords, it appears to me that these considerations are decisive of the present case. The Bath justices, when sitting as the compensation authority under the Licensing Act of 1910, may not be a Court; But they are performing a judicial act for it  is their duty alter hearing evidence and  listening to arguments to pronounce a decision which may vitally affect the interests of the persons appearing before them. This being so, the justices who are members of the authority are bound to act judicially and not to sit if they are subject to that which is Reg. v. Rand (6) was referred to by Blackburn. J as a "real likelihood of bias"; and I cannot doubt that in the case of those three justices who took part in instructing a solicitor to oppose the renewal  of the licence of the Seven Dials such a real likelihood of bias existed. It is said that the justices in question did not themselves instruct the solicitor but only directed their clerk to do so; but this appears to me to be an unreal distinction.....and I fail to see how under these conditions the justices who had instructed him and whom he represented could be free from all suspicion of bias when sitting to adjudicate upon his argument."

Lord Sumner held at page-613-615:

"What, then is the real likelihood of bias in the minds of members of the compensation authority, who have previously sat at the Renewal sessions and have voted to refer the licence as redundant, when such a course, as is here in question, is pursued? It would be pedantic to expect that a justice who has recently held the Seven Dials to be  redundant, must come to the compensation  meeting with his mind as open as if he had never formed any opinion at all. Nevertheless, he has to take part in a hearing de novo, where fresh evidence may be given or old evidence may be improved or shaken by new considerations, and he ought to be capable to giving and to be likely to give these things his best attention. Again he may say, "I voted against the Seven dials before. I did not like the house though I own I did not quite know why but this gentleman's speech puts the objection admirably and I need trouble no more about the matter. "Half a dozen other things may be put, all leading to his voting as before and acting on the compensation authority more as a dormant partner than as an open mind. It is quite true on the other hand that if no solicitor were instructed the same justice might still act and think in the same way. He might even be himself as persuasive an advocate, when the members of the compensation authority retire to consult as the solicitor could have been during the actual hearing. Again it is quire true that he may be specially on his guard just because he has been into the matter before and has made up his own mind and has decided that a solicitor shall be engaged same direction. He may, on the other hand have forgotten all about it, and be able to take in the whole thing afresh. He may even change his mind and his vote too. Without intending the least disrespect to any of the justices of the county borough of Bath, I think the latter series of mental operations distinctly less probable than the former and consequently that, in the circumstances of the case, there existed in the justices, whose conduct is impugned, such a likelihood of bias as the parties interested in the renewal could not justly be called upon to risk."

113. In the case of Cooper v. Wilson (1937)1KB 309(AC), the Chief Constable purported to dismiss a Sergeant of Liverpool Police Force and his appeal was also dismissed by the Watch Committee in a meeting where the Chief Constable was also present in their deliberations in dismissing the appeal. In the Court of Appeal, Greer L. J. held at page-323-4:

“---- I think he is fairly entitled to complain that the presence of one of the respondents to his appeal on the Bench when they were deliberating as to whether they would or would not affirm his sentence was contrary to natural justice and that it thereby invalidated the decision of the watch Committee and entitled him to have a declaration to that effect. I ask myself what would any one have thought who came into the room where the Committee were sitting after the plaintiff had come out while they were considering their decision and found sitting on the Bench with the Committee one of the respondents to the appeal who had opened the case, though he had left the calling of the witnesses to superintendent Hughes. Such a person, if reasonable would have been likely to say to himself: "There has been an opportunity here fir one of the parties to influence the judgment of the Committee and it looks as if justice may seem not to have been done.

And Scott L. J. held at page-344:

"But even if the presence of the respondent sitting to all appearances amongst the members of the Tribunal could be said not to vitiate the proceedings, the fact that he remained with them when the Court was cleared for the Committee to consider its decision is fatal to the validity of the proceedings. It makes no difference whether he then discussed the case with them or not: the risk that a respondent may influence the Court is so abhorrent to English notions of justice that the possibility of it or even the  appearance of such a possibility is sufficient to deprive the decision of all judicial force, and to render it a nullity.

114. In my view this action is open to the same objections as the Committee's conduct in allowing the Chief Constable really the prosecutor on the rehearing and respondent on the appeal, to sit on the Bench with them but in a more acute degree as there was from the appellant's point of view secrecy and the risk of bias through the tribunal seeing one party without the other being present.

Scott L. J. concluded at page-348:

"However well intentioned the Watch Committee may have been personally in their desire to do their duty, which I do not doubt the Committee, constituted as a quasi-judicial Court to hear the appeal failed to confirm to those requirements."

115. In the case of Manak Lal, Advocate V. Dr. Prem Chand Singhvi AIR 1957 SC 425, a complaint was filed against an advocate on the allegation of professional misconduct and the complaint was sent for enquiry to the tribunal nominated by the Chief Justice of the High Court of Rajasthan. It was contended that the tribunal was improperly constituted since the Chairman of the Tribunal who is a Senior Advocate, appeared on behalf of the complainant himself in the proceeding in question itself he was disqualified From acting as a member of the said tribunal. Accepting this argument Gajendragadkar, J, observed at para-6:

"If Shri Chhangani was disqualified from working as a member of the tribunal by reason of the fact that he had appeared for Dr. Prem Chand in the criminal proceedings under S.145 in question then it would not be necessary for Shri Daphtary to prove that any prejudice in fact had been caused or that Shri Chhangani improperly influenced the final decision of the tribunal. Actual proof of prejudice in such cases may make the appellant's case stronger but such proof is not necessary in order that the appellant should effectively raise the argument that the tribunal was not properly constituted."

Although the appeal was dismissed on another ground but his Lordship held at para-7:

"We would, therefore, hold that Shri Daphtary is right when he contends that the constitution of the tribunal appointed by the Chief Justice of the High Court of Rajasthan suffered from a serious infirmity in that Shri Chhangani who had appeared for Dr. Prem Chand in the criminal proceedings in question, was appointed a member of the tribunal and in fact acted as its Chairman."

116. In the case of Metropolitan Properties Co.(F.G.C) Ltd. V. Lannon.(1969)1 QB 577(CA),  while Mr. John Lannon, a solicitor was assisting his father, in a dispute with his landlords about determination of lair rent occupied by his father as a tenant, he was appointed as a Chairman of an appeal tribunal to hear appeals from the rent officers, of which the same group of landlords were parties, although, in another area. But objection as to his bias was raised. Lord Denning M.R. found at page 598 G:

"So far as bias is concerned, it was acknowledged that there was no actual bias on the part of Mr. Lannon, and no want of good faith. But it was said that there was, albeit unconscious a real likelihood of bias."

Thereafter, his Lordship considered the issue at page-599 B-F:

"It brings home this point: in considering whether there was a real likelihood of bias the court does not look at the mind of the justice himself or at the mind of the chairman of the tribunal or whoever it may be, who sits in a judicial capacity. It does not look to see if there was a real likelihood that he would, or did, in fact favour one side at the expense of the other. The court looks at the impression which would be given to other people. Even if he was as impartial as could be nevertheless if right-minded persons would think that in the circumstances, there was a real likelihood of bias on his parts them he should not sit. And if he does sit his decision cannot stand. There must be circumstances from which a reasonable man would think it likely or probable that the justice, or chairman as the case may be would, or did favor one side unfairly at the expense of the other. The court will not enquire whether he did in fact favour one side unfairly. Suffice it that reasonable people might think he did. The reason is plain enough. Justice must be rooted in confidence: and confidence is destroyed when right-minded people go away thinking: "The judge was biased.

And his Lordship held at pages-599G and 600 A-E:

"Applying these principles, I ask myself: Ought Mr. John Lannon to have sat? I think not. If he was himself a tenant in difference with his landlord about the rent of his flat he clearly ought not to sit on a case against the selfsame landlord, also about the rent of a flat, albeit another flat. In this case he was not a tenant, but the son of a tenant. But that makes no difference. No reasonable man would draw any distinction between him and his father, seeing he was living with him and assisting him with his case.

No man can be an advocate for or against a party in one proceeding and at the same time sit as a judge of that party in another proceeding. Everyone would agree that a judge or a barrister or solicitor (when he sits ad hoc as a member of a tribunal) should not sit on a case to which a near relative or a close friend is a party. So also a barrister or solicitor should not sit on a case to which one of his clients is a party. Not on a case where he is already acting against one of the parties. Inevitably people would think he would be biased.

I hold, therefore, that Mr. John Lannon ought not to have sat on this rent assessment committee. The decision is voidable on that account and should be avoided."

117. The case of R V Bow Street Metropolitan stipendiary Magistrate and others ex parte Pinochet (no. 2) (1999)1 All ER 577(HL) arose out of a petition filed on behalf of Senator Pinochet, praying for setting aside the earlier decision of the House of Lords allowing the appeal. The appeal was filed on behalf of the Commissioner of Police of the metropolis and the Government of Spain praying for restoring the second international warrant issued on 23rd October, 1998. The Amnesty International (A.I) was granted leave to intervene in the proceedings. After hearing, the majority members of the House held that Senator Pinochet was not entitled to immunity and restored the warrant. Lord Hoffmann did not give his separate reasons for allowing the appeal but agreed with the speeches delivered by lord Nicholls and Lord Steyn. Subsequently, the instant petition was brought on the ground that Lord Hoffman was a director and chairperson of Amnesty International Charity Ltd which had been incorporated to carry out A l's charitable purposes. There was, however, no allegation of actual bias against Lord Hoffmann. The objection was based on the requirement that justice should be seen to the done as well as actually being done. In allowing the petition Lord Brow -Wilkinson held at page 586 code:

"The fundamental principle is that a man may not be a judge in his own cause. This principle as developed by the courts has two very similar but not identical implications. First it may be applied literally: if a judge is in fact a party to the litigation of has a financial or proprietary interest in its outcome then he is indeed sitting as a judge in his own cause. In that case the mere fact that he is a party to the action or has a financial or proprietary interest in its outcome is sufficient to cause his automatic disqualification. The second application of the principle is where a judge is not a parts to the suit and does not have a financial interest in its outcome but in some other way his conduct or behaviour may give rise to a suspicion that he is  not impartial for example because of his friendship with a party. This second type of case is not strictly speaking an application of the principle that a man must not be judge in his own cause, since the judge will not normally be himself benefiting, but providing a benefit for another by failing to be impartial.

His Lordship further held at page 588 def:

"The rationale of the whole rule is that a man cannot be a judge in his own cause. In civil litigation the matters in issue will normally have an economic impact: therefore a judge is automatically disqualified if he stands to make a financial gain as a consequence of his own decision of the case. But if, as in the present case, the matter at issue does not relate to money or economic advantage but is concerned with the promotion of the cause the rationale disqualifying a judge applies just as much if the judge's decision will lead to the promotion of a cause in which the judge is involved to together with one of the parties. Thus in my opinion if Lord Hoffmann had been a member of Al he would have been automatically disqualified because of his non-pecuniary interest in establishing that Senator Pinochet was not entitled to immunity."

His Lordship concluded thus at page 589 b:

“---my decision is not that Lord Hoffmann has been guilty of bias of any kind: he was disqualified as a matter of law automatically by reason of his directorship of AICL, a company controlled by a party. Al.

In the said case, Lord Golf of Chieveley, held at page 592 c d e f:

"The effect for present purposes is that Lord Hoffmann, as chairperson of one member of that organization, AICL is so closely associated with another member of that organization, Al, that he can properly be said to have an interest in the outcome of proceedings to which Al has become party. This conclusion is reinforced, so far as the present case is concerned, by the evidence of AICL commissioning a report by Al relating to breaches of human rights in Chile and calling for those responsible to be brought to justice. It follows that Lord Hoffmann had an interest in the outcome of the present proceedings and so was disqualified from sitting as a judge in those proceedings.

It is important to observe that this conclusion is, in my opinion, in no way dependent on Lord Hoffmann personally holding any view or having any objective, regarding the question whether Senator Pinochet should be extradited nor is it dependent on any bias or apparent bias on his part. Any suggestion of bias on his part was of course disclaimed by those representing Senator Pinochet. It arises simply from Lord Hoffmann's involvement in AICL; the close relationship between Al, AIL and AICL which here means that for present purposes the can be regarded as being in practical terms one organization; and the participation of Al in the present proceedings in which as a result it either is, or must he treated as, a party.

In the case of Porer V. Magill (2002)1 All ER 465 H.L., in 1989, a number of local Government Electors raised objections about the policy of selling council-owned properties as such, Mr. John Magill an auditor was appointed who conducted a detailed enquiry. In January, 1994, the auditor stated his provisional view about the culpability of the conservative leaders in a press conference. In due course in 1996, the auditor made his final decision concluding that the policy was unlawful and they had been guilty of misconduct causing financial loss to the council. The appeal against the said decision of the auditor was dismissed but reversed by the Court of Appeal. The matter went before the House of Lords. One of grounds for consideration was whether the auditor's statement in January, 1994, had given rise to the appearance of bias. Considering the issue on bias, the House modified the reasonable likelihood and the 'real danger' tests earlier propounded in the dictum of Lord Goff of Chieveley in R V. Gough (1993)2 All ER 724, preferred the reasonability test and Lord Hope of Craighead approved the following conclusions drawn by Lord Phillips MR in re Medicaments and related Classes of Goods (no 2)(2001)1 WLR 700,(at page 726-727 para 85) quoted in his judgment at page 507:

"When the Strasbourg jurisprudence is taken into account, we believe that a modest adjustment of the test in R V Gough is called for, which makes it plain that it is in effect, no different from the test applied in most of the Commonwealth and in Scotland. The court must first ascertain all the circumstances which have a bearing on the suggestion that the judge was biased. It must then ask whether those circumstances would lead a fair minded and informed observer to conclude that there was a real possibility, or a real danger, the two being the same, that the tribunal was biased."

Thereafter, Lord Hope drew his own conclusion at page 507 d,e:

"I respectfully suggest that your Lordships should now approve the modest adjustment of the lest in R V Gough set out in that paragraph. It expresses in clear and simple language a test which is in harmony with the objective test which the Strasbourg court applies when it is considering whether the circumstances give rise to a reasonable apprehension of bias. It removes any possible conflict with the rest which is now applied in most Commonwealth countries and in Scotland. I would however delete from it the reference to 'a real danger'. Those words no longer serve a useful purpose here and they are not used in the jurisprudence of the Strasbourg court. The question is whether the fair-mined and informed observer having considered the facts would conclude that there was a real possibility that the tribunal was biased."

His Lordship Further adds at para 105 b:

"The question is what the fair-minded and informed observer would have thought, and whether his conclusion would have been that there was real possibility of bias."

118. The auditor in calling the press conference made an error of judgment which may create a risk of unfair reporting but not a case of bias.

119. This reasonability test has got no quarrel with what Lord Hewart C.J. declared in the case of King R V. Sussex Justices ex p. Mc Carthy (1924)1 K.B.256.

120. In the case of The King V. Sussex Justices (1924)1 K.B. 256, the deputy clerk retired in the usual way with the justices, taking with him the notes of the evidence and that the justices came to their conclusion without consulting him. But objection was raised on the ground that the Deputy Clerk was a member of Messers. Langham, Son & Douglas, a firm solicitors, engaged in the conduct of proceedings for damages against the applicant in respect of the same collision as that which gave rise to the charge that the justices were considering Quashing the conviction, Lord Hewart C.J. held at page 259:

“---it is not merely of some importance but is of fundamental importance that justice should not only be done, but should manifestly and undoubtedly be seen to be done. The question therefore is not whether in this case the deputy clerk made any observation or offered any criticism which he might not properly have made or offered; the question is whether he was so related to the case in its civil aspect as to be unfit to act as clerk to the justices in the criminal matter. The answer to that question depends not upon what actually was done but upon what might appear to be done. Nothing is to be done which creates even a suspicion that there has been an improper interference with the course of justice."

121. If the test propounded by Lord Hope of Craighead in the case of Porter V. Magill, is applied to the facts of the above case, it would still produce the same result of quashing of the conviction of Mc Carthy.

122. As such, the contention of Mr. Hosein that the new test propounded by the House of Lords in the case of Porter V. Magill overruled the ratio decidendi in the case of King V. Sussex Justices has got no substance. The principle glorified in that case is that of ensuring fairness in a judicial proceeding and for that matter also in a quasi-judicial proceeding like the one in hand.

123. It appears that the relevant facts are not in dispute. It is admitted that Mr. Hosein appeared in the hearing of the Writ Petition no.313 of 2003 on behalf of the Chairman of the governing Body of the College and that he also participated as a member of the Syndicate of the National University on 22.8.2003, in its deliberations which approved the removal of the petitioner from the post of principal of the college.

124. On these facts, let me quote Lord Denning M.R. in the case of Metropolitan Properties Co. V. Lannon at page 600 B:

"Test it quite simply; if Mr. John Lannon were to have asked any of his friends; "I have been asked to preside in a case about the rents charged by the Freshwater Group of Companies at Oakwood Court. But I am already assisting my lather in his case against them about the rent of his flat in Regency Lodge where I am living with him. Do you think I can properly sit?" The answer of any of his good friends would surely have been; "No, you should not sit. You are already acting or as good as acting against them. You should not, at the same time, sit in judgment on them."

125. It should be noted, however, no body not even the learned Advocate for petitioner alleged any actual bias on the part of Mr.Hosein but as in the case of Lord Cottenham in Dimes V. Grand Junction Canel or like Lord Hoffmann in the case of Ex p. Pinochet Ugarte, Mr. Hosein may not be guilty of actual bias but he was disqualified as a matter of law by reason of his being the Advocate for the 'prosecutor in the earlier writ petition and a 'Judge' (member of the Syndicate) which approved the ultimate removal of the petitioner. Incidentally he is also the learned Advocate for and on behalf of the Chairman of the Governing Body in the instant writ petition.

126. Three incidents in this connection may be considered, such as, (a) appearance of the learned Advocate on behalf of the Chairman of the Governing Body of the college in the Writ Petition no. 313 of 2003. (b) his participation in the deliberations of the syndicate of the National University which approved the removal of the petitioner and (c) his appearance on behalf of the Governing Body, in the instant writ petition where the said order of removal of the petitioner has been challenged.

127. Now if the question which, Lord Hope asked in the case of Porter V. Magill in the last sentence of para 103, is also asked in the instant case, such as:

"The question is whether the fair-minded and informed observer, having considered the facts, would conclude that there was real possibility that the tribunal was biased."

The inevitable answer from a fair minded reasonable man who is aware of the facts of the case and its background would be that there was real possibility that the Syndicate was biased.

128. As such the said approval of the Syndicate of the National University, in its meeting held on 22.8.2003, in respect of the recommendation of the Governing Body of the college for removal of the petitioner is a nullity and the order of removal of the petitioner, communicated to him by the letter ref; no. এস বি পি সি সি/০২/০৩ dated 22.8.2004 [Annexure-I(1)], is liable to be declared illegal.

Allegations of Malafide:

129. Now the allegations of malafide raised on behalf of the petitioner against the respondents.

130. Mr. Mustafa Niaz Mohammad, the learned Advocate for the petitioner submitted that it all started with the issuance of a notice to show-cause dated 10.11.2002 (Annexure-C) by the respondent no.7 to the petitioner, containing 7(seven) charges but when he replied on 19.11.2002 to the said allegations contained in the notice and raised objections, the respondent no.7 again by its memorandum dated 4.1.2003, enclosing a report containing 24 pages, in a malafide manner asked the Governing Body of the college to take action against the petitioner, by removing him from the post of the principal of the college on the basis of the self-same charges contained in the earlier notice dated 10.11.2002. This memorandum dated 4.1.2003 was challenged in the Writ Petition no.313 of 2003 and a Bench of the High Court Division issued rule on 7.1.2003 and stayed operation of the said memorandum dated 4.1.2003. In the said writ petition, the Chairman of the Governing Body of the college was respondent no.3 (Annexure-D-1). But inspite of the said order of stay the Chairman of the Governing Body, the respondent no.3 in the instant writ petition, by its memorandum dated 1.2.2003, in a malafide manner issued a notice to show-cause containing 5(five) charges, all of which are vague, still the petitioner replied to the said notice but prayed for clarification in respect of certain charges and by another letter requested to hold the meeting of the Governing Body on reopening of the college after Eid vacation but the Governing Body, without considering his prayer or even refusing it, in hot haste on consideration of the report of one Dr. Nurul Islam, which was not even forwarded to the petitioner at all at any time and unknown to him, suspended him two days prior to Eid ul Azha although all the charges against the petitioner were vague and nominal. Referring to the letter of suspension dated 10.2.2003 (Annexure-F-2), the learned Advocate strenuously argued that the Governing Body had no right to suspend the petitioner on the basis of the report of Dr. Nurul Islam, which was prepared behind the back of the petitioner and according to the learned Advocate another instance of melafide conduct on the part of the members of the Governing Body. The respondent no.3, also appointed the respondent no.4 as the principal-in-charge superseding as many as 21 (twenty one) Senior teachers including 3(three) Vice-Principals, 9(nine) Associate Professors and 6(six) Assistant Professors (Annexure-M). He drew our attention that Syed Shah Alam, the former Chairman of the Governing Body was a Joint Secretary to the Government of Bangladesh, the present Chairman is also a Joint Secretary and incidentally, the respondent no.4, is the wife of another Joint Secretary.

131. The learned Advocate for the petitioner also drew our attention to the enquiry report dated 6.7.2003 (Annexure-6) and submitted that it has no nexus whatsoever with the charges contained in the notice to show-cause dated 1.2.2003 and a totally perverse one, still the petitioner was removed from the post of principal of the college at the behest of the interested persons in the Ministry of Education in accordance with directions given in the Memorandum dated 4.1.2003 which was earlier set aside in the Writ Petition no.313 of 2003.

132. The learned Advocate further submitted that the Governing Body considered the recommendations to the enquiry committee on 18.8.2003, its decision to remove the petitioner was approved by the Syndicate on 22.8.2003 and the order of removal of the petitioner was issued on the same date on 22.8.2003. According to the learned Advocate, this hot haste manner in removing the petitioner also highlights the malafide on the part of the concerned authorities.

<u>133. Since we have already found that the disciplinary proceedings taken against the petitioner did not satisfy the requirements of the relevant provisions of law and both the principles of natural justice and not fair under the circumstances, we need not enter into those allegations of malafide.</u>

<u>To sum up, we found as follows:</u>

<u>1) The charges contained in the notice to show-cause dated 2.1.2003, were vague and the notice itself was defective.</u>

<u>2) The enquiry was held in the absence of the petitioner without affording him reasonable opportunity of being heard in person as prayed for in the reply dated 3.2.2003 of the petitioner.</u>

<u>3) The enquiry committee did not consider the charges as stated in the notice to show-cause dated 1.2.2003 or the replies of the petitioner thereto, as such, it was no enquiry in the eye of law and the report dated 6.7.2003 is a perverse one.</u>

<u>4) The decision dated 22.8.2003 of the Syndicate of the National University in respect of the petitioner is a nullity on the principle of bias.</u>

134. Under such circumstances, the order contained in the Memorandum No. এস বি পি সি সি/০২/০৩ dated 22.8.2003 issued under the signature of the respondent no.4 [Annexure-I(1)], removing the petitioner from the post of the principal of Shaikh Burhanuddin Post-Graduate College, is declared illegal.

In the result, this Rule Nisi is made absolute but without any order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Mr. A. K. Badrul Huq, J: Shahana Begum alias Bakul (hereinafter referred as victim Shahana Begum) Was subjected to gang rape. Convict-appellants Nuruddin alias Shahahuddin and Mohiuddin and live (5) other persons had been depicted as the authors of commission of offence. Heinous incident occurred on 8.6.1999 in a jungle of Forest Department of Nijum Dhip. 

2. Gravamen mounted against convict-appellants Nuruddin alias Shahabuddin and Mohiuddin and other five persons Ibrahim, Fariduddin alias Mirasuddin, Mohiuddin, Belal and Shafiullah alias Shafi forcibly was that they carried victim Shahana Begun from her house to the jungle of Forest Department of Nijum Dhip and they committed rape upon latter. Victim Shahana Begum as a result of gang rape became senseless and her half naked body was recovered at midnight. 

3. Following commission or gang rape upon Shahana Begum, law was set on roll on lodgment of a First Information Report by Sultan Ahmed, father of victim Shahana Begum as Informant with Police Station. 

4. Victim Shahana Begum was placed before a Magistrate. First Class for the purpose of recording her statement under section 164 of The Code of Criminal Procedure and her statement was recorded by Md. Shafaul Karim, Magistrate, First Class (PW 12).

5. Victim Shahana Begum had been medically examined by a Medical Board and Medical Board could not express any opinion whether she was exposed to forceful sexual intercourse or not. Medical Board found that victim Shahana Begum was pregnant and pregnancy was of Six months. 

6. Nuruddin alias Shahabuddin by way of a Judicial confessional statement recorded under section 164 of The Code of Criminal Procedure confessed his guilt that he along with other accused persons committed rape upon victim Shahana Begum, Judicial confessional statement of Nuruddin alias Shahabuddin had been also recorded by Md. Shafaul Karim, Magistrate, First Class ( PW 12). PW.12 also recorded judicial confessional statement of accused Ibrahim and Merasuddin. 

7. Nuruddin alias Shahabuddin and Mohiuddin and other live persons having been indicted liar offence of section 6(3) of Nari-O-Shishu Nirjatan Daman (Bishesh Bidhan) Ain (For short The Ain of 1995) faced trial before Nari-O-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Adalat (Briefly Bishesh Adalat) in Nari-O-Shishu Nirjatan) Daman Case No. 66 of 2002. 

8. Prosecution in proof of twill of accused Nuruddin alias Shahabuddin and Mohiuddin and live other accused persons put on witness box twelve (12) witnesses. 
9. Defence adopted by accused Nuruddin alias Shahabuddin and Mohiuddin and live titers were innocence and false implication. 

10. Bishesh Adalat found Nuruddin alias Shahahuddin and Mohiuddin guilty of charge of section 6(3) of The Ain of 1995 and convicted them thereunder. Consequential sentence was imprisonment for life. Bishesh Adalat did not find other live accused persons guilty of offence and delivered a judgment of acquittal upon them. 

11. In challenge of Judgment of conviction and sentence convicts Nuruddin alias Shahabuddin and Mohiuddin from Jail presented two Petitions of appeal before this Court and Petitions of appeal has been numbered as Jail Appeal No.564 of 2003. 

12. Convicts Nuruddin alias Shahabuddin and Mohiuddin shall he described as convict-appellants. 

13. The only question that services for determination in this Jail appeal is whether the conviction and sentence recorded upon convict-appellants warrant any interference by this Court in the exercise of its appellate jurisdiction. 

14. The question posed he approached and answered. 

15. Victim Shahana Begum was examined was P.W 2. In her evidence Shahana Begum made a blow-by-blow account of commission of gang rape upon her by convict- appellants and other accused persons. She clearly identified convict-appellants Nuruddin alias Shahabuddin and Mohiuddih. She offered request to accused persons not to commit rape upon her disclosing that she was pregnant. She laid hare that as a result of commission of gang rape upon her she became senseless but before that she could very much Identify convict-appellants Nuruddin alias Shahabuddin and Mohiuddin. Evidence of victim of crime Shahana Begun is very much  clinching and trustworthy. 

16. Dr. A.B.M. Abdul Motaleb (PW 11) examined victim Shahana Begum along with) other members of the Medical Board. PW 11 standing on witness box gave evidence that victim Shahana Regum was pregnant though, no opinion could he passed whether there had been foreibly Sexual intercourse upon her or not. Medical evidence of PW 11 lent support to evidence of PW 2 victim Shahana Begun ho is the star witness in the case. 

17. Convict-appellant Nuruddin alias Shahabuddin by way of judicial confessional statement recorded by PW 12 Magistrate, First Class marked himself and the other convict-appellant Mohiuddin and other accused persons as the persons who committed rape upon victim Shahana Begum. PW 12 gave evidence that he recorded judicial confessional statement of convict-appellant Nuruddin alias Shahabuddin and confessional statement was voluntary and free. 

18. Confession made by a confessing accused can he very much relied upon awarding  conviction upon confessing accused himself but confession of a co-acused implicating other co-accused can be also a basis for awarding conviction upon the non-confessing accused if the confession is supported by other evidences on record. Confessional statement of convict-appellant Nuruddin alias Shahabuddin implicating himself and other convict-appellant Mohiuddin stand very much corroborated by credible ocular evidence of victim Shahana Begum who well recognized and identified convict-appellants during commission of rape upon her and victim Shahana raised accusing linger towards the other non-confessing convict-appellant Mohiuddin. 

19. The trustworthy ocular evidence of victim Shahana Regum medical evidence and judicial confessional statement of convict appellant Nuruddin alias Shahabuddin in respect of his involvement and also involvement of the other convict-appellant Mohiuddin in the revolting offence unerringly points their guilt and only conclusion that can be reached is that convict-appellants were the culprits who committed rape upon victim Shahana Begum. 

20. Bishesh Adalat appeared to have approached and decided the case in correct direction and decision rendered by Bishesh Adalat, reasons canvassed in rendering decision and conclusion reached demonstratively transpires to be well justified and well merited. We are also in lull agreement with the decision rendered and conclusion reached by Bishesh Adalat. 

21. No interference is therefore, called for.  

22. Jail appeal got no merit and it stands dismissed. Judgment of conviction and sentence dated 20.7.2003 passed by Nari-O-Shishu Nirjatan Bishesh Adalat, Noakhali in Nari-O-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Case No.66 of 2002 is maintained. 

23. Lower Court's Record he sent down as immediate as possible.

End.
