full_judgment:
Mohammed Fazlul Karim, J : Plaintiffs-petitioners in a suit for declaration of title simpliciter seek leave to appeal against the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division dismissing the appeal affirming those of the trial Court dismissing the suit.

2. Sahani Bibi, the predecessors of the petitioners as the plaintiff filed the suit for declaration of title to 44½ decimals of land of the northern portion of C.S. Plot no. 114 under Khatian No. 124 of Mouza Brahmancharan stating, inter alia, that C.S. Plot No. 112 measuring .53 acre and C.S Plot No. 114 measuring .89 acre of Mouza Brahmancharan were owned by Sk. Mainuddin, who orally sold the same to Chand Bepari at a consideration of Tk. 75/-; Chand Bepari died leaving two sons and 5 daughters; these heirs of Chand Bepari instituted Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 against their co-sharers, Sultan Hossain and others for partition of joint properties, including the aforesaid two plots, in the 5th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka; this partition suit was decreed on contest and plaintiffs of that suit got saham which included the aforesaid two Plot Nos. 112 and 114 and the plaintiffs of that suit took possession through Court; by amicable partition Saburunnessa and Jahura Bibi got those two plots in their Saham and sold those two Plots with some other lands to Kari Samiruddin Ahmed by registered sale deed dated 10.04.22 and Kari Samiruddin took possession of his purchased land; Kari Samiruddin. by a registered deed dated 30.05.29 gifted half of the aforesaid Plots to Munshi Md. Nawab Ali who, in his turn, transferred the same to Sarma Sundari Guha by registered sale deed dated 05.01.30; by amicable partition amongst the co-shares, Sarma Sundari Guha got the northern portion of the Plot Nos. 112 and 114 and subsequently sold the same to Rdmjan Ali by registered deed of sale dated 08.12.38; Ramjan Ali died leaving wife Faizun Nessa Bibi, 5 sons Abbas Ali, Ahmed Ali, Ansar, Abdur Razzak and Md. Giasuddin and two daughters, Amena Khatun and Sahera Khatun; 34 acre of Plot No. 114 was recorded in the name of Faizunnessa in the State Acquisition Khatian as Plot No. 473 and .37 acre of Plot No. 114 was recorded in the name of Shamsuddin Mia (who purchased from Asahuddin Mia purchaser from heir of Md. Nowab Ali Mia) and the remaining 18 decimals of the said Plot was recorded in the name of Province of East Pakistan in the khan Khatian No. 1; all the heirs of said Ramjan Ali transferred 31½ decimals of land to Sahani Bibi. predecessor-in-interest of the petitioners and 13 decimal of land to Md. Son Mia from Plot No. 114 by two separate sale deeds dated 16.02.65 and the purchasers were given possession in their respective land; Md. Sona Mia subsequently. transferred his 13 decimals of land to Sahani Bibi by registered sale deed dated 12.11.66 and put her in possession of the same Sahani Bibi. predecessors-in-interest of the petitioners, thus acquired total 441/2, decimals of land in the northern portion of C.S. Plot No. 114 and got her name mutated in the' S.A Khatian in place or Faizunnessa (wile of Ramjan Ali) and others in respect of 34 decimals and mutation of 10½ decimals was done through Court by a proceeding under section I 43A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act; Sahani Bibi paid rent in respect of the said land upto 1983; Sabani Bibi has been in possession all along cultivating land through laborers and growing cauli flowers and paddy etc. therein and R.S. record was prepared in her name; defendants claimed title to the suit land as grand children of Sk. Moinuddin (defendant of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916) and got the R.S. record changed in their names; such action having clouded the title of the plaintiff (Sabani Bibi) she was constrained to institute the suit.

3. The successive heirs of Sk. Moinuddin, defendants nos. 1-9 contested the suit by filing one written statement and the added defendant Nos. 10-18 (who purchased some interest from the heirs of Sk. Moinuddin) contested by filing a separate written statement. It was contended by defendant Nos. 1-9, inter alia, that the suit property was owned by Sk. Moinuddin and his name was correctly recorded in the C. S. record of right. Sk. Moinuddin possessed the suit proper) by constructing but there son and cultivating portion of land. Ile died leaving behind two sons. Abdus Sattar and Abdul Halim. There was no partition of the suit property amongst the co-shares of Chand Bapari and possession was not taken through Court by decree-holder; deed of gift in favour of Md. Nowab Ali in respect of 2 decimals of land of Plot No. 114 in favour of Sarma Sundari Guha is false. Ramjan Ali did not acquire any title by purchase from Sunlit Sundari Guha; the suit land was vacant nal/land and remained under water most of the year; the suit land had been in possession of the defendants from the time of their predecessor-in-interest and the same stood recorded in their names in the S.A. and revisional settlement Khatian and rent had been paid by them in respect of .the suit land; defendant Nos. 1-9 are heirs and successors-in-interest of Abdul and Abdus Sattar sons of Sk. Moinuddin, the plaintiff Sahani Bibi has got no title to or interest in the suit land and her deeds of title are collusive and without consideration.

4. The trial Court on consideration of the evidence on record dismissed the suit which was duly affirmed by the High Court Division.

5. Mr. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Counsel appearing for the petitioners submits that no issue having been raised by the defendants as to identity of the suit land in their written statement and the point having been urged for the first time at the time of hearing argument in the suit and the plaintiff appellant even, at that time prayed for holding local investigation for settling the question as to identity of the suit land which was rejected; the trail Court seriously erred in law in holding that from the description of the land in Ext. I (plaint in Title Suit No. 167 of 1916) as shown by boundary it was not possible to ascertain whether the schedule of Ext.1 attracted suit plot No. 114 and no attempt was made on the side of the plaintiff to prove the identity of the suit land with reference to the schedule of Ext. 1 and High Court Division erred in affirming such finding of the learned trial Court. The learned Counsel next submits that in view of the final decree in favour of the predecessor of the plaintiff in Partition suit No. 167 of 1916 and successive transfers from 1922 of the land of the suit Plot No. 114 under C.S. Khatian No. 124 of Mouza Brahmanchiran, evidenced by Exhibits 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9 and mutation of the names of Sahani Bibi plaintiff in respect of 34 acre through proceeding; before the revenue officer and in respect of 10½ decimal (wrongly recorded in the names of Government) by proceeding under section 143 A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the rent receipts Ext. 13, 13(a) and 13(h) all subsequent to the C.S. record of right Ext. A in the name of Mainuddin Kochwan, High Court Division erred in law in holding (without considering all these evidence) that the presumption of Ext. A had not been rebutted. Ile next submits that the trial Court as also the High Court Division misconstrued transfer document Ext. 5 reading –প্রকাশ থাকে যে, ৬নং তফসিলে নাল জমি ষোল আনা দীর্ঘকাল যাবৎ আমার খাস দখলে আছে উহার হিস্যা। আট আনা উত্তরাংেশের অত্র দলিল মূলে আপনার দখলে অর্পন করিলাম ও আপনার খাস দখলে বুঝাইয়া দিলাম।  and erred in concluding  that the transfer was only of .02 acre of the suit plot inasmuch as item 6 of the schedule of that document related to Plot No. 114 under Khatian No. 124 of Mouza Brahmanchiian, northern hall of which amounted to. 44½, acre. The learned Counsel next submits that a reading of the evidence of the P. Ws. shows that there was no contradiction in their evidence as found by the High Court Division and their evidences were consistent on the point that the plaintiff was in possession by producing cauli flower pumpkin etc. through borgadar P.W. 3 and such possession of the plaintiff is consistent with the averments made by the defendant Nos. 1-9 in their written statements in paragraph 18(3) together with the evidence of D.W. 6, Md. Shaljahan son of Kamrunnessa (defendant No. 9) that they possessed in the southern part of the suit plot. The learned Counsel lastly submits that in view of the long lapse of time from the decree Ext. 2 and the evidence of possession on record, the High Court Division erred in law in delving into question of the decree Ext. 2 being nullity giving no title to Saburunnessa and Juhura Bibi on the ground that minor sons of Mainuddin Kochwan not being properly represented by Court guardian and transfers made by the heirs of Abdul Halim as late as in 1981 during the pendency of the suit.

6. Mr. Moksudur Rahman. learned Counsel appearing for respondent Nos. 17 and 21 supported the impugned judgments submitting that plaintiffs have failed to establish title and possession in respect of the suit land and as such the suit is not maintainable under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.

<u>7. On perusal of the impugned judgment it appears that the petitioners alleged to have filed an application for local investigation before the trial Court but the same having been rejected no step was ever taken either challenging the same in revision nor any ground  as taken in the Memorandum of appeal against the rejection. of the prayer for holding local investigation or even renewed the prayer at the appellate stage and the learned Advocate though submitted that the Court of appeal below should have sent the case partly on remand invoking the provision of order 21 rule 25 of the Code of Civil. Procedure which provides for a remand but only if the Court below has omitted to frame or try a issue and has failed to determine a question .of fact essential to the right decision of the ease on merit. Moreover it' the appellate Court is of opinion that a particular issue should be framed and tried and that certain findings of fact arc necessary for the proper disposal of an appeal and that further evidence should be taken on these points, the proper procedure is to make an order under this rule and not remand the whole case; but the said provision tinder the circumstances was not applicable as the application for local investigation was already rejected and the order does not appear to have suffered from illegality and the petitioners as well did not agitate taking any ground in the memo of appeal but at the hearing of the appeal the Matter though agitated afresh but the Court was of the view that the order rejecting local investigation do not suffer from infirmity inasmuch as there was no vagueness as to averment in the plaint that C.S. Plot No. 114 attracted the property described in "Cha" and "Tha" of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 and the identity of the suit land had not been challenged and the issue as to the vagueness of the suit land was not material in the facts and circumstances of the case in view of findings as to title and possession of the suit land on the basis of the evidence on record being recorded in the case and considered by both the Courts below against the plaintiff petitioners.</u>

8. As regards next submission of the learned Counsel for the petitioners that the Courts below illegally have not relied upon documents filed by the plaintiff which are subsequent to the decree of the same may be ancient antiquity but no presumption is attached to them being private documents and the plaintiff as well could not prove the same inasmuch the basic document was found to be interpolated in respect of Plot No. 124 making the same to be Plot No. 114 by over writing inasmuch as Ext. 6 shows that Sarma Sundari Guha transferred 44½ decimals of land from plot No. 114 whereas the schedule of Ext 5 showed she purchased only .2 decimals of Plot No. 114 and as such could not transfer 44½ to Remjan Ali and his heirs could not transfer .3½ and  13 decimals of land to Sahana Bibi and Sona Miah by Exts. 7 and 8 respectively inasmuch as Ext. 13, the rent receipt in favour of Ramjan Ali, the predecessor of plaintiff had not been proved by producing counter foils or adducing evidence through witnesses to prove the same as required in accordance with law and as such the plaintiff could not fall back upon the same as a basic documents of title of the suit land. Ext. 5 the document of transfer in favour of Sarma Sundari Guha by Munshi Nawab Ali (which is interpolated as to the C.S Plot No. 114 in place of C.S Plot No. 124 ) show only 02 acres of land out of the suit plot was transferred and as such she was not competent to transfer 44½ decimals of land to Ramjan Ali, who could only transfer .02 decimals by Exts. 7 and 8 to the plaintiff and Sona Mia.

9. As regards the possession of the suit land by the plaintiff, the High Court Division as the final Court of fact has assessed the evidence of the P.Ws. and held on consideration of the evidence on record that the evidence of the P.Ws 1, 3 and 4 as regards possession suffers from contradiction and no reliance could be placed on these witnesses and upon proper evaluation of the deposition arrived at a finding that the plaintiff has failed to prove her possession in the suit land, on the contrary, on assessment of evidence on record found that defendants could prove their possession in the suit land from the time of their predecessor-in-interest Moinuddin Kochwan and accordingly affirmed the finding arrived at by the trial Court on consideration of the evidence on record. As the plaintiff tiled the suit for declaration of title simpliciter and having failed to prove the possession, both the Court below concurrently found that the suit is not maintainable under the provision of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.

10. The Courts below on consideration of the evidence on record arrived at the concurrent finding of fact that the plaintiff could not prove the title and possession of the suit land. On perusal of the impugned judgment and materials on record we find no reason to differ with the aforesaid findings of the Courts below. In the case of Chief Joseph Wobo and others Vs. The Attorney General for the Federation of Nigeria and another repelled in 9 DLR (PC) 616 the Privy Council observed: "This appears to raise a question of fact upon which there are concurrent findings by the Courts below and in accordance with their long-established practice their Lordships would not think it proper to disturb such finding unless the appellants could clearly show that those Courts had fallen into some serious error."

11. We are in respectful agreement with the aforesaid observation and of the view that there is no such serious error in the impugned judgment compelling us to interfere with the concurrent findings of fact.

12. As to the next submission of the learned Counsel regarding decree in partition suit of 1916, it appears that the decree in Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 was never put into execution within 12 years and as such the decree-holder plaintiff including plaintiff nos. 4 and 5 (Safunnessa and Jahra Bibi) could not get into possession in the decretal land particularly in 'Cha' and 'Tha' of the schedule upon evicting the defendants including the sons of Moinuddin Kochwan, the defendant no. 21, the substituted heirs of defendant no. 21-Kha Abdus Sattar. the predecessor-in-interest of defendant nos. 6-9 and Abdul Halim, the substituted defendant no. 2 I -Ga, the predecessor-in-interest of defendant nos. 1-5, the transferors of the defendant nos. 10-17. We also noticed the legal infirmity in the said decree in Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 that defendant no. 21 Moinuddin Kochwan died during the pendency of the suit his two minor sons Abdus Sattar and Abdul Halim were not legally represented in the suit but by appointing Court guardians as required under the mandatory provision of Order 32 rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The appointment of guardian ad-litems is not a mere formality. It is an imperative duty. of the Court. It is the duty

of the Court to see that minor's interest is properly represented as a decree passed against a minor without proper guardian-ad-liem being appointed for him is a nullity (1929 Cal. 586) and accordingly the decree against the said minors was a nullity and the same was not binding upon them. The High Court Division on consideration of the Ext. 1 and 2, found that the plaint, the preliminary decree and the final decree have mentioned -the substituted heirs of Moinuddin Kochwan defendant No. 21, namely, Abdus Sattar and Abdul Halim as defendant Nos. 21-Kha and 21-Ga described as minors and they were not represented by any court guardians duly appointed under order 32 rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Moreover, their addresses were also not shown therein and the suit as well was decreed exparte against them and as such the minors defendants being totally unrepresented by a Court guardian appointed by the Court, the decree against them was wholly void and nullity and could not be enforced against them and their heirs defendant nos. 1-9 and the transferee defendant nos. 10-17. Reference in this regards was made relying the case of Rain Chandra Arya V. Man Singh and others reported in AIR 1968 SC 954 where a decree was passed against a lunatic in contravention of Order 32 rule 15 of the Code of Civil Procedure and a sale was held in execution of the said decree but as the lunatic was not represented by a guardian appointed by the Court the said decree was held to be a nullity and is void and not merely voidable.

13. The impugned judgment of. the High Court Division is concluded by concurrent findings of fact arrived at on consideration of the evidence of record.

14. Accordingly, we do not find any substance in the submissions of the learned Counsel for the petitioners. We also do not find any illegality or legal infirmity in the impugned judgment for our interference.

15. The petition is accordingly dismissed.

End.

full_judgment:
Mr. Sheikh Abdul Awal, J:- By this Rule the opposite party was called upon to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 05.09.2000 (decree signed on 14.09.2000) passed by the Subordinate Judge, 11 Court, Dhaka in S.C.0 Suit No.1 of 1999 dismissing the suit for ejectment of monthly tenant shall not be set aside. 

2. The facts relevant for the purpose of disposal of this Rule are as follows: The petitioner as plaintiff filed S.S.0 suit No. 1 of 1999 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka against the defendant-opposite party for ejectment of monthly tenant. The father of the petitioner named. Dr. Abdul Monayem Khandaker was the owner of a tin-shed shop situated at holding No.34 Sideward New Circular Road, Police Station-Ramna, District-Dhaka. The defendant opposite party entered into the said tin-shed shop as monthly tenant under Dr. Abdul Monayem Khandaker, the father of the petitioner-Khandaker Mahmud Hasan on 01.04.1984 by executing a monthly tenancy deed. The father of the plaintiff-petitioner during his life time gifted the suit holding to him and since then the defendant and other tenants of the suit holding started to pay the monthly rent to the petitioner. The last rate of rent of the suit shop has been mutually fixed at Tk.1400/= per month. The plaintiff brought the suit for ejectment of the defendant from the said shop room on the grounds that the defendant was a defaulter in payment of rent and that the plaintiff bonafide required the room amongst other rooms of the suit holding which were let out to other tenants. The bonafide requirement has been stated to be for constructing a multistoried building as per plan passed by RAJUK. 

3. The defendant appeared in the suit and filed written statement denying the material allegation of the plaint and stating, inter-alia, that the defendant was not a defaulter and that the plaintiff had no bonafide requirement of the suit shop room. Moreover, since the plaintiff had other rooms of the suit holding let out to other tenants, the plaintiff should not have chosen the particular room of the defendant as target of eviction for bonafide requirement. 

4. At the trial the plaintiff examined 3 (three) witnesses and the defendant also examined 3(three) witnesses and both the parties filed series of documents to prove their respective claims.

5. The Trial Court on consideration of the evidence and circumstances of the case dismissed the suit by impugned judgment and decree dated 05.09.2000 (decree signed on 14-09-2000). 

6. Aggrieved thereby the plaintiff-petitioner approached this Court and obtained the present rule. 

7. Mr. Mohammad Ali, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner in the course of argument after placing the Revisional Application and other connected papers including plaint, impugned judgment and deposition of witnesses submits that the learned S.S.C. Judge on misconception of law and facts most illegally and mechanically dismissed the suit even though the plaintiff made out a clear case for bonafide requirement for construction of a multistoried building as per plan of RAJUK. The learned Advocate next submits that PW-1, plaintiff himself stated in his deposition that the defendant was a defaulter inasmuch as he did not pay any rent since December, 1998 to February, 1999 and thereafter, the defendant on pretext started to pay the rent through postal money order. Mr. Mohammad Ali further submits that the judgment of the learned S.S.C. Judge is not based on correct evaluation of the facts and materials on record and as such the impugned judgment is not a proper judgment which is liable to be set-aide. The learned Advocate in support of his submissions relied on the cases reported in 43 DLR (AD)-225, 9BLT(AD) 69, 6 BLC (AD)-36 and 5 BLD(AD)-77. 

8. Mr. Mohammad Ali finally on referring Exts.4, 5, and 5(ka) submits that on several occasions the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was returned as undelivered which shows that the defendant-opposite Party deliberately with ill motive avoided to receive the notice and therefore, it cannot be said that no notice was served as per provision of section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. The learned Advocate in support of this contention relied on the cases reported in 34 DLR(AD)-271 and 12 BLD-406. 

9. On the other hand, Mr. Md. Mosiul Alam, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-opposite party after placing the impugned judgment and the depositions of PWs. and DWs. submits that the learned S.S.C. Judge was right in finding that the petitioner failed to prove the bonafide requirement for purposes of a multistoried building. He next submits that the Trial Court was right in holding that since the advanced security money is not adjusted the question of defaulter in respect of payment of rent does not arise at all. He further submits that the approved plan of RAJUK does not contain the area of suit shop premises and thus, the plea of so-called bonafide requirement of suit-shop is false and malafide. Mr. Mosiul Alam finally submits that the findings of the S.S.C. Judge based on correct evaluation of the evidence on record cannot be disturbed by this Court unless it is shown that the decision is based upon gross misreading of evidence or it has been founded on misapprehension of law or otherwise it is perverse being contrary to law. The learned Advocate to fortify his submission relied on the cases reported in 31 DLR (AD)-155, 55 DLR(AD)-63 and 46 DLR(AD)-121. 

10. These are the points which were argued by the learned Advocates for the respective parties. Now, to deal with the contentions raised by the learned Advocates for the respective parties from a correct angle let me see the evidence and other materials on record. 

11. PW-1, Khandaker Mahmud Hasan, as plaintiff stated in his deposition that on 01.12.1980 his late father let out the shop premises to the defendant. This witness also stated that 
"নভেম্বর ১৯৯৮ মাসের ভাড়ার টাকা ৩০/১১/৯৮ তারিখে পরিশোধ করেন। আমি মুড়ি বই মাধ্যমে বিবাদীনীকে ভাড়ার রশিদ প্রদান করতাম। আমি মুড়ি বই প্রদর্শনী-২দাখিল করেছি। তৎপর বিবাদীনি আর ভাড়ার টাকা প্রদান করেনি। This witness also stated that: নালীশি জায়গার উন্নতির জন্য আমি রাজউক হতে প্লান পাশ করায়েছি। জুলাই ১৯৯৭ সনে রাজউক হতে ঐ প্লান পাশ করাই। এটা হচ্ছে মূল অনুমোদিত প্লান ও রাজউকের প্লান অনুমোদন করার চিঠি। আমার আরো কয়েকটি মামলা আছে। তাই ঐ প্ল্যানের ও রাজউক  এর উক্ত স্মারকনং- নক্স/৭৫৪/৯৭/২০৬৮ তারিখ এর সত্যায়িত ফটোষ্ট্যাট কপি যথাত্রমে প্রদর্শনী ৩, ৩(ক) দাখিল করেছি। নালিশী জায়গার উন্নয়নের জন্য নালীশী দোকান ঘরটি আমার প্রয়োজন। আামি মৌখিক ভাবে ও মোহাম্মদ আলী সাহেব মাধ্যমে বিবাদীনিকে উহা জানিয়েছি। বিবাদীনিকে সহ অন্যান্য ভাড়াটিয়া গণকে দোকান খালি করে দেননি। This witness also stated that: বিবাদীনি একজন ডিফিলটার। আমি বিজ্ঞ এ্যাডভোকেট মোহাম্মদ আলী মাধ্যমে বিবাদীনিকে ১০৬ ধারার নোটিশ দেই। এটা সেই নোটিশের কপি। ২৯/৭/৯৯ ইং তারিখে উক্ত নোটিশ দই। উহা আমার কথামত লেখা হয়। আমি রেজিষ্ট্রি পোষ্ট এডি সহ প্রেরণ করি। উক্ত নোটিশের কপি প্রদর্শনী ৪, ১টি ডাক রশিদ প্রদর্শনী ৫ এবং উহার এ,ডি প্রদর্শনী ৫(ক) দাখিল করেছি। প্রদর্শনী ৫(ক) বিবাদীনির স্বাক্ষর আছে। 

12. PW-2 Quayum Mohammad is one of the tenant under the same holding of the plaintiff-petitioner stated that the plaintiff obtained plan for construction of building in the suit shop premises. This witness denied the defence suggestion that সত্য নহে যে, আমি বাদীর অধীনে ভাড়াটিয়া নই বা বাদীর কথামত তার পক্ষে মিথ্যা সাক্ষ্য দিলাম বা বাদী নালিশী হোল্ডিং এ দালান নির্মান উন্নয়ন করতে চাননি বা নালিশী হোল্ডিং টিনশেড এখনও অত্যান্ত ভাল আছে বা আমার সাথে বাদীর কোন সমঝোতা হয়নি। 

13. PW-3, Md. Shahidullah, in his deposition supported the evidence of PW-1 and PW-2 in respect of all material particulars. 

14. DW-1 Amirul Islam is the husband of plaintiff-Anjir Asma, who on behalf of his wife testified that his wife took rent the suit shop premises from the father of plaintiff on 01.04.84 by executing an agreement. This witness also stated in his deposition that the plaintiff did not give rent receipt regularly. In cross-examination this witness admitted that প্রদর্শনী-১ হচ্ছে উক্ত ভাড়াটিয়া চুক্তিপত্র। উক্ত চুক্তি পত্রের ২নং কলামে লেখা আছে যে, আমার স্ত্রী রশিদমূলে ভাড়া দিবেন। ঐ এগ্রিমেন্ট অনুসারে প্রতিমাসের ভাড়া প্রতিমাসে দিচ্ছি। উক্ত চুক্তিপত্রের ৬ নং ক্লজ-এ লেখা আছে মালিক ছাদ ঢালাই করলে আমরা দোকান ছেড়ে দিব। In cross-examination he denied the suggestion of the plaintiff that সত্য নহে যে, নালিশী  হোল্ডিংটা টিন সেডটি বহুপুরাতন ও জরাজীর্ণ বা বাদ উহাতে বহুতল বিশিষ্ট দালান নির্মানের জন্য প্ল্যান পাশ করায়েছেন ও আমাদেরকে ছেড়ে দেবার জন্য নোটিশ দেই বা আমরা দোকান ছেড়ে দেবার জন্য বাদীকে আশ্বাস দেই। In cross-examination this witness also denied the suggestion of the plaintiff that সত্য নহে যে, বিবাদীনি ডিফলটার বা না দোকান বাদীর উন্নয়নের জন্য প্রয়োজন হওয়ায় বিবাদীনি ডিফলটার হওয়ায় বাদী তার আইনজীবির মাধ্যমে ১০৬ ধারার বিধান মতে বিবাদীনিকে নোটিশ দেন। বিবাদীনি ঐ নোটিশ গ্রহণ জবাবে বিবাদীনি বাংলা ভাষায় স্বাক্ষর করেছেন। DW-2, S. M. Sanwar and DW-3. A.F.S. Abdul Hady both of them in their respective testimony corroborated the evidence of DW-1 in respect of all the material particulars. 

15. It appears form the impugned judgment that the S.S.C. Judge dismissed the suit mainly on two count:- Firstly, the plaintiff could not prove his bonafide requirement of the suit premises for his own use or for the purpose of building. Secondly, the plaintiff could not prove that the defendant was a defaulter in payment of rent. 

16. I have examined the averments of plaint and find in the plaint the plaintiff clearly stated that he required the suit primness for construction of a multistoried building as per approved plan of RAJUK. It also stated that বিবাদী একজন খেলাপী ভাড়াটিয়া এবং দোকান ঘরটি উন্নতি করার জন্য বাদীর একান্ত প্রয়োজন। (বোনাফায়েড নেছেছিটি) তজজন্য বাদী তাহার নিয়োজিত এ্যাডভোকেট জনাব মোহাম্মদ আলী মারফত বিবাদীকে সম্পত্তি হস্তান্তর আইনের ১০৬ ধারায় নোটিশে ভাড়াটিয়ার স্বত্বের অবসান করিয়া দোকান ঘরটি দখল ১৯৯৯ ইং সালের ফেব্রুয়ারী মাস অন্তে বুঝাইয়া দেওয়ার অনুরোধ করেন। 
It thus, appears that the plaint do disclose clearly that the defendant was a defaulter in payment of rent and the plaintiff needed the suit shop primness for construction of a multistoried building as per approved plan of RAJUK. 

17. On assessment of the evidence on record, it appears that PW- I , PW-2 and PW-3 all of them in their respective testimony stated that in order to develop the suit shop room amongst other rooms of the suit holding which were let out to other tenants the plaintiff obtained a plan from RAJUK. It also appears that the rented shop situated at 34, Sideward New Circular Road, Police Station Ramna District Dhaka wherein other adjacent holding contained multistoried building. It also appears that DW-1, defendant himself in cross-examination admitted that প্রদর্শনী-১ হচ্ছে উক্ত ভাড়াটিয়া চুক্তিপত্র। উক্ত চুক্তিপত্রের ২ নং কলামে লেখা আছে যে, আমার স্ত্রী রশিদমূলে ভাড়া দিবেন। ঐ এগ্রিমেন্ট অনুসারে প্রতিমাসের ভাড়া প্রতি মাসে দিচ্ছি। উক্ত চুক্তিপত্রের ৬ ক্লজ-এ লেখা আছে মালিক ছাদ ঢালাই করলে দোকান ছেড়ে দিব। 

18. Now, let me examine the legal position in this regard. In the case Chand Miah Sawdagar Vs. AMA Rahamn reported in 43 DLR (AD)-225 where, it has been laid down that: 
"The plaintiff-appellant was not required to adopt the language of the statute to make out a case for rebuilding of the suit house. Whether "addition, alteration and renovation" of the suit house amounts to cosmetic improvement or entails reconstruction after demolition is a question of fact which must be decided on evidence. The respondent did not agitate in the Courts below that the sanctioned plan did not involve demolition. It is now too late to raise fresh issues of fact. 
The only objection taken by the two Courts is that the sanctioned plan cannot be seriously considered in the absence of any averment in the plaint regarding its existence. But the fact is that the SCC suit was filed in 1980 whereas the building plan was sanctioned in 1978. There is no finding that the sanctioned plan was forged and spurious as contended by the defendant-respondent. The learned SCC Judge evidently misread the plaint when he found that the plaintiff did not state in the plaint that the suit premises was required for the purpose of rebuilding. The plaintiff-appellant was not required to state in the plaint as to what proof he had with regard to the requirement of rebuilding. A plaint contains facts, not proof. On both counts, namely, (a) bonafide requirement for his personal use and the use and occupation of his family members and (b) bonafide requirement for rebuilding, the plaintiff appellant has adequately stated his case in the plaint and has proved the same. The two Courts below failed to apply the provisions of proviso (e) to sub-section (1) of section 18 of the Ordinance, to the facts and circumstances of the case. For all the reasons above we hold that the learned SCC Judge and the High Court Division wrongly dismissed the appellant's suit and incorrectly applied the test of bonafide requirement." 
In the case Zahir Ahmed Vs. Manik Sarder reported in 9 BLT(AD)-69, it has been laid down that: 
"It is for the appellant to decide-- which premises out of many is required by him bonafide. The learned Single Judge took a wrong view that the appellant picked up the shop room let out to the respondent malafide on the plea of bonafide requirement without requiring other shop rooms let out to other tenants for the reason that choice for other shop room will be confronted with the same argument leading to a absurd situation. The right of bonafide requirement is always with landlord but he is under legal obligation to prove that he needs the premises for such requirement. Expansion of existing business of a landlord run in a shop room adjacent to the shop room let out to a tenant involves element of must have and constitutes bonafide requirement. Thus, we do not find any reason to uphold the judgment and order of the learned Single Judge and accordingly we set aside the same and restore those of the learned S.C. C. Judge and Assistant Judge and decree the suit." 
This view gets support from the case of Abdus Salam Babari Vs. Shamsun Nahar reported in 6 BLD-36. 

19. From the above evidence, averment of the plaint vis-a-vis the principles as laid down in those decisions. I do not find any possible reason to agree with the finding of the of the S.S.C. Judge that the plaintiff could not prove his bonafide requirement of the shop room for the purpose of building inasmuch as there are consistent evidences both oral and documentary available on record to corroborate the landlord's bonafide requirement of the suit premises. Moreover I find that the disputed suit shop is situated at 34, Siddeswari New Circular Road, Police Station Ramna, District-Dhaka wherein, other adjacent holding contained multistoried building and if construction is raised it will be beneficial to all the parties and will meet the need of the day. Thus, 43DLR (AD) 225 has not been correctly appreciated by the learned S.S.C. Judge. 

20. It is true Sub-section (1) of section 18 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance protects a tenant from eviction as long as the tenant pays rent to the full extent allowable by this Ordinance and performs the conditions of the tenancy". This protection is given "not-withstanding anything contained in the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, or the Contract Act, 1872" The protection is not available if he is a defaulter and/or in the contingencies mentioned in clauses (a)-(e) of the proviso to sub-section (1) of section 18, namely. "(a) where the tenant has done any act contrary to the provisions of clause (m), clause (o) or clause (p) of section 108 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, or (b) where, in the absence of any contract to the contrary, the tenant has , without the consent in writing of landlord, sublet the premises in whole or in part, or (c) where the tenant has been guilty of conduct which is a nuisance or any annoyance to occupiers of adjoining or neighboring premises, or (d) where the tenant has been using the premises or part thereof or allowing the premises or part thereof to be used for immoral or illegal purposes, or (e) where the premises are bonafide required by the landlord either for purposes of building or rebuilding or for his own occupation or for the occupation of any person for whose benefit the premises are held of where the landlord can show any cause which may be deemed satisfactory by the Court". The last clause (e) of the proviso allows the Court to order eviction of a tenant "where the landlord can show any cause which may be deemed satisfactory by the Court". 

21. It is thus clear, that bonafide requirement of the premises in suit by the owner for his own use or for the purpose of construction of building is a matter exclusively with landlord but still then he is under legal obligation to prove that he needs the premises for his own use or for construction of building through the evidence of reliable witness. In this case I have already indicated that there are sufficient corroborative evidence both oral and documentary available on record to arrive at a finding that the plaintiff petitioner has been able to prove his bonafide requirement of the suit shop premises for purpose of multistoried building. 

22. There is another aspect of the case which needs to be addressed as it involves an important question of law. 

23. In the present case it appears from the materials on record (Exhibits 4, 5, and 5-ka) that on several occasions the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was posted in the address of the suit-shop but all the times the same was returned as undelivered. 

24. In the case of Rokeya Begum Vs. Shah Md. Yeamin another reported in 12 BLD-406, it has been decided that: 
"In the instant case, as already indicated, the notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act had been posted on September 14, 1986, on pre-payment with correct address. The postal peon called at the address four times within the period from September 16, 1986, to September 22, 1986, although as per his own admission in the written statement the tenant had been carrying on business at the address. There was no evidence to show that he had been away from the premises during the period and there was none who could accept the letter on his behalf. If he was not away there was no reason why the registered letter could not he served on him. As he was in arrears, there could also be no reason why the landlord should have withheld the service. In the circumstances the failure of the postal peon to actually deliver the letter would be attributed to the tenant's conduct. In the aforesaid circumstance, the learned small Cause Court Judge, on a reference to the principle enunciated in the cases reported in 22 DLR(Dhaka) 664 and 31 DLR(FICD) 269, took the view that there was due service of the notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. In my opinion the learned Judge, in arriving at the said finding, committed no error of law which can be said to have been occasioned a Failure of justice." On an analysis of the aforesaid decision. I am led to hold that in this case there was due service of notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act inasmuch as I have already noticed that in the present case it appears from the materials on record on several occasions the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was posted in the address of the suit-shop to the defendant-opposite party but all the times the same was returned as undelivered. 

25. There is another aspect. Admittedly, the plaintiff brought allegation against the defendant-opposite party that he was a defaulter with regard to payment of rent for the period of December, 1998 to February, 1999 although, the defendant claims that the plaintiff on pretest did not pay the rent receipt for that period after taking rent. In this connection on assessment of the entire evidence on record I find that the defendant did not or could not adduce any documentary or corroborative evidence to prove that he was not a defaulter with regard to payment of rent for the period of December, 1998 to February, 1999. 

26. III order to meet the grievance of Mr. Mosiul Alam that the approved plan of RAJUK does not contain the area of suit premises, I have examined the connected papers including the approved plan of RAJUK, it appears that the plan of RAJUK contained the suit shop premises. Therefore, I do not find any substance in the submission of the learned Advocate on this point. As to the observation given by the Trial Judge that since the advanced security money- is not adjusted the question of defaulter does not arise at all to which straightforward answer is the same can not be the basis dismiss the suit while landlord's bonafide requirement of the suit shop premises for purposes of building has been established by sufficient corroborative evidence both oral and documentary. 

27. Mr. Md. Mosiul Alam, the learned Advocate tried his best to convince me that the learned S.S.C. judge has rightly arrived at a finding that the principles enunciated in the decision reported in 43DLR (AD) 225 are not applicable in this case. In this connection I have already noticed that the principles laid down in said case are attracted in its entirety in this case and therefore, I am unable to accept the submission of Mr. Mosiul Alam on this point as well. 
The decisions cited by the learned Advocate for the defendant-opposite party is distinguishable on facts. Be that as it may, the proposition of law is well settled that once a tenancy comes into an existence the tenant cannot convert his tenancy into a permanent one by doing any act adverse to the landlord. 

28. Having given my best consideration to the materials on record both oral and documentary and the legal position I hold that the trial Court below committed gross illegality in dismissing the S.S.C. suit, which calls for interference. 

29. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The impugned judgment and decree dated 05.09.2000 (decree signed on 14.09.2000) passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, I' Court, Dhaka in S.C.C. Suit No.1 of 1999 is hereby set, aside. The defendant-opposite party is directed to vacate the rented suit shop premises within 4(four) months from date. 

30. Let a copy of the judgment along with LC record he send down at once. 

End.

full_judgment:
Mr. Miria Hussain Haider. J: This Rule, issued on 22.10.2000 upon an 
application filed under section 25 of the Small Causes Courts Act. 1887, at the instance of the Defendant/Petitioners calling upon the plaintiff/opposite parties to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order, dated 6.8.2000 passed by the Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court and SCC Judge, Sylhet in S.C.C. Suit No.2 of 1988 decreeing the suit and directing the eviction of the defendant /petitioners from the suit property should not set aside and / or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

2. Facts necessary for the disposal of this Rule, in short, are that the opposite parties Nos. Ito 4, 6, predecessor of opposite parties No.5 (a) to 5(h) and predecessor of opposite parties No. 7(a) to (e) as plaintiffs instituted Small Causes Court (SCC) Suit No. 2 of 1988 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court and S.C.C. Judge, Sylhet, against one Abdul Wahid, predecessor of the present defendant /petitioners, who was a monthly tenant under the predecessor of the plaintiffs/ opposite parties, for eviction from the suit premises for defaulting in paying rent and on the ground of bonafide requirement of the suit premises. During the pendency-of the suit Abdul Wahid, the sole defendant died on 03. 10.1995 and the present petitioners were substituted as his legal heirs. Thereafter, the original plaintiff Nos. 5 and 7 also died during the pendency of the suit and their legal heirs, plaintiff No. 5(a) to 5 (h) and 7(a) to 7 (e) were also substituted as plaintiffs in their places. It is alleged in the plaint of the SCC Suit that the deceased Abdul Wahid took monthly lease of the suit premises from the predecessor of the plaintiffs, late Jobeda Khatun, by executing a 'Bharanama agreement' dated 03. 10. 1979 at a rental of TK. 450/- per month payable within 5th day of the next following month according to the English. Calendar. The said landlady during the subsistence of the said tenancy agreement died on 27.8.1987 and as such the tenancy right of the defendant Abdul Wahid stood terminated. But the defendant without vacating the same has been running his business in the tenanted premises as an illegal occupant. Thereafter, on the death of the landlady Jobeda Khatun, her heirs became the owners of the suit premises by inheritance and asserted that with the death of the landlady the tenancy right stood terminated and the tenant became an illegal occupant in the said premises. It is further  alleged that the defendant defaulted in paying rent of the suit premises till his death and as such liable to be evicted from the said premises on the ground of being illegal occupant and default and also for bonafidc requirement of the suit premises for necessary repairing, development and use as office/reception hall and dining room of the plaintiffs' hotel business which had been running under the ownership of the plaintiffs on the adjacent part of the suit premises. It is alleged in the instant revisional application that the plaintiffs accordingly sent a notice on 7.7.1 988 under registered post terminating the tenancy under the provision of Transfer of Property Act 1882 asking the defendant to vacate the suit premises on the expiry of the last day of July. 1988. The notice was received by the defendant Abdul Wahid on 9.7.1988 but he did not vacate the suit premises. Hence, this suit for eviction of the defendant from the suit premises. 

3. Abdul Wahid, the original defendant contested the suit by filing written statement denying the material allegations of the plaint contending, inter alia, that he never defaulted in paying rents and the plea of bonafide requirement of the plaintiffs is untrue and unfounded. After the death of the defendant Abdul Wahid on 3.10.1995 the present petitioners were substituted as defendants as they are the legal heirs and successor of the said Abdul Wahid. The defendant/petitioners filed another written statement on 31.12.1996 denying the material allegations of the plaint contending inter alia that the original defendant Abdul Wahid had been running a business or grocery in the suit premises as a monthly tenant under Jobeda Khatun, the predecessor of the present plaintiffs, since long before, at a rental of TK. 450/- per month payable within 15th day of every month next following, according to the English Calenader. It is further asserted that Jobeda Khatun received TK. 30,000/- on 306 December, 1984 from late Abdul Wahid, the original tenant, as advance rent on condition that it would be adjusted towards the monthly rents but the same had not been adjusted as per promise. The defendants regularly paid rent upto July 1987 and were granted receipts for such payment of rents. The rent for the month of August, 1987 was offered to the plaintiff No. 2 Khondaker Karim Uddin Ahmed, who used to collect rents on behalf of Jobeda Khatun during her life time. But said plaintiff No. 2 having refused to accept the same, Abdul Wahid sent the said rent, on 6.9.1987, by postal money order which the plaintiffs refused to accept on 9.9.1987. After return of the said refused money order the original defendant Abdul Wahid deposited the rent for the said month with the House Rent controller Sylhet in House Rent Case No. 68 of 1987 on 27.9.1987 and thenceforth had been depositing rents with the House Rent Controller, Sylhet in the said case regularly. It is further denied that the plaintiffs had any bonafide requirement of the suit premises and the plea of use of the some as reception room for the boarders of the hotel and dining hall of the said hotel is bogus, unfounded and malafide pleas for causing illegal ejectment of the defendant petitioners. As such it is claimed that the suit for ejectment of the defendants was filed with malafide intention to let out the same to others at an enhanced rate and therefore the SCC suit was liable to be dismissed. 

4. During the trial the plaintiffs examined three witnesses including plaintiff No.2 as P.W.1 who deposed in support of the plaint case. The defendants examined two witnesses out of which Lutfur Rahman, the defendant No. 1(ka) deposed as D.W.1.0n consideration of the evidence on record the S.C.C. Judge decreed the suit for ejectment by the impugned judgment and order dated 6.8.2000 holding that the defendants were defaulters and thereby directed the defendant/petitioners to handover the vacant possession of the suit premises within 60 days from the date of order. 

5. As against the said judgment and order dated 6.8.2000 passed in SCC Suit No.2 of 1988 the defendants moved this Court and obtained the instant Rule. 

6. The rule was duly served upon the plaintiffs/opposite parties pursuant to which ultimately the learned Advocate Mr. S. H. Md. Nurul Huda Jaigirdar appeared and argued in the case on behalf of the plaintiffs/ opposite parties. 

7. Mr. J.N. Deb, the learned advocate appearing on behalf of the defendants/petitioners upon placing the impugned judgment submits that the plaintiffs having claimed that the relationship between the land lady and the tenant being terminated on the death of the land lady Jobeda Khatun on 27.8.1987, the defendant Abdul Wahid became illegal occupant in the suit premises as such a notice dated 6.7.88, registered on 7.7.88, was served upon the defendant directing him to hand over the possession of the rented property to the plaintiffs by 31.7.88 and also asking the defendant to pay Tk. 25/- per pay from 28.8.87 till 31.7.88 for such illegal occupation of the suit premises and therefore, the clear case made out by the plaintiffs is that the defendants are not the tenants under the plaintiffs. Such an assertion in the plaint clearly made the SCC Suit No. 2 of 1988 as not maintainable. The learned Advocate contends that as the plaintiffs do not admit that the defendants are their tenants, the relief as prayed for in the plaints does not fall within the provision section 15 and Article 4 of the S.C.C. Act, and as such the suit is not maintainable. In this respect Mr. Deb relied on the decision of the case of Managing Director, Rupali Bank Limited and others vs. Tajazal Hossein and others reported in 44 DLR (AD) 260 and submits that the Appellate division has held in that case "that the jurisdiction is the root of everything 'and if there is no jurisdiction of the Court to try the suit everything shall fall apart." As such Mr. Dev submits that the suit being not maintainable as SCC suit the SC Court has no jurisdiction to try the instant suit and the. Judgment and order passed by the SCC Judge is a nullity and is liable to be struck down by this court. 

8. The learned Advocate Mr. J.N. Dev further strenuously argued that learned SCC Judge committed serious illegality in coming to the finding that the irregularity in depositing rent after the institution of the Rent deposit case has implication on the question of alleged default made prior to institution of rent deposit case since the deposit of rent is only referable to the cause of action of the eviction suit.

 9. The learned Advocate Mr. Deb finally argued that the question of bonafide requirement of the tenanted premises by the plaintiffs for the purpose of using the same as reception room and dining hall and of their hotel is not honest and genuine reason for eviction which the defendants were able to prove by adducing corroborative evidence which the learned SCC Judge did not consider. In this respect the learned Advocate referred of the case of Mst. Shamshennessa Sakeba Bayou and others vs. A.H. Mohsenuddin Ahmed and others, reported 27 DLR 643 and submits that the word bonafide has been defined in the said case as equivalent to honest and a kind of genuine and present need and not a colourable pretext. According to the learned Advocate Mr. Dev, the evidence of the Advocate commissioner as P.W. 3 does not come into any assistance to the plaintiffs as to proof of bonafide requirement and as such the same has not established the claim of the plaintiffs. Mr. Dev contends that since the plaintiffs does into recognize the defendant as tenant, there remains no question of paying rent and default. And as such the impugned judgment and order passed by the SCC Judge 'is not sustainable in law. The learned Advocate prays for making the rule absolute. 

10. On the other hand the learned Advocate Mr. S.H. Md. Nurul Huda Jaigirder, appearing on behalf to the plaintiff/opposite parties strenuously argued that the notice under section 106 of the transfer of property Act 1882 as well as the plaint itself manifest that the plaintiffs although depicted the defendant as illegal occupant but the law recognizes the defendant as tenant by holding over and as such the total assertion of the Notice and the statement in the plaint would clearly show that the original defendant was tenant under the plaintiff /opposite parties after the death of the original land lady. Because, when the defendants admitted that the defendants are the tenants of the present plaintiffs the question of jurisdiction of the SC Court does not arise because of acquiescence. He submits that the defendants in both their written statements as well as in their evidence categorically admitted that the plaintiffs become their landlords after the demise of the original landlady. The learned Advocate Mr. Jaigirdar further argued that the said plea of maintainability of the SCC suit was never taken by the defendants at an earliest opportunity before the SCC Judge and as such the defendants cannot come up now in the revisional application with a fresh plea that there is no landlord and tenant relationship exist and accordingly the suit under SCC Act is not maintainable. Referring to the case of Ahmed Hossain Chowdhury vs. Zakia Khatun reported in 20 DLR 578, Mr. Jaigirder further contends that the defendants having not repudiated the relationship of landlord and tenant in a lawful manner it cannot be said that the relationship has been terminated. The original landlady although died on 27.8.87 but the notice was served on 7.7.88 asking the defendant to vacate the suit premises by 31.7.88, showing the defendant as an illegal occupants in the premises when nearly eleven months after the death of the landlady the tenancy subsisted and the tenant had been paying rents in the House Rent Controller. The learned Advocate Mr. Jaigirdar next submits that the irregularity in depositing rent with the House Rent Controller after the institution of the rent deposit case is obviously a ground to treat the tenant as defaulter because section 19(1)(b) of the Premises Rent Control Act 1991 categorically provided that the tenant shall continue to deposit rent with the House Rent Controller within fortnight till the decree is passed. In this respect he relied on the case of Ramjan Ali Misery Vs. Md. Hedayetullah reported in 31 DLR (AD) 183. 

11. Mr. Jaigirder further submits that the defendant in their written statement did not plead as to when the refused money order was received by the defendant nor in their evidence they said anything as to such receipt. But apparently on the face of the refused money order (Exhibit -Kha") it appears that the refusal wan made on 9.9.1987 and in the absence of any date mentioned in the written statement, the filing of the House Rent Control (Rent deposit) Case No. 68 of 1987 on depositing the rent on 27.9.1987 is clearly falls beyond the statutory period of 15 days as contemplated in section 19 (1) of the premises Rent Control Act 1991 as such the defendant cannot get any protection of law under the said Act. 

12. Mr. Jaigirder next submits that although the trial court did not consider anything in the impugned judgment as to the bonafide requirement but fact remains that the pleading clearly contained the ground of bonafide requirement and to that extent sufficient evidence has been adduced by the plaintiffs including the advocate commissioner to establish the genuineness
of the requirement. The learned Advocate prays for the discharge of the Rule with costs. 

13. Heard the learned Advocates of both the sides and perused the revisional application along with annexures and other materials on record. I have considered the arguments advanced at the Bar. 

14. In the instant Rule three pertinent questions are involved i.e. SCC Suit No. 2 of 1988 was, maintainable, the defendant/ petitioner was defaulter and there was bonafide requirement of the plaintiff in evicting the defendant/ petitioners. 

15. In appreciating the first ground it appears that the plaintiffs did not assert in the plaint that the defendants were tenant under them rather the plaintiffs stated that the original defendant Abdul Wahid was a tenant under Jobeda Khatun, the predecessor of the plaintiffs. It has been alleged in the plaint that with the demise of the plaintiffs' predecessor Jobeda Khatun the bharanama agreement' seized to exist. It further appears from notice dated 7.7.1988 issued for terminating the tenancy that it also does not contain the assertion that the original defendant Abdul Wahid was admitted as a tenant under the plaintiffs rather he was depicted as illegal occupant. But it transpires that the admitted fact is that the original defendant entered into the suit premises on the basis of a `bharanama agreement' entered into with the original landlady and thereafter the landlady died and the plaintiffs entered into the shoes of the landlady as her heirs. It has been alleged that the tenant offered rent for the month of August 1987 to the plaintiff No. 2 who refused to accept the same on 5.9.1978 and thereafter, sent the same by money order on 6.9.78 the same being refused on 9.9.78 the original defendant started depositing the rent with the House Rent Controller Sylhet, in House Rent Case No. 68 of 1987 and continued to pay the same till the House Rent Control case was disposed off. It is also an admitted fact that in the meantime, on 7.7.1988, the plaintiffs issued a notice for eviction upon the defendant which clearly proves that the defendant was admittedly in possession of the suit premises from the date of beginning of the tenancy under the landlady at least till issuance of the notice wherein the defendant was asked to vacate the suit premises by the ends of July 1988. Reading the notice itself and the plaint as a whole, it appears that the defendant was admittedly a tenant under the original landlady and was in possession of the suit premises as such. So the entry of the original defendant in the suit premises was legal who continued to be the lawful tenant till the death of the landlady. Thereafter although, the plaintiffs refused to accept the original defendant as a tenant under them but the provision of section 111 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 provides that in such a case the tenancy cannot be treated as terminated on the demise of the landlady. It appears that the plaintiffs having inherited the property asked the defendant to vacate the premises after one year of the death of original landlady practically allowing the defendant to deposit the rent with the Rent Controller. Therefore, I hold that admittedly the tenant was neither a trespasser in the suit property nor the relationship of landlord and tenant was terminated. A tenancy for which no term is fixed is a lease running from month to month, terminable upon proper notice. But section 111 of Transfer of Property Act 1882 provides as to the point of time when the relationship terminates. The conditions laid down therein can be a ground for termination of tenancy under such situation. Again there is no provision of law in determining the tenancy on the ground of a tenant becoming an "undesirable tenant" unless a tenant ,comes within the mischief of forfeiture under section H 1(0 of the Transfer of Property Act 1882 as decided by their lordships in the Appellate Division in the case of Maria Keshi D' Rozaio vs. Hassan Movies Ltd. reported in 41 DLR (AD) 135. Again section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act 1882 can be looked into wherein the nature of such tenant has been described as holding over tenant but question remains that the tenant by holding over in the premises pre suppose a condition that requires acceptance of the rent from the tenant, But in the present case I hold that the tenancy in question is a tenancy by sufferance. Because as the inherited landlords refused to accept the rent from the existing tenant the tenancy cannot be termed as a tenancy by holding over. No doubt the tenant being in possession of the suit premises upon entering into the same as a lawful monthly tenant and had been paying the rent regularly to the original landlady then refusal by the plaintiff No.2 to receive the rent from such tenant made the tenancy a tenancy by sufferance. 

16. Therefore, I hold that when a tenant remains in possession of the suit premises on termination of a tenancy, due to land lords non-action or negligence in not evicting him to enforce the land lord's right to re-enter, such tenant, who therefore continues his possession by land lord's negative permission is a "tenant by sufferance" who, is not a trespasser nor he could be treated as remaining upon the suit property by wrongful means. In the present case the original land lady died on 27.8.1987 and the defendant was served with notice for eviction on 7.7.1988. So due to negligence of the plaintiffs the tenant was not evicted from the suit premises, who continued paying rents to the House Rent Controller for last eleven months. Moreover, the plaintiffs asked for the premises on bonafide requirement. Thus under all circumstances the tenancy subsists and filing of the suit under the Small Causes Court's Act is very much maintainable and the decision of the Judge of the Small Cause Court is not without lawful authority. That since the suit filed in Small Cause Court is maintainable 1 am of the view that the finding and decision of the trial court i.e. Small Cause Court, arrived at on the basis of the evidences on record are squarely lawful. The argument as advanced by Mr. Deb in this respect fails. 
17. The contention that the tenancy right is a personal right which ceases with the death of either party may be an age old proposition but the same has been negated by the Appellate Division in the case of Pradip Das Vs. Kazal Das reported in 44 DLR (AD) 1. It transpires that a tenant under the premises Rent Control Ordinance means any person by whom, or on whose account the rent is payable for any premises and includes a legal representative as defined in the Civil Procedure Code. Thus a person continuing in possession after termination of a tenancy, if any, is also a tenant under this definition. Therefore so long the tenancy subsists the same is terminable by notice under section 106 of the Transfer o Property Act 1882 by 15 days notice expiry with the end of a month of the Tenancy Thus the plaintiffs rightly issued notice terminating the tenancy asking the defendant to vacate the suit premises by the end of July 1988. This action of the plaintiffs clearly indicates that the relationship between the landlord and tenant subsisted till 31.7.1988 Moreover, the defendants never denied that Abdul Wahid was not a tenant under the legal representatives of deceased landlady Jobeda Khatun. 

18. Now turning to the second ground of the plaintiff/ opposite parties let me examine whether the finding of the trial court on the point of default is correct. The trial court in the impugned Judgment observed that admittedly the original defendant paid rent upto July 1987 and the rent for the month of August 1987 was offered to the plaintiff No.2 on 5.9.1987 on the death of the original land lady which was refused by plaintiff No. 2. Thereupon, the 55 day being the Government holiday, on 6.9.1987 the said defendant sent the rent for the month of August 1987 through Money Order to the owner of the house. On perusal of exhibit "Kha" i.e. the Money Order Coupon No. 803 the Court below found that the above statement is correct and it is further found from the said exhibit that the same was refused by the owner on 9.9.1987. But the learned trial Judge found that it is not possible to ascertain as to when the same returned to the said defendant nor it can be -ascertained that the sane returned to defendant on 13.9.1987 because the said exhibit does not contain any date as to when the same was returned to defendant. On a negative approach the Court observed that the D.W.1 did not deny that the Money order was not returned to him on 13.9.1987. But the plaintiff did not produce any evidence to show that the Money Order returned to the defendant before 13.9.1987. Thus the SCC Judge held that it can be presumed that the Money Order was returned on 13.9.1987 and as such the findings of the learned Judge in Rent Control Case No. 68 of 1987 filed on 27.9.1987 can be accepted as being filed within time. 

19. Such approach of the trial Court cannot be accepted because of the fact that in exhibit "Kha" there being no date as to when the Money Order was returned to the defendant-tenant nor there being any assertion in the defendant's written statement as to when the Money order was returned as such the presumption of return of the Money Order on 13.9.1987 is not sustainable under the law. The defendant having not stated in the written statement about the date of receipt of refused money order and no specific evidence having been adduced to that extent presumption cannot be made on the data of receipt of refused Money Order. The date which has been mentioned in the Money Order Coupon, exhibit "Kha" being the date of refusal on 9.9.1987, it cannot be said that the House Rent Control Case No. 68of 1987 which was filed on 27.9.1987 as filed within fortnight as contemplated in .section 19 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance I986,. which was the prevailing law at the relevant period.

20. The other finding on the question of default as arrived at by the court below is that the Exhibit No. 8 filed by the plaintiff, which is the information slip obtained on 27.6.2000 of the Rent Control Case No. 68 of 1987 showing that the defendant defaulted in depositing the rent with the Rent Controller subsequent to filing of the House Rent Control Case, which led the Trial Court to hold that the defendant did not deposit rent in time since Exhibit 8 shows that the defendant tenant paid the rent for the month of October 1990 on the 19th day of next month. Similarly the rent for the month of November 1998 and December 1998 were deposited together on the 12th day of the next month i.e. January 1999. Again rent for the month of November and December 1997 were deposited together on the 13th day of next month i.e. January 1998. The rent for the month of November 1999 has been deposited on the 13th day of next month and the rent for the month of September 1995 has been deposited on the 5th day of next month whereas the "Bharanama" agreement dated 3.10.1979 shows that the rent is to be paid on the 5th day of next month. Thus the Trial Court held that the defendant defaulted in depositing the rent with House Rent Controller and as such he is a defaulter. 

21. In this respect section 19 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance 1986 is to be looked into. Section 19(1) and (2) of the said Ordinance are the relevant sections which attracts the present case. On perusal of the aforesaid provision of law it is clear that `when the land lord refused to accept any rent remitted by postal Money Order by a tenant of any premises, the tenant may deposit such rent within fortnight from the date on which the rent, so remitted, is retuned to the tenant by the postal authorities as undelivered and unless the landlord signifies by notice in writing to the tenant his willingness to accept any subsequent rent which becomes due in respect of such premises it may also deposit such subsequent rent within a fortnight of the date on which such rent becomes due, from the expiry of the time within which such rent is required to be paid under section 18(5) of the ordinance together with the cost of transmission by postal money order of the money deposited, to the landlord' .Similarly sub section 2 of section 19 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance 1986 says 'wherein any bonafide doubt or dispute has arisen as to the person who is entitled to receive any rent referred to in section 18 in respect of any premises the tenant may deposit such rent and may continue to deposit every subsequent amount of rent which becomes due in respect of such premises until such doubt has been removed or such dispute has been settled by the decision of any competent court or by the settlement between the parties, within a fortnight of the date on which such rent becomes due or from the expiry of the time within which such rent is required to be paid under section 18,(5) of the Ordinance'. In this connection section 18 of the Ordinance is also to be looked into. Section 18says that 'no order shall be made for eviction so long the tenant pays the rent in full extent and fulfills the condition of the tenancy', Section I8(5)says that 'no tenant shall be entitled to the benefit of the section in respect of any premises unless he pays the full rent due to him in respect of such premises within stipulated date and time fixed in the contract with his land lord or in the absence of such contract by the fifteenth day of the month next following that for which the rent is payable or unless the tenant has deposited such rent or any subsequent rent in respect of the premises as provided in that section together with the cost of transmission referred to in that sub section within the time specified in sub section 1B of the said section'. So it appears that if it is taken that the agreement subsisted then the tenant is supposed t. deposit the rent within fifth day of the next following month as per the agreement date. 3.10.1979 and in case if it is taken that there is no agreement existing then the tenant is liable  to pay the rent on the 15th day of the next following month. 

22. In the present case it appears that the tenant deposited rent for the month of October 1990 on the 19th day of November 1990; the rent of November and December 1998 were deposited together in the month of January 12th , 1999. Similarly, the rent for the month of November and December 1999 were deposited together on the 12th day of the next month i.e. January 2000. Although due to year end vacation of the Civil Court the defendant was bound to deposit the rent on the opening day of the Courts in January. So it appears that the rent for these months were not deposited with the House Rent Controller within the 15th day of the following month. So construing section 19 (I) and (2) of the ordinance along with deposit of rent for these months it appears that the defendant tenant have failed to comply with the provision of law in depositing rent within the fortnight of next following month. In this respect Mr. Deb contended that default in making deposit with the Rent Controller cannot be the criteria to determine the tenant as defaulter because of the fact that the default in depositing rent subsequent to the cause of action for the filing of the suit has no implication on the cause of action of the suit. In this respect he referred the case of M/S. Binning & Co (Bangladesh) Ltd. Vs. M/S Nasirabad Properties Ltd. reported in 40 DLR (AD)89. On the contrary Mr. Jaigirdar relying on the decision of Ramjan Ali Mistry vs. Md. Hedayetullah reported in 31 DLR (AD) 183 submits that the expression as long as tenant pays rent indicates that the point of default on the part of the tenant will be not only the date of filing of the suit but will continue till decree is passed. It does not, however, mean that if the tenant subsequent to the filing of the suit has deposited the rent with the Rent Controller the default incurred earlier is cured. On the contrary the tenant's liability for default even after the filing of the suit continues till passing of the decree, In the said decision it has been said that 'protection of the tenant against ejectment is on the fulfillment of certain conditions. He should pay rent to the full extent allowable by the Ordinance and if he does so he is protected from ejectment on the ground of default in the payment of rent.' It has further set out the terms of payment of rent that it is to paid within the time fixed by the contract and in the absence of any such contract within the fifteenth day of the month next following for which the rent is payable or he can deposit the rent with the rent controller in terms of section 19 of the Ordinance. The provision for depositing rent is in section 19 of the Ordinance wherein the provision has been made for deposit of rent to meet diverse contingencies. This provision is contained in section 19(1) of the Ordinance. It clarifies the earlier provision regarding the tender of rent by the tenant. The section says that when, the landlord has refused to accept rent in terms of section 18 of the Ordinance he is to remit it through postal money order and the tenant may deposit the rent with the Rent Controller within the fortnight of the receipt of the undelivered rent. sent through the postal authorities. Section 19(1) (la) of the Ordinance categorically says about the deposit of subsequent rent within a fortnight and section 19(2) (b) of the Ordinance says that he may continue the deposit of every subsequent amount of rent, which becomes due in respect of such premises, within a fortnight of the date in which such rent becomes due until such doubt has been removed or such dispute has been settled by the decision of any competent court or by settlement between the parties. 

23. On perusal of the decision as referred to by Mr. Deb reported in 40 DLR (AD) 89 it appears that the same is not applicable in this particular case. Therein the Appellate. Division held that the statutory restriction relating to payment of monthly rent within 15th  day of the next month, if disregarded by the tenant that will disentitle him to the protection against eviction for default in payment of rent. Mere acceptance of rent by the landlord without objection or protest is not sufficient to constitute waiver. Mr. Deb relied on paragraph No.7 of the said decision and on perusal of the some it appears that that it was not the decision of the honorable court rather the same is the submission made by the learned Advocate of the respondents. Rather in paragraph No. 8 of the said decision it has been held by the Appellate Division "  We are unable to accept the contention that the defendant petitioner is not a defaulter." In the said decision, it has been held that payment of rent in lump for two/three months together does not save a tenant from the mischief of default. 
Thus, by cross referring these two decisions reported in 40DLR (AD) 89 and 31 DLR (AD) 183 and on referring through the sections 19(1) and (2) of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance 1986 I am of the view that the defendant tenant having not deposited the rent subsequent to filing of the House Rent Control Case No. 68 of 1987 in accordance with law i.e. within the fortnight of the next following month the tenant became a defaulter. Moreover, law provides that the defendant is to pay rent to the landlord or deposit the same with the House Rent Controller wither the period as stipulated in the contract and in the absence of any contract within fortnight of the next following month. Thus the submissions of Mr. Dev, the learned Advocate for the defendant/petitioners that the default in depositing rent subsequent to filing of the suit does not entitle the landlord to a decree for eviction is of no substance, meaning that to get the protection of law the tenant is to pay or deposit the rent in accordance with law till the disposal of the eviction suit either to the landlord or to the House Rent. Controller within the stipulated period of time in the contract or in the absence of contract within fortnight of the next following month, as contemplated in section 18(5) and 19(1) and (2) of the Ordinance failing which the tenant cannot avoid his liability of being a defaulter and as such liable to be evicted. Thus in the present case the tenant having failed to deposit the rent with the House Rent Controller for the month as mentioned above within fortnight of the following month, he is a defaulter in the eye of law and once a defaulter is always a defaulter. Hence he cannot avoid the liability of being evicted. 

24. The last question which has been raised in this Rule is whether the plaintiffs had any bonafide requirement of the suit premises? In this respect the legal notice and the plaint is again to be considered. In both these documents the plaintiffs asserted that they required the premises for the purpose of extension of their hotel to be used as office/reception room and dining room of the said hotel situated adjacent to the suit premises. To prove the assertion the plaintiff examined the witnesses who deposed in favour of the plaintiffs. Moreover, on the prayer of the plaintiffs local investigation was held by an Advocate Commissioner as to ascertain whether the suit premises is adjacent to the plaintiff's Hotel and whether the same is required by the plaintiff bonafide. The Commissioner after investigation submitted his report and deposed as P.W.3 Categorically 'stating as to the terms of reference that the requirement of the plaintiffs is correct and genuine. On the contrary the defendant could not produce any evidence to contradict the requirement of the plaintiff as not bonafide. Thus the grounds for eviction of the tenant-defendant from the suit property for the purpose of bonafide requirement is established. 

25. So the ground taken by the defendant /petitioners in this Rule are found against the defendant petitioners and as such the suit filed in SCC Court is maintainable and the defendant/tenant/ petitioners are found to be defaulters and liable to be evicted so also the plaintiffs required the suit premises for their bonafide requirement. As such 1 do not find any merit in this Rule which is liable to be discharged. 

26. Accordingly, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The judgment and order dated 6.8.2000 passed by the Subordinated Judge 2nd Court and SCC Judge Sylhet in SCC Suit No.2 of 1988 is hereby affirmed. 

Let a copy of the Judgment along with the LCR be sent down at once. 

End.
